speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER-PROPOSED ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY BY QUEBEC LEGISLATURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a few days ago I raised a question of privilege regarding the regularity of an action taken in connection with the repatriation of the Canadian constitution. I now want to add to what I said on that occasion, for no further opportunity will come, and unless action is taken now it will be too late.
What I am referring to is an act before the legislature of the province of Quebec in connection with the repatriation formula. In order to found my question of privilege I must place before the house the wording that now appears on the order paper of the legislature of that province, which reads as follows:
Mr. Lesage-Quebec Parliament Act-Motion-
That an humble address be presented to Her Majesty the Queen in the following words:
To the Queen's most Excellent Majesty:
Most Gracious Sovereign:
We, Your Majesty's most dutiful and loyal subjects, the legislative assembly of the province of Quebec, in parliament assembled, humbly approach Your Majesty praying that you may graciously be pleased to cause a measure to be made before the parliament of the United Kingdom, to be expressed as follows:
Then the act is set out to provide for the amendment in Canada of the constitution of Canada in the terms that appeared in the white paper.
I rise, sir, to say that it is not constitutionally proper for any province to be placed in a position of exercising the right of address to the sovereign. Such addresses to the sovereign, asking for action in the British parliament, cannot, according to constitutional authorities, be made by a province or any of the provinces. To do so would be to permit the provinces to circumvent parliament, which alone can pass such addresses.
I raise this question because it is a matter upon which we must have a clear and unequivocal statement from the Prime Min20220- 808i
ister. Has there, on the part of the Prime Minister of Canada or the government, been any arrangement made with the premier of Quebec whereby an address regarding the repatriation of the constitution shall be made directly by the legislature of that province? What will be the position of the Prime Minister when this matter is brought before the Sovereign? Will he, as her adviser, inform her that it is in order for her to accept an address from the province? If he will not, then all that will be done, should this be passed, would be a nullity. If, on the other hand, as her adviser he informs her that it is in order that any one province may do this, rather than that the consent of the provinces shall be made known to the parliament of Canada, then in effect by this advice he will have accepted the theory that there can be sovereign states within this nation.
It is a matter that must be raised now before this-I was going to say anachronism- before this unusual step can receive the fullest consideration of parliament. I raise it at this stage because on the face of it the Quebec parliament act and the address being directed to the Queen of Canada, in her dual capacity as Queen of Canada and Queen of Great Britain, would bring about a constitutional difficulty in this country that needs no further explanation.

subtopic: POLICY ANNOUNCEMENT RESPECTING ASSISTANCE TO SECONDARY AIRPORTS

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: POLICY ANNOUNCEMENT RESPECTING ASSISTANCE TO SECONDARY AIRPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 5 last I announced that certain assistance was being given to three airports in Ontario, Sarnia, St. Catharines and Waterloo-Wellington. At that time I indicated that consideration was being given to a new policy with respect to assistance to secondary airports, that is airports which are not used by scheduled air lines generally. The government has now reached a conclusion about this matter, and I think I should communicate it to the house as briefly as I can if that will be agreeable to hon. members.
As a result of this change in policy there have been substantial changes in the capital assistance program for building local and other smaller airports. Federal assistance to municipalities and other public bodies was hitherto limited to 50 per cent of the capital cost of local and development airports up to a federal share not exceeding $100,000. Treasury board has now approved a policy under which the 50-50 limitation will be dropped. The new policy will be based instead upon the firm requirement that in every case a local body must assume full responsibility for operation and maintenance, and as well, if land is required in support of the development, then the municipality or other public

body must provide the land required. Each case will be the subject of individual study and the amount and percentage of the federal contribution determined on the merits of the case.
The limit on grants which may be approved in any one fiscal year to all airports shall not exceed an approved ceiling of $1 million. A restriction that runways must be built to "DC-3 or larger" standards has also been lifted so that small communities may now develop a basic turf aerodrome at minimum cost. Outright contributions for small aerodromes in remote areas have also increased from $50,000 to a maximum of $100,000.
The new proposal reflects the growth of all types of civil air operations other than air line in Canada, which in terms of hours flown are about three times as extensive as air line route operations. I think this will surprise many hon. members. Special studies have shown this proportion to have been maintained in the past three years.
The policy is expected to be of benefit to larger communities with relatively ambitious airport plans as well as to smaller communities which do not need and could not afford the kind of airport supported under the former scheme. The new policy also opens new possibilities for vacation and convention areas where an annual influx of summer tourists justifies a landing strip, but where the small resident population cannot afford one without considerable financial assistance.
Main line and auxiliary airports required for air line operations are not affected by the change, as the transport department either owns and operates or provides maintenance subsidies to municipalities operating them. Support for seaplane base facilities will now be made within the same general classifications as land airports; main line, auxiliary, local, development and remote.
The department estimates federal contributions under the new policy may total up to $10 million over the next 10 years. Full details of the new policy will shortly be available from the air services regional offices very shortly.
May I also say that I learned this morning with great gratification that the United Kingdom government through the agency of the minister of air transport, Mr. Jenkins, had agreed to have Air Canada fly a shuttle service on the route Montreal-Halifax-Ber-muda, or simply Halifax-Bermuda, whichever is more convenient to the air line. The British government has been very understanding of our needs and wishes in this

matter, and I wish to express great satisfaction and gratitude.

I am thinking, for example, of airports that were once serviced by Air Canada and where a program of expanding and strengthening the existing runways had been embarked upon.

subtopic: OTTAWA-TENDERS FOR CONSTRUCTION OF PERFORMING ARTS CENTRE

speakeroldname: Hon. Lucien Cardin (Minister of Public Works):
subtopic: OTTAWA-TENDERS FOR CONSTRUCTION OF PERFORMING ARTS CENTRE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 5 last in response to questions I advised the house that because of the complexity of the project for the Canadian centre for the performing arts and the desired completion date of June 30, 1967, my department was proposing special tender procedures to select a general contractor for this project. I also announced that this involved a cost plus invitation tender from a selected group of contractors.
This action was commenced on the day of my announcement. However, concurrent with this the Department of Public Works and treasury board have been reviewing the proposal in detail, examining it on the following basis: first, a possible increase in cost due to the accelerated program; second, the degree of detailed planning of requirements and design of sophisticated mechanical and electrical systems; third, the degree of certainty of meeting the completion date of June 30, 1967 to a satisfactory provision of facilities and standard of construction.
As a result of the review it is evident that a substantial increase in cost would be involved in premium overtime and bonus for the manufacture and delivery of equipment. The status of the plans, in spite of the best efforts of the consultants as well as the various committees establishing requirements, was such that a guarantee of completion by June 30, 1967 and maintaining the high standard of facility desired is not probable.
Having regard for these factors, the government has decided that the time of completion should not be the controlling factor in the project; hence we do not intend to proceed with the cost plus contract.
The government now proposes to continue with the existing contract and undertake additional work on the portion of the underground structure; however, tenders will not be called for the main portion of the project until the detailed plans are completed. Work will, however, be continuing on the site and the preparation of the balance of designs
Inquiries of the Ministry will receive priority to ensure completion of the project at the earliest possible date.
The revised schedule now contemplates that the centre will be completed to a point where it will add distinction to the capital in the centennial year. Interior completion will continue throughout the year, and the centre will be ready for the launching of a festival in 1968, in the first year of the second century of confederation.

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Wednesday, March 24, consideration in committee on Bill No. C-136, to establish a comprehensive program of old age pensions and supplementary benefits in Canada payable to and in respect of contributors-Miss LaMarsh-Mr. Lamou-reux in the chair.
On clause 1-Short title.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am very happy to take part in the debate on the Canada pension plan bill which is no doubt the most important piece of legislation introduced in this house at this session.
This importance stems in a large measure from the fact that it represents a danger for the economy, and especially for our democratic institutions. But I should like to make it clear, to avoid any misunderstanding on the part of our opponents, that we Creditistes are definitely in favour of a most generous old age pension. Personally, and all the members of our group share my opinion, I believe the present pension should be doubled. Furthermore, the pension should be paid to all those who are 65 years of age and without any means test. On the other hand, an investigation should be made in the case of those who would apply for a pension at age 60. Instead of passing this bill, since Canada can physically and materially afford it, the existing act should be improved so that a couple who has been married for at least five years may receive the pension at 65 years of age, and if the husband reaches 65 first, the pension should also be paid to his wife whatever her age may be.
At the present time, the pension is inadequate for a single person and I never could understand why a married couple had to live on a pension calculated for a single person, a pension which makes it hard for one person to make both ends meet. It is inhuman and unaccountable in a high production country like ours. All members of parliament should
Canada Pension Plan
be concerned about that situation, which should become enough of an obsession to disturb our sleep as long as the problem is not solved. Certainly the legislation before us is no solution to this problem, and here is why.
This legislation takes away part of the purchasing power of those who already do not have enough, so that they may use it in 10, 15, 20 years from now, or even later. We might as well tell those people: Do without bread or other material goods which you have legitimately earned, to which you are entitled and of which there is plenty right now in order that you may enjoy them a little in 10, 20, 30 or even 35 years from now, without knowing, besides, whether or not you will live long enough to enjoy them.
Such are, in brief, the provisions of this pension plan. I know that the citizens of the province of Quebec where I live, will not directly participate in the federal pension plan, but I know that the Quebec government is preparing a pension plan based on the same principles as those of the federal government, and everything I have to say of the federal pension plan applies also to the Quebec pension plan.
In short, Mr. Chairman, the purpose of the government with this pension plan is lofty, generous and most human, for the idea is to find means of enabling old people to enjoy a larger share of the consumer goods which raise the standard of living and increase comfort, all that in about 10 years. Therefore, I admit that the purpose is sound, lofty, human, and logical.
Nowadays, and increasingly so in the future, people 60 years or over will be excluded from production jobs. Automation increases total production and individual productivity to such an extent that even now there are not enough jobs on the labour market for young and energetic people, educated or not. This situation is bound to get worse from day to day, and yet statistics show that production increases rapidly. I am not speaking of the costs of production but of its volume.
Since production will be higher in the future, is it logical to take away from the public, by compulsory contributions, purchasing power which is already inadequate in relation to the volume of products on the market, and keep it in reserve in order to buy an even more abundant production in the future?
We all recognize that the abundant production, present and potential, is and will always be the result of two basic causes: science

Canada Pension Plan
and life in society. It is obvious that if we lived isolated from one another, without contacts between us, a lot of inventions and commodities would never have seen the light of day; on the other hand, as science does not belong to anyone in particular it is an heritage which reverts equally to everyone. Hence everybody is entitled, free of charge, to part of the material goods resulting from science. In a profit sharing organization each shareholder gets what is coming to him. It is according to these principles that our senior citizens are entitled to a share of the overall production. Through a lifetime of work they contributed to make Canada what it is today. Most of them brought up a family, thus providing the country with human capital, the greatest asset a country could have. They made sacrifices for the education of their children and went without a great many of the comforts they could have had. They also paid a considerable share of the taxes which were used to build up Canada. I would go even further. Most of them would still be willing and able to serve industry and continue their productivity. However, they can no longer work and, as a result, they have to be satisfied with a pittance which, for several years to come, will be ridiculous, pitiful and unworthy of a country as rich as Canada, a country which has become wealthy thanks to the labour of its inhabitants.
I believe that the main reason why the government wishes to proceed thus with this bill is because the two old line parties, the Conservative and the Liberal parties, look at this problem from a false angle. Since the government looks at it from the financial angle it is primarily concerned about determining the amount of money required to give a mere pittance to those elderly people. Naturally, it endeavours to find the most practical and least painful means. Something marvellous came out of this effort, since the government will kill two birds with one stone. First, it will obtain the necessary funds to pay an allowance to the aged by levying a compulsory contribution. Second, it will also be able to use those funds to make up its deficits, since this compulsory contribution will bring in billions of dollars within a few years. Therefore, it will be in a position to tell the people that it set up an old age pension plan without increasing taxes, because it will never be admitted that a compulsory contribution is a tax in disguise, a shameful tax, even more discriminatory than the personal income tax. I say that this compulsory

contribution is a hypocritical and ignominious tax whereby dog eats dog, as the communists would say.
What do our elderly people want? A shelter, wholesome and plentiful food, proper clothes, medical and surgical care, drugs when needed, and some recreation. I do not believe that such requirements are exaggerated; on the contrary, they are perfectly reasonable and particularly deserved.
Who, in or out of this house, would claim that Canada cannot supply this minimum of comfort to persons who have reached the age of 60? I am not talking in terms of money, but in terms of products. If this is the intention of the government, if those people are entitled to this, why then exact from them a tax in order to give them something to which they are entitled in all fairness? If the objective of the government is the same as ours, that is to grant those people well-deserved amenities, then it is worthy of our congratulations.
What we cannot accept is the method used to finance this program. Why deprive the present generation of part of the goods and services produced in order to make it available to future generations?
Does the government fear a large decrease in production or its complete stoppage? The only reason why the government requires such a contribution, which is a dictatorship in disguise, is because it is the slave of a monetary and financial system controlled by bankers who disregard their responsibilities to the people.
It is criminal to accept such bondage. In this way the people are misled, but those who control money and credit are satisfied. It is pure and simple gangsterism.
When money is needed to help the people or give them what belongs to them taxes are collected first. When $200 million are needed to save the English pound sterling, this amount is issued and made available to Great Britain.
If it is proper and possible for the Bank of Canada to issue $200 million for our "mother-in-law", Great Britain, why could it not be proper and possible to issue the credits required to finance the Canada pension plan?
Why must the Canadian government start by depriving the Canadians of today in order to give to the Canadians of tomorrow, when everyone is sure there are enough goods at present and there will be still more in the future?

I am dead set against communism, because everybody, including the Liberal party, denounces communism. Yet, the proposed method of financing for the pension plan amounts exactly to the application of the basic principle of communism, which consists in depriving some people of their property in order to distribute it to others, to spread poverty around instead of well-being, rather than trying to raise the standard of living of everybody. Why is the government acting in this way?
When billions are being spent on safeguards against communism and its propaganda, why does the government attempt to force on the people communist-inspired legislation?
The government takes such action simply because instead of playing its part, that is carrying out the mandate they received from the people, to give leadership, they prefer to yield to the requirements of high finance where their party funds come from, and comply with the old financial system that cheats the people to the benefit of high finance.
The government, on the occasion of the establishment of a pension plan, had an opportunity to show that they really practise democracy and that they administer by the people and for the people, in creating the credits required for the administration and the implementation of this project.
Let them not tell us that it would be illegal under the law, because to my mind laws should be passed to help the people and not to do them harm.
If some people are adversely affected by certain acts, it is not the people but the acts, especially those benefiting a small group of financiers, that should be changed. The government has here the opportunity of supporting what it had in mind when it voted with the Creditiste party in 1963 to have a debt free monetary system; if the government does not take this opportunity, the Liberals will once again be accused of being phonies, liars and turncoats, interested only in votegetting schemes.
I am asking the Liberal members, on behalf of the people, to give us the truth. You have approved debt free money. Why then, when the time has come to use that system, do you say it is impossible?
Mr. Chairman, we the Creditistes are opposed to compulsory financial contributions and suggest that the Bank of Canada should issue the necessary credits to implement this act since production is high enough. It should
Canada Pension Plan
make such credits available to all those who qualify and they will then be able to select for themselves whatever products are on the market.
The terrible thing about this plan is that the small wage earner is made to contribute while there are restrictions on those who could make larger contributions.
If we Creditistes were in power here is what we would do: we would pay a monthly pension of at least $150 to all those who are 65 years of age, and, furthermore, the expenditures involved would be financed from the credit issued by the Bank of Canada. That is my suggestion to the government today.
The compulsory contributions imposed under the government pension plan are nothing but a new means of taxation which is more odious, more hypocritical, than anything we have seen yet. Canadians will be required to make compulsory savings but 20 years hence the dollars thus saved will probably not buy half of what they can buy today.
To me it is the most socialistic legislation ever introduced in this house. It is a further step toward communism, that doctrine we condemn and want to fight with billions of dollars worth of armaments, but that we are establishing little by little here in Canada.
Let us be frank and honest with ourselves. If communism is bad, condemnable and monstrous, why try to imitate it in our legislation instead of providing measures which would show that democracy is, and by far, the system best suited to our mentality, to the private individual and to the Canadian people?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman,
having been the joint chairman of the special committee of the Senate and House of Commons appointed to consider Bill No. C-136, an act to establish a comprehensive program of old age pensions and supplementary benefits in Canada payable to and in respect of contributors, I think it is not inappropriate that I make some comments on Bill C-136 before clause 1 is carried.
The Canada pension bill is undoubtedly the most important legislation of its kind ever to be brought before the Canadian parliament. The very comprehensiveness of the measure and the number of persons who will be protected under its aegis, the many millions of dollars involved and the benefits payable are bound to have a very direct and material effect on the future welfare of millions of Canadians and our political maturity.

Canada Pension Plan
The committee itself was a strong one, as any member may judge for himself by referring to the personnel constituting it. It included amongst its numbers two former federal cabinet ministers in the persons of the former minister of health and welfare, the hon. member for Perth, and the former minister of trade and commerce, Senator McCutcheon. It also included a former Ontario provincial cabinet minister whose special responsibility had been matters affecting the social welfare of the residents of Ontario, Senator Croll; a member of this house noted for his leadership in labour circles, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre; the chairman of the board of a large life insurance company, again Senator McCutcheon; chartered accountants, economists, distinguished representatives of all fields of public endeavour, including business and the professions.
The procedure followed by the committee may be of interest to some hon. members. In the first instance, during a period of about three weeks the committee had the advantage of detailed explanations of the bill from the deputy minister of welfare, the deputy minister of justice, the assistant deputy minister of national revenue, taxation division, the deputy minister of finance, the chief actuary, the director of pensions and social insurance, Department of Finance, technical adviser to the department of welfare, who was also technical adviser to the committee; and there were very many other highly placed and knowledgeable civil servants.
We were given in retrospect the actuarial formulae and the legal language in which they were clothed. We had clearly explained the principles incorporated in the bill. We were given in complete detail how the act would be handled from an administrative point of view. This part of the work of the committee was an education in itself.
The information thus obtained is of course available in the minutes of proceedings and evidence, both in English and French, to all members of the house. I can only regret that all hon. members did not have the same advantage of hearing it, and express the hope that from the minutes of proceedings and evidence they have obtained a clear understanding of the scope of the bill and of the security and peace of mind that will be the end result to our fellow citizens. Canada can and should be proud of its civil servants, who are unsurpassed anywhere in the world.
Following the explanation of the bill and the procedure in regard to its administration,

we then had the advantage of hearing from the chief government actuary as to the actuarial basis and the actuarial implications of the bill. We also had the benefit of hearing from the deputy minister of finance as to its economic implications and from the director of the pensions and social insurance division, Department of Finance, as to the proposed integration of civil service pensions with pensions under the bill.
Following this course of study, and with the information which had thus been made so readily available, the committee invited all national organizations which had appeared before the King-Lesage committee to submit briefs if they so desired, and an invitation was also extended to the general public to appear before the committee to submit briefs if they so desired and to make their views known to the committee. Most of the national organizations referred to accepted the invitation and submitted briefs. Through their properly accredited representatives they appeared before the committee to support their briefs and submitted themselves to intensive questioning by members of the committee.
In addition to the many national organizations that appeared before the committee there were also many private individuals who had intimated their desire to appear and who did appear and presented briefs and arguments. It might be proper to say also that by invitation Dr. Robert Clarke, economist, Mr. R. J. Myers, chief actuary of the United States social security program, Mr. W. M. Anderson, chairman of the board of the North American Life Assurance Company and Mr. J. E. Kilgour, president of the Great West Life Assurance Company, voluntarily appeared and gave the committee the benefit of their special and extensive knowledge and experience about the subject matter of the bill, on which they were experts.
In addition many letters, statements, etc. were received and filed as exhibits. Each member of the committee was supplied with a copy of the briefs which had been filed in order to enable him or her to study the briefs and be prepared to ask whatever questions they thought necessary and advisable in respect of the material contained therein. The briefs were all printed in full as an appendix to the minutes of proceedings and evidence, and are available for the information of all hon. members of the house.
The minutes of proceedings and evidence are extensive and cover some 2,100-odd pages of printed material. Included therein is information supplied by the technical adviser to the committee, by other branches of govern-

ment relating to the subject matter of the bill, and also information requested by hon. members.
As all hon. members are aware, the bill received approval in principle on second reading and was then referred to the special committee for study. There was no restriction placed on the committee by its terms of reference, and during the course of the proceedings I think it is quite fair and quite honest to state that all points of view not *only had an opportunity to be presented but were in fact presented to the committee and given thorough consideration. I know the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka felt that the hands of the committee were tied to a degree. With this thought I cannot agree. The committee were free to bring in whatever findings they saw fit notwithstanding the fact that the principle of the bill which they were considering had already been approved in the house.
It is worth noting that from the beginning emphasis was placed on the argument that persons now in retirement or shortly to be on retirement would receive no benefits under the legislation. It was also argued that there was no need for a Canadian pension bill and that the needs of those now in retirement, or hereafter to come into retirement, could be best met by an enlargement of the coverage and benefits under the Old Age Security Act. It was argued that the old age security legislation, which had been recommended by the King-Lesage committee and which has worked so satisfactorily since it was enacted, with improvements, was the answer. This is an argument that was advanced by the life assurance officers' association representing more than 100 Canadian and British life insurance companies, the life underwriters' association and by many of the actuaries who appeared before the committee in their personal capacity, although many of them were employees of life insurance companies or in some way connected with pension schemes as advisers and consultants. It is to be noted that the life underwriters were of the opinion that there would be increased sales of pension insurance as a result of the publicity given to the bill.
The life insurance officers' association suggested in detail improvements that could be made to the Old Age Security Act. They were significant, and undoubtedly would have constituted a major step forward in our development of adequate retiring allowances. They felt there was no need for an earnings related scheme. On the other hand the
Canada Pension Plan
principle of the bill was supported by the large employers of labour such as the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, the retail council of Canada, the Canadian construction association, labour organizations including the Canadian congress of labour, welfare agencies and also by organizations representing persons now in retirement.
The principle of the bill was supported by the Canadian welfare council, and in particular I draw attention to their recommendation that an appropriate body such as a royal commission be constituted to study all aspects of social security in which the dominion government has a direct or indirect responsibility, and more particularly to make recommendations with respect to (a) gaps in existing provisions and priorities in dealing with unmet needs; (b) the appropriate methods of providing social security benefits, whether by social insurance, statutory social welfare payments, public assistance, or by a combination of these methods, in respect of old age, unemployment, sickness, disability, death of the breadwinner and the cost of child rearing; (c) the development of a more integrated system of social security; (d) federal-provincial co-operation in the field of social security; (e) the negotiation of reciprocal agreements with other countries in order to provide social security coverage on an equitable basis for immigrants to Canada and for Canadians residing in other countries; (f) other questions having to do with the design, content and administration of Canada's total social security system. The wisdom and soundness of this recommendation commends itself very strongly to me.
The committee held in all some 51 sittings. They sat while the house was in recess, and they were in a position to submit their report to the house when it reconvened on February 16. The committee, toward the end of its hearings, had the privilege of receiving a brief from the Ontario government, and may I say that they were greatly heartened to hear of the statement made in the provincial legislative assembly of Ontario by the prime minister of that province that the province of Ontario for the reasons given decided that it would be in the best interests of the people of Ontario and in the best interests of Canada that we in Ontario accept the Canada pension plan in principle and lend every effort to make this plan truly national in scope for the benefit of all the citizens of Canada.
The brief submitted by the Ontario government was ably presented by Mr. Coward,

Canada Pension Plan
chairman of the pension commission of Ontario, and his associate, B. W. Stevenson, director of the economics branch of the department of economics and development. Their suggestions as to improvements in the bill were given very careful study and consideration. The suggestion, however, that contributions under the Canada pension bill should be used to pay benefits to persons who were not contributors under the bill did not prove acceptable to the majority of the committee.
The desirability of making additional payments to persons now in retirement or shortly to come under retirement was in no way questioned. The objective of $100 a month is reasonable and is much nearer realization as a result of the study of the Ontario government. I think it might be fair to state, and at least it is my opinion, that the Old Age Security Act and the Canada pension bill taken together will provide the means for assuring to Canadians, including those now in retirement or shortly to come into retirement, a measure of security sufficient to assure a reasonably adequate standard of living for the great majority of Canadians. With regard to those persons who do not come within that classification it was, of course, thoroughly understood and agreed, certainly in the committee, that supplementation will continue to be necessary in such particular cases. My own thinking leads me to the conclusion that in addition to bringing down the age for receipt of pensions, thought must be given to upgrading the benefits as age increases.
The committee did not adopt nor was it necessary to bring in a report dealing with the arguments pro and con or giving reasons why the proposal for improvements to the Old Age Security Act was not sufficient to cover the problem, or arguments as to why the Canada pension plan in conjunction with old age security would have the result which I have indicated. Criticism has been made of the bill on the grounds, inter alia, that it benefits most those who need it least. One answer at least to that argument is that the bill provides for a wage related scheme of contributions for the purpose of ensuring adequate retirement allowances and the maintenance in retirement of a standard of living comparable with that whilst in employment.
Features of the bill which commended themselves to the committee are set forth in the committee's report.
In addition may I mention the benefits of portability, which is a feature of the bill

applauded by everyone, especially by employers and employees. The recommendations concerning the bill are set forth in the report. As all hon. members know, the government has accepted the recommendations, except that the recommendation of a 20 per cent drop-out allowance made by the committee was reduced to a 15 per cent drop-out allowance. Then, too, the government has seen fit to do what the committee had declined to do, that is to reduce progressively the age at which old age security benefits will be payable so that a few years from now benefits under that act will be payable as of right to everyone attaining their 65th birthday. In doing this the government has established an important principle.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, may I say it is my considered judgment that the Old Age Security Act, improved as it will be from time to time both in scope and as to the amount of its benefits, and the Canada pension bill as it now stands and as it will be refined and improved from time to time, offer to the Canadian people one of the most comprehensive and well thought out assurances of adequate and meaningful retirement allowances that it is possible for human ingenuity to devise, and at the same time remain financially responsible in its implication. As Canadians, regardless of party affiliations, we have approached the problem with open minds. While we may have some disagreements with regard to changes in the bill, there is no doubt that the bill is a credit to the members of this house and to the people of Canada generally.
In answer to the argument advanced by the hon. member for Red Deer I wish to say without qualification that Bill No. C-136 is a social security pension for income earners with supplementary benefits to and in respect of contributors.

speechtext:
I do not wish to take up much time of the committee, but there are some comments I should like to make before this legislation passes through the committee stage. There are a number of gaps in the coverage which this bill provides for those whom it was intended to protect. This party to which I have the honour to belong made an effort to cover those gaps, both in the special committee which was set up to consider the pension legislation and in this committee of the whole house. Its proposals for improving the legislation have followed, in some respects, along the lines of the suggestions offered by the province of Ontario, such as the recommendation providing for uni-

versal coverage. This party wishes everyone to be covered and no one to be left out.
Another Ontario recommendation was that a pension of $25 per month should be provided for all contributors. This, together with the old age security flat rate pension of $75 per month, would have provided all Canadians on their retirement with a minimum of $100 per month. Our party strongly supported this suggestion. Other improvements were suggested by speakers within this party and by other opposition parties. I still support the principle of a contributory old age pension, but this bill falls far short of what I and many others hoped would be provided. It is a far cry from the original pay as you go proposal which was first offered to the electors of Canada during the election campaigns of 1962 and 1963.
I note that the premier of Ontario, according to a recent press dispatch, has indicated that while Ontario, for the sake of national unity, is prepared to accept the program as it is, the province looks forward to amendments in the near future which will cover the gaps and weaknesses in the legislation. I point out, Mr. Chairman, that the most careful consideration should be given to these proposals and any desirable amendments should be included in the legislation now. It is most regrettable that the province of Quebec, so far, has not been able to convince itself it should follow the example set by the province of Ontario and accept this national program for the sake of national unity, thereby making it a truly national undertaking. Perhaps this hope may yet be realized.
The provisions of this bill have been widely discussed, except one which I intend to deal with now. I have been and continue to be, in common with many of my colleagues on this side, strongly opposed to the opting-out provision contained in clause 3 of this bill. It has been pointed out that this pension legislation covers matters which originally came under provincial jurisdiction and therefore any province that may wish to do so can remain outside the program. However, it is my belief that this legislation should cover all the provinces or none. I do not believe it is in the interests of this country for nine provinces to come under the legislation and leave one province outside of it. This, I submit, will destroy national unity rather than promoting it. I repeat, therefore, that the legislation should cover all the provinces or none.
Canada Pension Plan
Now I may point out that in times past the policy was for Canada to move ahead as one country. If one or more of the provinces could not agree with proposals that were made, the proposals had to be dropped until unanimous consent could be given. We got along in this way for 98 years. I feel it would be wiser if this country continued to move ahead as one even if progress is slower by following that course.
Hansard will indicate that I opposed the opting-out principle provided in the youth allowances legislation. I also dealt with this matter of opting-out under Bill No. C-142. I believe this principle of opting out is wrong, that Canada has to move together as one country. The shared programs were contracts entered into in good faith by both federal and provincial governments, just as this pension program should be. The reason for sharing such programs as this and others is to make possible a better distribution of our national income. Through the media of these shared programs it has been, and will continue to be, possible to convey assistance from the higher income provinces to the lower income provinces. The necessity for equalizing income and, therefore, the desirability of our shared programs continues to be as valid today as when the first arrangements were made some years ago. It is impossible to arrive at any other conclusion than that the only reason for these opting-out proposals in connection with this legislation is to promote and create in Canada that which is envisaged in the concept of associate states.
I attempted to make my position clear in this respect during the debate on Bill No. C-142 on March 22 last, at which time I put on the record a number of press clippings and other things designed to set forth the implications of the term "associate states". This was not done for my own sake but was done for the sake of the thousands of people I have the honour of representing and for the sake of this country. The concept of associate states in Canada brings fear to the minds and hearts of many Canadians.
They fear that this concept of associate states, if implemented, will transfer authority from the central government to the provincial governments to such an extent that the provincial governments will dominate the political scene in Canada and, in the course of time, Canada will become balkanized.
Our central government in its dealings with the provinces may be likened to a farm father with a family of sons. As long as the

Canada Pension Plan
father retains title to the property and control of the operation, the family works as a unit. If the property and the control are transferred to the sons the family tends to pull apart and no longer continues as a unit. The authority of the father is lost because he has no favours left to bestow. This is what could happen to Canada if the authority of the federal government is dissipated. The permission for opting out, as contained in clause 3 of the bill, sets one or more provinces apart from the others. It isolates that province or those provinces and creates a division in the unity of the nation.
There has been persistent criticism throughout this unprecedented, long and wearisome session of parliament that the opposition has obstructed business. I submit that this criticism is unjust. The basic reason for the length of debate has been the determination of the government to lay rough hands on the delicate matters of our federal-provincial relationships, and to remould those relationships to a shape unacceptable to an overwhelming majority of the citizens of the country.
The Liberal party did not offer to the people of Canada, during the election campaigns to which I referred or at any other time, a clear understanding of what it intended to do to the federal-provincial relationships of this country.

The kindest action the government can now take is to recommend dissolution of this parliament and offer to the people of Canada an opportunity to express their views concerning the record of the government, and their wishes with regard to the establishment of the concept of associate states, as provided in clause 3 of this bill.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have not spoken on the Canada pension plan to date, and I feel I should speak briefly about it. In my opinion this is one of the most far reaching pieces of legislation to be brought before any parliament.
I am in favour of a Canada pension plan, but not a plan that makes the rich richer and the poor poorer, not a plan that gives little or nothing to two and a half million Canadians, and not a plan that does little or nothing for the person who has low income, due to low productivity that may be the result of sickness, disability or chronic illness, whether he be self employed or employed by another person.
It seems to me that in their scramble to gain individual advantage the politicians have gone a long, long way from the original plan, which was to have guaranteed an essential, minimum pension for all Canadians. But what a travesty of justice is this plan which is introduced in the name of helping the Canadian people. Now the Canada pension plan is all mixed up, mixed up in providing capital for power hungry and money hungry provinces to use for economic development, and not for the people who have built this country with their initiative. It is to provide capital under rules that would not be allowed by any insurance company or any privately operated funds. It will not provide as much in the way of returns as would a private pension plan.
The government must have taken one of two attitudes; either that there is no further need to help the poor people of this country, or that we have no low income people in Canada and that only a contributory savings plan is required. Let us look at the facts. Canadian welfare costs are the third highest in the world. They are the highest on this continent. Surely this does not indicate that we do not need more help for the poor people of the country.

I am sorry to interrupt my hon. friend, but I am sure he does not want to mislead the chamber. If he has read the speech I made when we first came to deal with the new resolution respecting old age security, he will have found that I talked there about a new assistance program which is to be a companion to the Canada pension
Canada Pension Plan
plan. I am quite sure that my hon. friend, who has taken a great interest in health and welfare matters, does not want to mislead the chamber and the country into believing that this program is intended to stand alone, and that it is the indication by the government that it is enough for the poor of the country.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
This is what I had in mind. But with the best intentions in the world, something can go wrong, and I suggest it did, in this bill. There is a clear indication that we do need a higher pension rate. This could have been brought about by raising old age security payments to $100 a month at the age of 65, possibly worked out over a five year period, if necessary. This would have cut substantially the drain on municipalities brought about by welfare costs of today.
Now we have a plan of forced savings. The government is saying, in effect: We will take your money because we know how to invest it much better than you do; we shall return it to you when you are 65; we may return all of it with a moderate rate of interest or we may return part of it plus a moderate rate of interest on your investment, or we may return only the principal. This is being done under the guise of a Canada pension plan to help out the poor people of this land. What does it do for the people on whom we have to spend welfare funds in Canada? Nothing. Twelve per cent of our budget is in this department.
This is a step which could eventually lead to state control of all investment. I am sure that most of us who live in one of the richest countries in the world, endowed with greater natural resources than any other country, would like the opportunity of handling and developing some of the riches of this world as our forefathers did when they came to Canada and made it the fine land it is today. We also want the people who worked so hard to develop this country, some of them during the hungry thirties, to be well looked after when they reach the age of 65. We want a decent living for those aged 65 and over. But we want to be left alone to develop

Canada Pension Plan
this country-with the help of government if necessary but not by way of interference with savings.
In conclusion, let me say I regret the failure to put a respectable pension floor beneath everyone aged 65 and over. I hope the government will see fit, though they have voted against it, to do the decent thing by a million of our people who are 65 and over, those who helped to bring about the prosperity of this land and make possible the things we enjoy today.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, if I have not spoken until now it is because several members have already said what I intended to say and also because, since the province of Quebec is opting out of the pension plan, I do not feel I should do more than I have done so far.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, Bill No. C-136 is a document of a wide social scope, the application of which will affect the well-being of all Canadians.
Because of its importance several Canadian associations have submitted briefs to the joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons.
Those associations, representing thousands of Canadian workers, suggested major amendments to the pension plan which would have given Canadians social legislation within their means.
Unfortunately, most of those briefs were turned down, and the bill now before us has not received the changes which were expected. I fail to understand the reasons why the government did not lend an ear to all those briefs which were submitted to it.
For instance, there is the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, established in 1871, with more than 6,000 members throughout Canada. It accounts for about 75 per cent of all goods manufactured in Canada. This association submitted a brief in which it suggested some changes which can be summed up as follows:
Negotiations should be resumed in order to give Canada only one pension plan. The high rate of preconsolidation should be reduced in order to collect only the funds necessary for the payment of benefits and the setting up of a modest stabilization fund for emergencies or contingencies.
There was also Alexander & Alexander Services Limited, consulting actuaries. That firm is one of the chief independent firms of consulting actuaries in Canada, and I believe that it deserves every respect in the actuary field.
[Mr. Rynard.l
That firm submitted to the committee a brief outlining some of the problems that the pension plan will create, namely the inherent instability of the consolidation plan, the eventual increase in the cost of the pay as you go plan and the permanent cost of the old age security benefits, the difficulty to prevent a certain number of contributors to private pension plans to receive a pension higher than the salary they were getting before their retirement.
Some aspects of the plan were the subject of unfavourable comments in the report of the 1964 royal commission on banking and finance. This plan will create problems in labour-management negotiations because it will be necessary to take into account additional costs to be borne by the industries when the federal plan is compared to the private plans now required by the labour unions.
We can add to this the potential cost of a compulsory health insurance plan. Furthermore, one can see, unfortunately, that the union movement does not seem prepared to admit the need to combine pension funds with the federal plan.
If the briefs submitted by those various Canadian associations had not been ignored, the difficulties that the pension plan will create could have been avoided or at least reduced.
Mr. Chairman, I would not want to gloss over the importance of private pension funds in Canada. In 1960, 9,600 funds were in operation in Canada, with a membership of 1,815,000, which is 34 per cent of the nonfarm labour force. The number of funds increased from 9,600 in 1960 to 12,000 in 1963. Therefore, we can say that this represents about 60 per cent of the non-farm workers whose employers already have a pension fund. Therefore, one can say, on the strength of the statistics I have just quoted that private pension funds are better suited to administer a pension plan than this government.
Mr. Chairman, I think that there is a need for a pension plan in Canada, but we are against the way the government is forcing its pension program on us. I think a national pension plan should in no way interfere with existing plans. We have no need for the plan as it is presented to us.
The implications of a national pension plan such as the one now before us will affect our national economy. If we assume that a national pension plan is desirable and that the benefits paid out must have the actuarial value of the contributions paid in, we will

set up a larger fund than what is anticipated. But the fact that this fund adds up to $5 or $10 billion is less important than to understand the fact that it represents a tremendous diversion of investments from the private sector to the public sector of our economy, and the government has a serious tendency to underestimate the scope of that diversion.
We should not overlook the fact that almost all existing pension plans to which employees must pay a contribution of 5 per cent of their income will be integrated with the Canada pension plan so that the total contributions of the employees, under both plans, will not be increased, with the result that large amounts of money are taken out of the private sector and handed over to the public sector. The implementation of such a pension plan will have a serious effect on the Canadian economy.
I would say that for the persons working at the present time the pension plan before us provides benefits that we are not prepared to grant to other people who deserve them just as much, if not more than we, and we are asking the next generation to contribute to a large extent to the benefit that we are expecting for ourselves.
A much wiser man than I said: "There will always be paupers among us". Therefore it is up to us to see that their interest is not jeopardized because the government is concentrating its efforts on a plan which will be much more beneficial to those who are already well off than to the needy.
Because of this let us make sure that Canadians of all ages and walks of life, but especially the needy, the indigent, will enjoy the best social security pension legislation which the country can devise and afford.
The government let itself open to criticism in saying that the Canada pension plan is not a social welfare measure but a social insurance measure based on some of the principles of group pension plans, with the government plan financed by means of taxes levied against wage earners for the benefit of non-earning pensioners, disabled persons, widows and orphans.
The great majority of the Canadian people have been less informed than misinformed by official statements and press releases as well as by statements made to the voters during the election campaign.
In this connection I should like to quote the official statement made in this house on July 18, 1963, by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh) concerning the Canada pension plan. Her statement 20220-809
Canada Pension Plan
was meant to create a favourable impression and went something like this:
The purpose of the Canada pension plan is to ensure that all Canadians will be able to retire in security and with dignity.
Those words were repeated during this debate.
I am sure that only those workers whose wages are near or above the average, and they would be the minority, will be able to retire in security and with dignity.
Mr. Chairman, I am sure that the Canadian people are unaware of the detail and nature of the official proposals. I think most people are in favour of something likely to assist the poor and those in need.
However, we must keep in mind that Canadians are a fair, intelligent, reasonable and humanitarian people. All Canadians, including Quebeckers, feel that their primary duty is to their poverty-stricken and less fortunate brothers.
I am sure that if Canadians were aware of the inadequacies of the proposed plan they would realize that it would be better for their present and future interests that the government should entrust the plan to experts in pension plans, who have all the proficiency, the skill and the means for that, without putting Canadians into a strait-jacket.
The great majority of Canadians would commend the government, the opposition and parliament for having taken the steps found necessary after a thorough study of the original plan. They would not only admire parliament for the intelligence and courage which it would display, but their faith in its wisdom and integrity would be increased.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, if I want to speak on clause 1 of Bill No. C-136, it is not in order to torture or massacre the French language, as the hon. member for Montmagny-L'lslet (Mr. Berger) said last week, but rather to point out to the house that I do not accept the recommendations of the government, which, under Bill No. C-136, is preparing to torture and massacre Canadian citizens for generations to come, by establishing a compulsory and arbitrary pension scheme that is nothing but a national fraud.
Mr. Chairman, I object to this pension plan above all because it is compulsory. In fact, this was often mentioned during the debate. Moreover, some members stated that the province of Quebec was not directly affected by this legislation. That is true, but if we think that the province of Quebec intends to

Canada Pension Plan
pass shortly legislation similar to Bill No. C-136-I rather think that Bill No. C-136 is similar to the one the province of Quebec intends to pass-I believe we cannot remain idly by if we consider everything which the government intends to do and which will have repercussions for years to come in our country. The members who agree to pass this bill, willingly or forcibly, will be responsible and will bear that burden for the rest of their lives, and their party will be branded accordingly.
Mr. Chairman, this bill is proposed to us as a boon for our old people. One of the few members on the government side to take part in the debate spoke this afternoon only about old age security benefits. He forgot to tell us about the contributions which must be paid by the Canadian workers. In fact, there is no mention about this. In my opinion it is easy to prove that the pension plan, as it will be financed, is nothing more than a direct tax levied at the source-a direct tax which must be paid for by the Canadian workers. Obviously, it is not called a direct tax, but a contribution. But for years the Liberal party made us familiar with changes in names. If we revert to the period of the second world war we will see that there was no conscription, but mobilization was decreed. There was merely a change in names.
For a few years, there has been no direct relief. However, there are winter works which are nothing but direct relief.
Today we have this bill which is intended to ensure a pension plan for workers. It is not mentioned that a tax is provided by this legislation; it is called contributions.
Mr. Chairman, Canadians cannot be hoodwinked. When this bill comes into force and when Canadians see that the amount of their pay cheques is decreasing, although at present it is far from too high, they will complain, but then it will be too late. Once more I object to the principle of this bill because it is compulsory. It is presented in this form by the government because it believes that the individual, the labourer, the worker cannot save in order to provide for himself a decent and appropriate pension.
If such legislation is necessary-and necessary is not the exact word-if it has become almost compulsory today, and if so many people must resort to subsidies from the government and apply for pensions or other benefits, it is because the old line parties imposed a system which brought extreme poverty upon a group of our people,
[Mr. Laprise.l
thus compelling them to claim an ever greater number of socialistic measures.
Mr. Chairman, if we go back 40 or 50 years we find that people managed to provide for their old age. They succeeded in saving enough to retire decently.
But today, with all those taxes, with the licences to be paid, it is impossible to provide for retirement. One has to pay taxes on everything.
Because of a haphazard administration three quarters of the population are living in dire poverty and cannot set anything aside to provide for their old age.
To prove that assertion I shall refer to a statement made in North Bay, Ontario, by the Ontario federation of labour and published in he Droit of October 5, 1964:
The federation recommends the setting up of a royal commission by the federal government to look into the problem of poverty in Canada. According to this report distributed at a seminar on political action held this week end, almost 4,000,000 Canadians are living in the most abject poverty or destitution.
Mr. Chairman, one readily realizes when faced with such figures, that those Canadians are unable to provide a decent retirement for themselves.
And further on:
Almost 2,500,000 Canadians, or over 13 per cent of the population, live in the most extreme poverty.
Do you think those 2,500,000 persons are able to save for their retirement years when they reach the age of 60 or 65? It is absolutely impossible. The contributions collected under the proposed pension plan will take a few dollars more out of these people's small income. Twelve dollars, $15 or $20 is still too much for a person who earns from $1,000 to $1,200 a year. Those people will be deprived of what they desperately need. Throughout the countryside and in urban areas some people live only on social welfare benefits. Some of our fellow citizens have had to depend on winter works for a living. Some of them had to drag themselves through the mud, this winter, to dig wells and reservoirs collecting water 150 feet from a lake. I saw it with my own eyes recently. What will be taken away from such people is still too much. They suffer hardship and need more purchasing power; yet, part of the pittance they earn will be taken away from them.
Mr. Chairman, no sensible person has the right to accept such a scheme. That is why I am opposed to it.

An enormous sum, billions of dollars, will be taken from the population in the ten years needed to get the act really working and will become a tremendous weapon in the hands of the bureaucracy which administers the government's business. It will add to the power of that fabulous bureaucracy monster to dictate to all the citizens of this country.
To administer this act a new pack of hunting dogs will come snooping around in the books of small as well as large employers, in those of farmers, independent workers.
There is in each locality, in each village, in each city a proportion of construction workers who are independent workers; investigations will be made everywhere they worked during the year to find out how much they earned and if they could not be made to pay 5 cents or 10 cents.
Mr. Chairman, the cost of those investigations will be very high. We need only consider what happened in other fields, with other legislation requiring investigations into people's businesses. It will just be a source of trouble for the Canadian people who already have quite enough with all the compulsory legislation they are subjected to. We already have to put up with a great deal of legislation but we are still in the process of passing a new one.
Mr. Chairman, I quite object to this situation. In my opinion, if we search through Bill No. C-136 for all its implications we shall realize that it endangers seriously the automony not only of Quebec but of all the provinces. The federal government will control anything where provincial action is required. Enormous sums of money made available to provinces, municipalities and school boards will become a terrible weapon in the hands of those leading the country.
Mr. Chairman, may I call it five o'clock?

Would the hon. member allow me a question?
Is the hon. member aware of the fact that in a paragraph of his speech he speaks of the "destitution of small wage earners," and later he speaks of the "fabulous amounts" that the pension plan will take away from those people who earn less than $6,000?

If we take off from this amount $5 billion and a few million dollars for the province of Quebec, 20220-809i

we arrive at the amount of about $15 billion, which represents their income for 1963.
Well, Mr. Chairman, this shows that more than six million workers with an income of $600, $800, $900, $3,000 and $4,000 will contribute to this plan, which will take away from them $160 a year. I contend that it is still too much.
If the hon. member for Drummond-Artha-baska (Mr. Pepin) will look carefully at those figures, he will see that the money taken away from Canadians through this tax is still far too much.
