The house in committee on Bill No. S-42, respecting Interprovincial Pipe Line Company -Mr. Wahn-Mr. Lamoureux in the chair.
On clause 1-Subdivision of capital stock.

Mr. Chairman, some of us who were members of the committee that examined the bill are not too happy about it. The purpose stated in the explanatory notes is as follows:
The purpose of this hill is to divide each of the 40 million authorized shares of the par value of $5 each of the capital stock of the company into five shares of a par value of $1 each.
It goes on to say:
The reason for the proposed subdivision is that the company considers it desirable that the small Canadian investors be encouraged and given an opportunity to invest in the equity of a successful and growing Canadian company.
Some of us have doubts that this is the real purpose of the bill before us seeking to authorize the splitting of the shares. The attitude that some of our members hold was quite well expressed in the committee, and at this time I should like to quote briefly from page 889 of the minutes of proceedings and evidence where the hon. member for Port Arthur had this to say:
In this explanatory note there seems to be a suggestion that there is some great virtue in the small investor and something wrong in the big investor. I would like to have things flat and on the line. I do not think it matters a darn whether it is a big investor or a small investor; it seems to me one of the reasons for a share split is the advantage to the company and the people who presently have the shares. I would like to see this put on the line instead of it coming in with

the people's capitalists propaganda. I am sure you are aware that some persons in our party would like to change some of the rules of the game, but because we are not in power I am content to let it go along as it is for now. I appreciate frankness and I feel, although you may have been frank in the introduction, that the explanatory note is too glorious.
When we examine the structure or ownership of the company we find that at the present time there are 5,087,282 shares outstanding. On the last page of the committee report, page 896, there is a list of the principal shareholders of the company, those holding 10,000 shares or more. It starts with Imperial Oil Limited holding 1,680,000 shares, British American Oil Company owning 360,000 shares, and shows a total of 3,166,501 shares held by shareholders owning 10,000 shares or more.
With regard to the major investors in the company at its inception, Imperial Oil Limited, British American Oil and Shell Oil held about 47 per cent of the shares of the company. They acquired their shares at minimum prices. Of the original shares there were 3,596,000 issued at $5 a share and later 3,600 shares were issued at $5.20. There has been a very great appreciation in the value of the shares of this company. At the present time the price on the market is approximately $90 a share.
So far as we can determine, there are not very many small shareholders at the present time and we doubt very much that there would be many more if the split took place. It is usually the case with large well established companies, which have a very good earnings record such as this company and pay a dividend of something like $350 on shares of a par value of $5, that there is little increase in market sales and the greatest benefit from such a change as proposed here is derived by the established shareholders of the company, who are usually large corporate enterprises. It seems to us that the splitting of the shares would not achieve the purpose set forth in the bill, namely to bring in small shareholders in large numbers. The small shareholder is not going to have the opportunity to buy many shares and the advantage will go to the existing shareholders.
The company has had a plan whereby certain employees have received shares over the years, and in the name of the employees at the present time there are about 11,000 shares. I suppose that is commendable but it is not very much when you consider the total issue of over 5 million shares outstanding at the present time. Therefore we can see no

particular merit in the bill. As I said before, it will not achieve what is set forth in the explanatory notes and it will be very much to the advantage of the existing shareholders. So we see no reason why the bill should go forward at this time.

Mr. Chairman, I saw the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Justice stand and I thought he was rising to support the comments of the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond. While I was not a member of the committee and did not have the opportunity to listen to the debate that went on in the committee that considered this matter, I too am of the opinion that the bill should not receive the endorsation of the house, primarily because I think the reasoning set forth in the explanatory notes is somewhat misleading.
To say the least.

To say the least. I do not say that the company did this deliberately. I think they probably just followed the example set by the Minister of Transport in the house, namely that it really does not matter what you do as long as you get the business accomplished. In the past we have seen other companies do the same sort of thing under similar circumstances. The reasons which this company has presented are not the true or correct reasons, and if the company, as set forth in the explanatory notes, really had at heart the interests of its employees in enabling them to become shareholders of the company to a greater extent, the company could have taken a different course.
The bill, if passed, as I understand it, would result, inasmuch as there is a five to one stock split, in the shares of the company numbering some 200 million. This is a fabulous number of shares to have as the share structure of a company. This will be the result if I understand what is involved correctly. If I am incorrect in my understanding,
I am sure the sponsor of the bill will put the true situation on the record. I just looked at the financial page of today's Globe and Mail and under the industrial quotations for March 24, 1965, which was yesterday, I note that Interprovincial Pipe Line Company shares were being traded at $91.75 to $92.25. They closed at a price of $92.25 per share.
This must be an extremely profitable venture since the value of the shares has increased from the original $5 by more than $90 as of yesterday. One part of the explanatory note reads as follows:
Private Bills
On June 10, 1964, the $5 par value shares of the company had a market value of approximately $85 to $85.50 each.
The value of these shares in this period has increased to $92, which is the figure I just quoted. I continue reading from the explanatory note:
This relatively high market value discourages investment by small investors.
Now, if the stock split takes place, the market value of the shares, in so far as I can gather, will be approximately $18 for the purposes of rough calculations. I spoke with a stock brokerage firm just today to find out the weight and importance which we should give to this statement, that this relatively high market value discourages investment of small investors. He told me that this is perhaps true with a stock that has a market value in the range of $90 or more as this one does. He said also that if the stock split takes place they can expect somewhere in the neighbourhood of a 5 per cent to 10 per cent increase almost immediately in the newly established market value.
We can, therefore, take the $18 which will be the market value of the shares of the stock split takes place, and almost immediately add somewhere between 5 per cent and 10 per cent. I will admit at the outset that predicting what any share will do on the market is a rather hazardous occupation. It is probably worse than predicting the outcome of an election. None the less, this is what a brokerage firm told me. If we add just 5 per cent to the $18, that would bring it close to $18.90 or nearly $19. If we add the 10 per cent, it brings it closer to $20 per share if this stock split goes through.
The broker told me that the small investors, as he knows them, are equally deterred by $20 a share as they are by $90 a share. It does not really matter to the small investor. They are not likely to buy these shares at the new market value as is implied in the explanatory note here. I think it is true to say that it is likely to discourage investment by small investors. Even after a stock split, the high market value will equally be discouraging to the small investor. I put it to you, therefore, that this attractive comment by the Interprovincial Pipe Line Company is misleading. I base these statements only on what people who are knowledgeable in the stock market field tell me.
The explanatory note goes on to point out another enticement or explanation as to why

Private Bills
it is necessary that this bill be passed. I quote:
The company recognizes that it is in the best interests of the company and investors in its stock that employees be enabled to become shareholders so as to give employees a sense of ownership in the company and active participation in its growth and profits.
I believe that is a laudable objective. The explanatory note continues:
Some time ago the company established a voluntary employees saving plan, to which the company contributes.
It would be interesting at this stage, perhaps, to know the details of the company's contribution to this employee savings plan.
I do not know if some statement has been made on this. It does have an element of fair play about it. I continue quoting from the explanatory note:
Under the terms of the plan the employees have the option of investing their plan savings in the stock of the company at current market prices. It is felt that with a lower unit market price this option will be more attractive to them.
I submit that last sentence indicates a sort of gilding of what the company intends to do for these worth-while people, as well as for those classified as small investors. If the company was seriously interested in attracting these employees to become owners of shares and thus to have what they call a more intense interest in the growth, development and profit structure of the company, then they could do it in a vastly different way. It has been, in fact, the practice of corporations of this size and larger to establish so-called stock options, mostly for their friends, relatives or board of directors. The stock option, as I gather, works in this way: The company guarantees to issue to certain preferred and selected people, mostly friends and relatives of members of the board of directors, shares in the company at a set price, and they usually establish this price at the par value.
We all know the story of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines where two people, whom the Leader of the Opposition at one time classified as Texas buccaneers, under a stock auction plan parlayed an $8 investment into a million dollar or more savings account. If this company wants its employees to become shareholders an arrangement should be made to offer the employees who, after all, have a greater interest in it than perhaps others, the option to buy shares at a fixed value, and set the value so that it is not subject to the fluctuations of the market. They do this with members of the board of directors; why can they not do it with employees?

Who has a greater stake in the profitable and efficient operation of a company than those who depend on it for their wages in order to earn a livelihood? Members of a board of directors usually have so many diversified interests in other companies that one board of directors does not matter too much.
I submit this is a way by which this company can entice its employees into becoming shareholders. If they do not wish to become shareholders then at least they can realize the profits by buying at the option price and selling on the market if the market price is higher. This would allow the employees to get some of the benefits that should accrue to them from the profitable operation of the company.
I submit that offering an option to their employees at whatever is market value is not an option at all unless the employees may save the brokerage fees. Under an employees saving plan, presumably money is taken from an employee's cheque and deposited in some trust fund. Then the employee, if he has the option, merely says, "I want to invest my amount of money in shares of the company at market value." Does this mean that the company sells out of the treasury shares which were given to it to promote at $5 and now sells them to its employees at $95 each? Or does the company take the amount of money in the fund, and when an employee exercises his desire to buy shares on the market, does the company act as his broker or agent, take that money out of the fund, phone up its stock broker and say, "Buy so many shares on the market for John Smith or Joe Brown"

or whoever the employee happens to be.
These are questions that require some sort of answer, and because this is the bill's first venture into committee stage in the house, which allows for a more informal type of debate, we should have an answer; but so far the sponsor of the bill has said nothing about this or any of the other aspects of it. These are questions which I think should be answered before the committee is asked to follow the enticement given by the company itself, namely that it will entice small investors and its own employees to become shareholders to a greater extent in the company. Unless we get some reasonably satisfactory answer we may well not be inclined to give passage to the bill at this stage.

Mr. Chairman, we are very interested in the Interprovincial Pipe Line

Company, and I feel sorry that the hon. member who is sponsoring the bill saw fit to do so. I say so because if he were aware of the history of this company, as are some of us, he would be aware that this is the type of bill that has not been matched among pipe line bills to come before parliament since 1949.
I am not aware how government members are selected to sponsor Senate bills, but I rather hoped he would have taken the opportunity to read some of the previous debates and look into the history of the company. If he had, he might have considered some of the complications involved and be willing to explain them. Or he might have thought it better not to raise this problem at all.
I have always wondered why a company should split stock. This is a good question for a layman to ask himself but I do not think we will get the answer to it today. However, it is interesting to note that this is not the first time this company has split stock. I seems to me that it is always after stock has reached a certain level of interest that a stock split is sought.
If we approve the splitting of this stock today it means this company will have 200 million shares of stock on the market. From a layman's point of view dealing with the mining industry, 200 million shares would mean approximately $200 million capitalization-very sizeable capitalization.
A special act of parliament was passed in 1949 establishing the Interprovincial Pipe Line Company to do a number of things. On September 5, 1952, the shareholders approved a ten for one split of common stock, and changed the par value from $15 to, I presume, the $5 figure at which it stands now. Approval was given following debate on February 11, 1953.
As the hon. member for Skeena has mentioned, it would be interesting to know why the present stock split is being made. Let me say without equivocation, I am as sure as I am standing here that it is not done for the reason given in the explanatory notes to the bill. This company could not care less about the common employees it employs. This stock split may well apply to the executive types in the company, and when you check down the list you can find the companies they represent; but the company does not really care whether its common employees buy stock or not.
If an employee were buying treasury stock it would not matter to him whether he bought ten $5 shares, one $50 share or even fifty $1 shares. He is going to have to raise $50 and
Private Bills
it does not matter whether he has a big sheaf of stock or a little sheaf of stock. We are not being fair to the wage structure system if we allow this method.
The reason this stock is being split is because the company is making a fantastic profit, and this is not unusual. I am highly perturbed about a company in my area operating in the trans-Canada pipe line agency, and I would like to refer to this because the profit motive of these companies is quite often the deciding factor.
I thought I had the news clipping here but I do not, and so I will have to describe from memory what took place. I may not be exactly right because the figures involved were very large. A meeting was held in Toronto the other day. I will not go into all the details of that meeting, but it was a very interesting one, for exactly the reason being discussed here, allowing the shareholders and common shareholders to have some control. Incidentally in this case the little shareholder did not get any hearing and was not able to put his nominee on the board of directors.
In two months Northern Ontario Natural Gas Company was able to make this enormous profit; it was able to increase its profits compared with the previous year by 34 per cent and make a profit in January and February of more than $1,300,000. This must be taken in conjunction with the fact that last year the company made a profit amounting to an increase of 50 per cent by comparison with the previous year. I would point out, too, that in northern Ontario there are only a few towns and that these are not densely populated.
All this means that shareholders receive so much money in relation to the amount of money invested that it becomes embarrassing. The Canadian public as a whole will eventually look at the profits declared by some of these companies and say: "This is not in the interest of Canada; this is an abuse of our natural resources and of their distribution." In my opinion this is the situation which it is hoped will be covered up here.
This company has a current rate of interest of $3.20 per share per annum paid regularly quarterly from September 3, 1963; 75 cents a share paid quarterly from June 1, 1962 to June 1, 1963, inclusive; 70 cents a share paid March 1, 1962, and December 1, 1961; 60 cents on March, June and September 1, 1961, and $2.30 a share paid in 1960. An extra 10 cents was paid on December 1, 1962; 40 cents was paid on December 1, 1961 and 50 cents in 1960. I have taken these figures from the Financial Post survey of 1964. In 1953 there

was the little matter of which I spoke earlier. The company had in 1953 paid $1.50 a share. This was followed, after the ten to one split, by an extra payment of 15 cents a share which really represents $1.50. Had there been no split, $3 would have been paid in 1953 on $50 stock, which is surely a reasonable amount of profit.
I intend later to put on record what the dividends have actually been. Hon. members should note that expenditures during this period have not been small. The company was able to twin its pipe lines from western Canada and extend the system to Sarnia and the Toronto area; there is now a twinned system established. At the very time the company was engaged in this terrific program of capital development it was able to pay $3 a share.
I will go on to give further figures. In 1954 it paid 45 cents. Of course, the shares have been split and this figure is really the equivalent of $4.50. In 1955, they paid 70 cents, that is, $7 in one year on a $50 share. A good stock to buy. In 1956 they paid $1.10. This amounts to $11 per share. By 1957 the dividend was up to $1.40. At the old rate it would have been $14 a share, coming very close to getting half your money back. In 1958 the shareholders got $1.40 plus 40 cents, that is, $1.80 or $18 a share on the old basis. In 1959 they got $2.25, or $22.50. By 1960 they were getting $2.30 plus 50 cents, that is, $2.80. So if a man held stock in this company it took only two years to pay off his initial investment because he made $28 per share on the old basis. In 1961 the company paid $2.50 plus 40 cents; in 1962 it paid $2.95 plus 10 cents, which comes to $3.05. In 1963 the shareholders got $3.10 which amounts to $31 on a $50 share. No wonder they come to parliament wanting to split the stock. Would hon. members agree that a $50 share was able to earn as much as this, unless you were stealing the money- that it would be able to earn $31 each year? Why, we would even run the moneylenders out of this country if they charged that kind of interest.
The man who pays for gas in Toronto, the man who pays for gas from the Lakehead Pipe Line Company which is a subsidiary outfit, is paying $31 to the shareholders of this company on the basis of a $50 investment.
Crude oil.

The hon. member raises a pertinent question. I have only had an opportunity of looking at this subject very recently. They did bring in crude oil.

The company was authorized to operate a crude oil pipe line extending 1,930 miles from Redwater, Alberta, via Edmonton, Regina and Gretna, Manitoba, across the international border to Superior, Wisconsin and thence via Sarnia to Port Credit, Ontario. A 93 mile extension from near Hamilton, Ontario, to Buffalo was completed in 1963 and transportation of natural gas liquids began in 1961. I learn that the original line has been progressively looped since its completion, resulting in a completely double system between Edmonton and Superior by the end of 1958. A further 167 miles of looping was completed in 1963, largely in the United States.
The article goes on to talk about the oil which has been carried. I gather that now the line has been twinned it is available for carrying gas. I may be wrong about this, but it does not really matter whether you buy oil in a can or whether you buy gas from a line into your house. In any case, the customers across Canada are supplying these profits and I have no hesitation in saying they are exorbitant profits-so exorbitant that I believe this question should be examined by the security commissions in the various provinces which are concerned.
In the circumstances I feel confident the hon. member would like to withdraw his support of the proposal before us because I am sure he would not wish to be associated with a company which has such an unreasonable profit structure as this one. We kicked the moneylenders out of the temple a long time ago because they were charging exorbitant interest rates. It seems to me that this company must be charging exorbitant rates for the transport of oil in order to allow it a profit amounting annually to more than half of the price of the original stock.
Now the company wants to reduce the interest rate which is apparently being paid. In order to do this, the stock issue has to be increased. May I say, in passing, that I have just been handed a note which is likely to be of interest to the hon. member. It indicates that the 1949 shares in this particular company would now be worth $950 if one had accumulated the interest on those shares. I am sure the hon. member will consider these things. We in this party have always been opposed to the extension of these pipe lines in the present manner, regarding these matters as directly involving the public interest and parliamentary control. Surely there is some machinery for giving consideration to what should be done when these companies make an unreasonable profit. It is eyewash,

literally eyewash, to say this. Listen to it. What a bunch of junk this is:
Under the terms of the plan the employees have the option of investing their plan savings in the stock of the company at current market prices. It is felt that with a lower unit market price this option will be more attractive to them.
If in 1949 they could buy one share and now find it is worth over $90, they must all have holes in their heads if they are not willing to take it at any price. This is all eyewash. It is a disgrace for any member to come into the house, put that junk on the record and endorse it. That statement is not true. It is not what they are trying to do. It is not even, in my opinion, an excuse for what they are trying to do. Under the plan their employees could make just as much money in the way I have pointed out. Did it really make any difference to them, splitting the stock ten to one? In 1953 they got $1.50; the stock was worth $50. Later in the year they got 15 cents. What difference does it make to them if they split it? Say they still got $3, so it does not matter if it is 15 cents or $1.50. The statement contained in the explanatory notes is not the fact. If they are going to take it out of their investment plan, then obviously arrangements could be made for the accumulation of money until you can pay for a $50 stock just as easily as you can pay for a $1 stock.
Maybe the house is in sympathy with this, and perhaps I am wrong. I am no financial wizard, by any stretch of the imagination. I have not been able to make 50 cents out of stock myself at any time, and I have worked for mining companies for many years. So I am not suggesting that I am a financial wizard. But reading the statement from the Financial Post, a statement made by those who look into these matters, I can only come to the conclusion that what is in the explanatory notes of this bill is not true; that this is not the reason. This is not the logical explanation of what they are trying to do and it is in no way an answer to the questions members of this house must ask themselves before they allow an amendment that will change the structure of the company that is operating in the public utility field.
Across the nation there is a growing desire for more honesty in agencies operating in the public utility field. I think that has been demonstrated by many of the remarks made in relation to bills in connection with telephone companies that come before us. It certainly is true in the case of gas and oil company bills that come before us. I know 20220-810

Mr. Chairman, I rise at this time to say a few words on this Interprovincial Pipe Line Company bill. I do so because this particular company is a monopoly organization and as such should be scrutinized with the greatest of care by the house, before we pass this bill. That scrutiny has not been given, either here or in the committee.
The real purpose at the back of this split and the reason this corporation is in a position to make this split has never been properly explained either to this house or to the Canadian people. I think that when a matter of this kind comes before a body such as is gathered here you should not pass it over, but you should look into it. I suggest this organization is a monopoly from beginning to end.
Some 39 per cent of the stock of this corporation is owned by Imperial Oil. Another percentage is owned by B.A. and another percentage still is owned by Shell. Out of this arises a combination of monopoly tactics. Those monopoly tactics have been levelled 20220-810i
Private Bills
against small operators who want to be in the oil business and who are anxious to develop the oil industry of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta.
To be sure, Mr. Chairman, this company will tell you that they have done this and done that as part of their policy. But I am telling you that wherever a corporation takes from the services which it is performing the amount which this corporation has been taking, they are relying upon their monopoly position in order to feather their own nest.
Now, Mr. Chairman, what has been said is that they want to sell shares to their employees; they want to get the employees in and let them buy. But let me tell you what is actually happening. These shares that are to be split five for one were at about $85 per share a short time ago. They are now up to $93 in anticipation of this split. If this split comes about they will probably bob up another $5 a share. And who would the shares be distributed to? Who would buy them? As a result of the excitement, being split five for one the price would come down to around $18 or $20 a share. What would happen? In the stock market each particular active issue has at least one sponsor. This means there is a sponsor backing the stock and that he has bought up a lot of the floating stock of this corporation. Therefore he and others are waiting to have this stock split, so that during the flurry which follows they can unload their shares on to unsuspecting people whom they call the small buyers. They might be speculators or anybody else who might buy the shares at that time. The people who own shares now are the ones who are going to profit. If you have had anything to do with the stock market you know that is true. Just watch the volume of transactions after a split of this kind takes place. The stock goes up and those who held shares unload them on the public.
This corporation has come to us stating that it wants to divide its shares so that its employees can buy more of them at a lower price. What utter nonsense. There might be a few employees who would buy shares, but what the company is up to here is the division of its shares so that those who now hold shares can make millions in the market. Since this is a monopoly corporation, I think that in the interests of everyone concerned we should give careful consideration to the policies of this company and how the incidence of those policies is affecting the growth of the oil industry in western Canada.

Canada Pension Plan
Mind you, it may be said that it is not unusual for corporations to split their shares after they have made profits that justify a split. It is quite a customary practice. We know that almost every corporation, once it has been in existence for a certain length of time, splits its shares. There is no question about that. But in the case of this company its policies and the amount of money it has taken from the people for performing a service need a better investigation by parliament before we pass this kind of legislation.
I see that my time is up and I have gone overtime. I do not wish to talk out the bill in any sense of the word, but I do think that we should call it six o'clock.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before the committee took recess at five o'clock I was saying 
that the huge amounts which will be made available to governmental bureaucracy would permit bureaucrats to rule the roost. They are the ones who will decide which areas will be developed, providing of course those areas are on the right side. They will be all-powerful because those amounts will total more than $8 billion within 10 years.
We are told that people are not intelligent enough to provide for their declining years and consequently they will be forced into it. They will be deprived of their purchasing power and thus browbeaten into conforming to government requirements. Then patronage and dictatorship will blossom out.
On May 26, 1964, La Presse published a report issued by the French service of William M. Mercer Limited, the most important actuarial consultant firm in Canada.
It stated:
The coming into force of the plan will cause the net income of the majority of the workers to fall off. This reduction, plus the one brought about by the last personal income tax increase which became effective on January 1, 1964, and taking into account future tax increases resulting from recent tax-sharing agreements, will bring about, we expect higher salaries and other inflationary measures. A plan offering such benefits will no doubt, at first, receive general public support, but as its effects on taxation and inflationary tendencies are fully assessed, this original support will be somewhat more restrained.
The government is only stressing the benefits accruing to the individual without telling him now what he will have to pay in the meantime and all the trouble he will have to go through.
Always take away from the weak and give to the strong. Workers having little or no income will get nothing or very little from this pension plan. Yet, they are the ones who will need it most. But those having the highest salaries will get the most from this pension plan, while they will need it the least.
At one of the first federal-provincial conferences held in 1941, Hon. John Bracken, then premier of Manitoba, said:
Our present taxation system seems to have been based on the evangelic promise: "For unto every one that hath shall be given; but from him that hath not shall be taken away even that which he hath".
Later, he said:
This unbalanced taxation system transfers the income of people with relatively low wages to those with relatively high income. The federal government's revenues from indirect taxation are largely used to cover debt charges which, in many cases, are paid out to people who bore a relatively lighter share of the dominion's taxes because, before the war, the federal government drew only a slight proportion of its revenues from direct taxation.

Thus, the income of relatively poor people goes to persons who are fairly rich. We will never set up a sound tax structure in Canada if we tax those in the low income group for the benefit of those in the higher income brackets.
Well, Mr. Chairman, that is practically what we have in this bill.
Yet, as far as old age security is concerned, it would have been much simpler and much more advantageous for everyone to provide for a minimum pension of $100 a month at the age of 60.
When the head of a family reaches the age at which he can draw his pension, his wife, even though she is younger by a few years, should also get this $100 pension, so that the two of them would not be forced to live on the same pension, as unfortunately happens too often at the present time and as happened in the past. In this way it would be easier for people, but it would perhaps be disastrous for lawyers like the hon. member for Lotbiniere who prefer obscure legislation which cannot be understood. I prefer results to complexities.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, to open my remarks on Bill No. C-136, may I sincerely thank all those who, directly or indirectly, helped in supplying to us the French version of the evidence given to the joint committee established to consider this bill. I hope that the appropriate decisions will be made by the staff authorities so that both the French and the English versions of the proceedings of the various committees will be distributed to all members.
Bill No. C-136 now before us, commonly called pension plan, was first introduced as a social measure; it underwent various amendments or revisions afterwards. It is easy to see, however, that the plan was prepared in order to supply the government with a source of capital; it is important to know- and all the Canadian people have a right to know-the scope of the provisions of the various clauses in Bill No. C-136 which might provide for a fair distribution of the social requirements to the Canadian people.
I am rather surprised to see that the supporters of the pension plan suggest that it is one of the best social security plans, but at the same time that it is drafted in such a complicated and incomprehensible manner.
I have already mentioned here in this house that there is something wrong, not with the number of pieces of legislation, but rather with the complexity of their drafting. In my opinion, the important thing in the drafting of legislation or the preparation of a plan is that it must be drafted in such a
Canada Pension Plan
way that it will be easily understood by those who have to comply therewith or contribute thereto one way or another.
I could quote various sections of Bill No. C-136 in which we find that we have to refer back to many other sections or paragraphs of the same bill to reach any conclusion at all.
Such drafting of laws or plans allows thereafter the officials responsible for their administration to find in them all kinds of loopholes, or to use in their correspondence in reply to taxpayers who are the victims of wrong decisions, some phraseology designed to create confusion rather than clarify the situation.
I could refer to a host of examples of the kind, but I shall limit my remarks in this field to quoting part of a reply sent to a citizen who was asking for supplementary social assistance; there are form letters prepared in advance, on which the official or the writer has only to add the address of the claimant.
The text is as follows:
The rate of your allowance was increased by $10 per month as of April 1, 1964; it is nevertheless possible for us to continue, at a reduced rate, the payment to you of the extra allowance which was previously granted to you pending the raise of new regular allowance.
Just imagine. What can a fellow understand from such double talk?
I pity some civil servants who sometimes have to resort to a great deal of ingenuity to make replies void of meaning in order not to commit themselves, and this is largely due to too large a percentage of ill-conceived laws.
As evidence of the administrative complexities of such a plan, I shall quote from a brief submitted to the committee by the E. B. Eddy Company on January 18, 1965.
This Canada pension plan could have been enlarged, made more encompassing, providing at the same time simplicity of structure which would lead to its more ready understanding and acceptance.
Judging from reported discussions on this bill, we must anticipate great confusion on behalf of our employees, together with much difficutly and expense in reconciling the plan throughout our day-to-day operations. Questions, correspondence and detail will be massive. Those learned in the way of finance and insurance have already demonstrated that the plan is not easily digested; and they have great experience.
How, then, can we expect a man earning $600 or upwards to be clear as to what he should contribute, what he will receive and when? It should not be overlooked that the cost of collecting from those in the lower income brackets might well surpass the returns.
And further down the brief goes on: Demand for refunds will be heavy, caused by two employers in the one year contributing more

Canada Pension Plan
than an employee should pay. An employee can obtain a refund and presumably there will also be redress for the employer. However, money will be paid which both parties know is not due; and will be returned in time and at expense. Much of this will be collected from those least able to part with it.
A brief submitted by the chamber of commerce of Canada on the same matter says clearly that:
In connection with integration, a major problem is created by the fact that the Canada pension plan indexing will make it impossible to integrate private plans with contractual benefits to a national plan whose rate of benefit would be changeable and unforeseeable.
Each time benefits under the Canada pension plan would be adjusted, a large number of private plans would have to be amended. The short transitory period of 10 years and the exclusion of incomes under $600 add to the complexity of integration?
As evidence of administrative complications, we notice that the supporters of the plan seem to have committed themselves by their longstanding promise of a social security program. I shall quote here a sentence from an article published in the Quebec newspaper L'Action on Monday, March 15, 1965, concerning the present pension plan. The author said that there had not been enough critics. Here are his words:
Allowing criticism from experts would have led at least to a complete revision and at the most to the withdrawal of the plan in favour of one or more suggested alternatives. However, neither the one nor the other was politically beneficial. Having committed themselves to the plan, the Liberals and the other parties are compelled to implement it, whether it is adequate or not. And to think that this will be described as a political victory when in fact it is a popular defeat.
I must mention here, however, that the government can expect a violent reaction from the people the moment they realize the excessive amount they will have to pay for a pension plan that the majority did not ask for, but that the government is seeking to impose through a publicity fanfare. It is obviously a means of taxation disguised so it can be accepted as a pension plan.
Actuaries have voiced their opinions in various ways. One of them, who had been a government employee for the last 13 years, even had the courage to denounce the pension scheme by stating that those who have investigated the plan have disguised its origin, hidden its true nature, concealed its effects to exaggerate the support it received in certain quarters and discredit its critics, adding that it was only because of propaganda and through fear that some members of parliament ended up supporting the plan.
The reaction of the supporters of the system was brutally evidenced when, the day after he made his statement to the press, this actuary who had enough courage to point out the errors in this pension plan, was fired.

This procedure more clearly points out the socialistic principles which underlie this plan.
He is not the only actuary who criticized this plan. In an appendix to a report of the meeting the committee held on January 18, a fellow of the society of actuaries, Mr. Dowsett, speaking on his behalf and on behalf of his organization said:
If all major parties want "a comprehensive plan to apply to as many people as possible in this country", surely they will express this desire in a strange fashion if they adopt Bill C-136 which channels current tax dollars-raised in the name of the plan-into some provincial government development program rather than into increases in income for the current aged.
Fortunately, this actuary is not a federal civil servant because he would be dismissed forthwith.
This is what he stated at page 120 of the same brief, dealing with portable pensions:
If a province wishes to raise funds for provincial development, the honest approach is to tell the voting public the reason for which the tax is adopted. By hiding a provincial development fund tax within the framework of the Canada pension plan, it is possible that the provincial and federal governments together might avoid the criticisms that would be forthcoming were the tax to be imposed directly, as a measure quite separate from the Canada pension plan. Combining a development fund tax with a social pension plan tax, and advertising the whole tax as a contribution to a pension plan may be politically smart, but it would not be forthright, and it would leave a legacy of problems to our children as well.
Giving as an example the application of the Unemployment Insurance Act, he stated:
Initially, the fund was supposed to be self-supporting, as is proposed for the pension plan. However, this actuarial soundness was destroyed when unemployment insurance benefits were extended to seasonal workers. The question is, of course, what guarantees can be provided so that the actuarial soundness of the Canada pension plan will not be destroyed in the same way by the future application of an opportunist policy.
I agree with the decision made to extend the provisions of the Unemployment Insurance Act to all workers, seasonal and others, but many of those who should be enjoying those provisions are not doing so at present, such as those who go to work across the American border.
Considering that the present plan cannot give security without interfering with the citizens' purchasing power, it is necessary to estimate what will happen in the future with the coming into force of the pension plan now under consideration.
Is it unreasonable to think that this plan will be used as a means to get the voters' support with their own money?

I suppose that the plan's supporters said to themselves: after all, what difference is there between increasing ordinary taxes and increasing taxes on the pay lists to meet the cost of the pension plan?
It is obvious that under the present plan many groups of people will not get benefits related to their needs.
Taking into account the circumstances and the manner in which this plan is drafted and presented, I find it impossible to support it because I find it inconsistent. If the financing methods advocated by the Creditiistes are not used, then I would rather see the present method used to pay for the government pensions. As it was said, it is completely unthinkable to collect contributions from workers whose income is still too low to enable them to live decently, in view of the increase in the cost of living.
At a time when a large number of workers have an insufficient purchasing power, it is not logical to draw further upon their resources by forcing them to contribute to a pension plan. This will simply compel the workers to demand wage increases, and the problem will become more complicated. On the other hand, in taxing enterprises, we run the risk of seeing their production costs increase, and the consumers will have to pay the shot.
This is the problem confronting us at present. Where should we get the money? Whom should we tax? From whom should we get the money in order to give it to somebody else? Under the present system, we rob Peter to pay Paul; it should not be necessary for those who are working at the present time to buy fewer products so as to permit older people to get enough. When you consider the present surplus of unsold products, it is obvious that the answer is no, but when you do not realize that it is simply because there is no money, then the supporters of the system foolishly answer yes.
It is not by increasing the cost of living and decreasing the purchasing power that we are going to satisfy people who are now doing without the necessities of life; with this plan in operation our governments are getting ready to pile up a great deal of money at the expense of the Canadian workers, because the cost of living will increase and the purchasing power will decrease.
Considering that the present system operates so as to keep the value of the dollar fluctuating, everyone will admit that you cannot buy as much with a dollar in 1965 as you could in 1935. And yet, the Creditistes are

not the ones who are managing the government.
Considering the rate of increase of the cost of living, what will the dollar be worth a few years hence, under a Tory or a Grit administration?
Instead of establishing a retirement pension plan, the government should seek to expand an assistance program for aged people by reducing the age at which they can receive benefits and by increasing the amount of the pension.
It would be much simpler to pay immediately the old age pension to people of 65 years and over without any means tests, than to work out a plan such as this one which seems to be put through in a great hurry, and which will carry with it a number of unforeseen mishaps and errors of all kinds. We find that instead of protecting the citizens suffering hardship, protection is given to the fund. Unemployed people are paid the smallest benefits possible. In fact, that is what happens with most social laws. Disabled persons are paid the smallest pension benefits possible, the victims of accidents are paid the smallest compensation possible.

Canada Pension Plan
That is what the people across Canada are saying about this plan. I say to you, Mr. Chairman, that this is a welfare measure and I know it is not popular to vote against welfare measures. But a welfare measure that leaves out hundreds of thousands of Canadians and imposes a huge burden on future generations cannot be accepted in silence. The government has plunged ahead with reckless haste in this measure. The minister was in a state of frenzy immediately after the election to get a plan, some kind of a plan, before the public. They brought forward a half-baked version that was immediately shot down in flames by business, farmers, labour and the provinces. They came out with another version that they could not sell to the provinces. Then Mr. Lesage got them off the hook by producing a version that was acceptable to the other provinces.
It was accepted because it offered a tremendous fund of $8 billion into which the provinces could dip with no federal control. This is one of the mysteries of this plan. I ask, Mr. Chairman, what control do we as a parliament exercise over the disposal of this fund? As far as I can see, the answer is none. Therefore we are taxing every person in Canada who has a job, or is in business, who is a farmer, a fisherman, or is on a payroll, in order to set up a huge fund with which the federal government can buy the support of the provinces. This fund will be set up with 3.6 per cent of the worker's payroll cheque.
People are being taxed twice what they ought to pay in regard to the benefits they are receiving, simply so this fund can be established. I cannot accept that it is parliament's job to set up huge funds having no defined purpose and to be spent outside the control of parliament, and that we should tax the Canadian taxpayer for such an unnamed and undefined purpose. I can say very definitely that people in my riding do not want to be taxed in order to set up a fund for provincial governments to play with. Thousands of people in my riding will derive little or no benefit from this scheme. In the first place, it leaves out the very people whose support the Liberal party sought when they promised a new pension plan in the last election. They were going to give to those people a new heaven and a new earth; that is, to the old age pensioners. Not one old age pensioner today will get any substantial benefit, except a slight cost of living rise, from this plan. No one now on old age pension in my riding will come under this plan.

Canada Pension Plan
In fact, no such person in all of Canada will come under this plan. This means that a million people will be left out. These are the very people the Liberals promised this new plan to; and now they have cast them aside.
I cannot agree with this procedure either by remaining silent or by voting in favour of the plan. As far as these pensioners are concerned, they are getting $75 a month now for the simple reason that we in the Conservative party, with no help from any other party in this house, forced the government to come through on their behalf. The Liberal party had left them with $46 a month, and even that was grudgingly handed out.
We raised it to $65 and hon. members opposite were going to leave it there; but we forced them up to $75. They showed that they had some sense of shame, which is something that has been lacking in that party ever since. Now they are leaving it at $75 and will leave millions of Canadians out in the cold.
I say that this is a crime against the present old age pensioners of this country. What of those whose incomes do not permit them to qualify? The sum of $600 may not seem much to hon. gentlemen opposite. I also realize it does not mean much to the Minister of Agriculture, after his having announced the farm policy for eastern Canada and stated that they could make a living out of six cows and two sows. Many people in my riding and the farmers of eastern Canada have not an income of $600 and they are going to be left completely out of this plan. Hon. gentlemen opposite have never thought of these people. They do not care about the small farmers, or the fishermen in Newfoundland, or the fishermen in all these places.
In view of these shortcomings surely it would be much simpler, more honest and easier to administer if the present flat rate pension were increased so that all those who are now on pension and those who would otherwise get little would at least get something under the plan which is not presently supplied.
I also understand that this plan will require every Canadian to carry a card with a number on it. This number will be supplied to the income tax department which will be collecting revenue for this plan. I want to say to the minister that I come from a long line of Canadians who are not accustomed to carrying cards with numbers on them. There are many people in my riding who have had experience in other countries of being required to carry a card bearing a number

and other identifying information. These people have seen the use to which these cards can be turned in exercising control over ordinary citizens. They do not like the idea of carrying such a card in a free country. If this government is going to force us to carry a card it is taking away our freedom. Out in western Canada they treat us like cattle. We turn the cattle out on the range in the spring, and we have a tattoo machine stencil a number on their ears. Perhaps the minister of national health would consider taking that step instead of requiring us to carry a card. They treat us like cattle anyway, so let them tattoo us on the ear and be done with it.
To these people from other countries the carrying of this card stands for regimentation and bureaucracy. This card will identify people for purposes of unemployment insurance, national revenue, social security and perhaps other matters. All the information contained in the files of other persons' incomes will be made available to these departments from the cradle to the grave. I and a great many other Canadians fear that by this process the government is erecting a gigantic system of regimentation and bureaucracy under which no person in this country will be able to call his soul his own.

Mr. Chairman, it was my intention to take part briefly in the discussion on clause 1 of the pension plan.
Some may wonder why we from Quebec, who will not be affected by the federal pension plan, have any objection to it. The reason is simple, Mr. Chairman. It is because that federal plan was prepared in cooperation with certain people in the province of Quebec, so that the federal and the Quebec pension plans would be, in the words of the Minister of National Health and Welfare herself, comparable or practically similar, in order to have a portable pension.
But we do not want a pension plan such as the one conceived, prepared and put forth by the federal or provincial government. And, I should like to take the opportunity which my presence in this house affords me to lodge a protest against this pension plan which will be imposed upon us later by the Quebec government; I also take the opportunity which is afforded me here, in Ottawa, to discuss this pension plan which is comparable

Canada Pension Plan
to the Quebec plan and to protest against the comparable plan which will be passed by the Quebec legislature.
Why are we protesting? The answer is quite simple. First of all, we are protesting because this plan tends to destroy the freedom of the individual since this will be a compulsory plan. Whether we like it or not, we will have to contribute to and pay taxes for the administration of this pension plan.
Take, for instance, a man 30 years of age who is suffering from cancer and who, according to the doctor, has but two years to live; this man will nevertheless continue to work for a year, fully aware that he will never benefit from the pension plan at 65 years. Nevertheless, he has to keep on contributing, knowing very well that he will get nothing out of it. This is the trouble with a compulsory plan. The individual is deprived of his liberty to act freely, to decide for himself what is good for him.
Mr. Chairman, we are against this plan because, first of all, it is a compulsory plan. We believe the Canadian citizen is intelligent enough to choose between various pension plans put forward by the federal or provincial governments or by private firms; he is intelligent enough to choose his own pension plan. We are against it because this is more or less a new tax and because we are trying to hide it in an hypocritical and sneaky way more than the others.
The government claims it is setting up a pension plan when, in fact, it is merely seeking to further deprive the public by accumulating funds in the federal treasury. It recognizes that there will be an accumulation of funds but it claims that this will constitute savings. That is what it calls compulsory savings. Savings for whom? For the man who will contribute, save and get benefits? If that were the case, the people could benefit from the scheme but no, it is the federal and provincial governments which will use those savings to make profits. This hidden tax will not benefit the citizen who will be forced to save but the government which will use those funds as it sees fit.
We claim that personal income is already overtaxed. Not so long ago, I pointed out that a 4 per cent old age security tax is levied against income. From now on, a further 3.6 per cent will be added for the pension plan. The private citizen has to pay unemployment insurance, union dues, and health insurance premiums; I am sure that before long most

Canadians will be more interested in getting their pay cheque stub than the cheque itself.
More money will be withheld than can be distributed. This is another tax which will not produce its equivalent for the individual.
We also protest against the fact that according to this pension scheme, too much is taken away as compared to what will be returned.
The other day the hon. member for Shef-ford (Mr. Rondeau) furnished examples of private companies' pension plans, and it was easy to see that with the same amounts of money being collected annually by the private companies, the individual received more, much more, at the age of 65, and that if he died before reaching the age of 65, his widow and his children received much more than under the federal plan or under the provincial pension scheme. Moreover, we protest against this pension plan since the well-to-do people, those who earn the higher salaries, will pay a lesser percentage of the taxes, under this pension plan, than those who earn smaller salaries.
Let us consider the case of an individual earning a yearly salary of $18,000. He is taxed only on $5,000, whereas the one who earns a yearly salary of $5,000 will be taxed at the same rate, on the $5,000. This means that the individual earning a salary of $18,000 will pay three times less, as a percentage, for his pension plan, than the one earning $5,000. The well-to-do will therefore pay a lower percentage of taxes-
