Mr. Chairman, there might be some mistake. A person earning $5,000 will be taxed on the minimum and maximum amounts of $600 and $5,000; someone who earns $18,000 will not be taxed on the amount exceeding $5,000 for the purpose of the pension plan. Therefore, an amount of $13,000, that is, the difference between $18,000 and $5,000, will not be taxable for the purpose of the pension plan. It is thus an advantage for those earning large salaries; the percent-

age of taxes will therefore be lesser on every $1,000 of their salary than in the case of the worker earning only $5,000.
I see the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) shaking his head, but this is exactly what the minister has just explained. As a matter of fact, a person earning $18,000 will be taxed on the difference between $600 and $5,000, but not on the excess from $5,000 to $18,000.
But, the individual earning $5,000 will be taxed on his whole salary, except $600. Consequently, it is easy to understand that high-salaried employees will pay a lower percentage of taxes for each $1,000 they earn, as compared to those who earn a salary lower than $5,000.
What is still more peculiar, is that the high-salaried employees will pay a lower percentage of taxes, but will get much more in return. Therefore, it is those people who are favoured all through their working years that will be most favoured when they reach age 65. The rich pay less but get more.
Furthermore, we protest against this pension plan because there are too many people forgotten. Thus, the worker who is unemployed for many years, and particularly during the last five or ten years of his life, and who has reached 65 years of age, will still suffer hardship, under this pension plan, while the other one who has earned a good salary all his life, who had a chance to put some money aside, will get a pension which will not be so very high, but at least he will get one. And, here again, the one who has lived in hardship all his life, who has received unemployment insurance benefits and social welfare allowances will once again be forgotten, at the age of 65.
Mr. Chairman, many reasons could be used to protest against this pension scheme, whether it is established by a provincial or the federal government.
We believe this measure has not been thought out long enough. It seems to us that the criticisms that have been heard in recent months should have opened the eyes of the Minister of National Health and Welfare and those of the Minister of National Revenue, so that they should have introduced a better plan than the one now under consideration.
As a matter of fact, why has not anyone thought of asking for suggestions from insurance companies? Why are no suggestions being asked for? I am sure the majority, if not all, of the companies that offer retirement plans would ask lower premiums than the federal
Canada Pension Plan
government is asking for at present. When an individual needs something, he should be free to approach those who can offer their services to him.
For instance, let us consider life insurance. The individual can choose his life insurance company.
Why should the same privilege not be granted a Canadian citizen respecting his pension plan? Why should the federal government not ask tenders from companies which offer pension plans and ask them the amount of their premiums toward a pension plan which would pay a certain superannuation to people who have reached the age of 65?
I am convinced that many companies would suggest premiums at a much lower rate, while offering higher benefits for a person reaching the age of 65.
However, tenders were not called and figures were not asked for. A system was established merely to accumulate funds, because at present the government is having difficulty in finding new funds. As a matter of fact, the government has borrowed so much over the last 25 years that it finds it practically impossible to do it today. Its only other source of revenue is to tax the Canadian people more, ostensibly to set up a pension plan, in order to accumulate funds to be used to develop some areas of the economy when the capital needed for the development of the Canadian economy should come from somewhere else than the Canadian taxpayers' pockets.
Mr. Chairman, we are not against the government finding capital to develop the economy, but we are against that capital being taken from the Canadian citizen. We are against that method because the Canadian citizens do not have enough money to five on as it is and more will be taken from them.
Mr. Chairman, on the motion for third reading, it is our intention to move an amendment to separate part IV of the bill from the three other parts, that is, we shall ask that the house vote on two different bills. First, the pension plan with premiums and benefits paid at the age of 65 and second, the continuation or improvement of the old age pension, such as it is now.
It seems to me that we should be allowed to vote on each part of the bill separately, since they do not have the same purpose, their terms are different, and they are not at all similar. We are going to ask that those two parts of the bill be kept separate and

Canada Pension Plan
we shall vote in favour of Part IV, while insisting that the old age pension be paid to everyone as of now, at age 65 without a means test, and at 60 with a means test.
Further, we shall ask an increase of the old age pension up to $100, and its payment to the wife as soon as her husand reaches 65 years.
Nowadays, Mr. Chairman, Canadian workers in industries, factories and other works are retired at 65. From then on, not only the husband but also the wife and all the family can no longer count on the salary of the family head because the latter, being 65 years old, is retired.
We suggest that the old age pension be paid to the husband and the wife as soon as the head of the family reaches 65 years old; that would solve the problem of the retired factory or industry workers. By giving $200 to a married couple the problem would be solved.
We then advocate the granting of the old age pension to everyone at 65 years old, without a means test, and at 60 years old following a means test, and that this pension amount to $100 a month and is given to both the wife and the husband when the latter is forced to be retired at 65 years of age. That would solve the problem and there would be no longer need for this pension plan and the taxes involved.
Mr. Chairman, we intend to move an amendment to that effect on third reading of the bill because we note that workers have continually fought for a salary increase. What is disgraceful is that the federal and provincial governments, municipalities and school boards all make a dash for the worker's pay cheque to try and take a little more out of it. So much so that when workers do get a raise, it does not show on their cheques because the government cashes in on those increases by levying new taxes. The government increases taxes and the pay keeps going down.
Mr. Chairman, I am convinced that in a country as immensely rich as Canada, a country with multiple and numerous possibilities, there must be enough to satisfy all Canadians at the age of 65 while leaving to the workers their whole remuneration for their work. There should be enough in Canada for people 65 years old to have a reasonable standard of living, as well as the workers.
I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that the minister has not given enough consideration to her
[Mr. Gregoire.l
pension plan. She has gone the wrong way about it. This is rather a tax, and the plan was never a social security measure. On the contrary, it has always been a way of impoverishing the general public.
No one will ever make me believe that taxes make people grow rich and constitute measures of social security. I think taxes impoverish Canadian families. People will have to work from 18 to 65 years of age in order to pay taxes or contributions to this pension plan and once they are 65 years old, the amounts already paid will still not be sufficient to permit them to have a decent standard of living.
We ask the minister to consider this carefully.
On the other hand, through the House of Commons I ask the legislature of the province of Quebec to be very careful not to pass such a plan, because taxes in Quebec have gone up so much in the last four years that the population cannot stand further taxes. According to the minister this pension scheme will be comparable to that of the province of Quebec, and I believe I have the right to take this opportunity to request the Quebec government not to accept a scheme comparable to that intended for the whole of the country, since this will only bring about an increase in taxes and weaken the economy of the province of Quebec.
Mr. Chairman, there is enough for everybody. Why tax some to give to others? The Minister of National Revenue, who is always on the lookout for new sources of revenue in order to meet expenditures, should consider a new economic system which would make it possible to distribute today the existing wealth, rather than to take away people's salary today in order to give it back to them later on. There is now plenty of production and wealth in Canada. Then, let the worker keep his salary, because he earned it, so that he may buy the production which exists in our country at this time.
Under the present system, a part of the income of Canadian citizens is always taken away from them.
On behalf of Canadian citizens throughout the country, who are fed up with taxes levied by all governments and with having their salary stolen by the federal government and the minister responsible for federal income tax, we want to protest against this pension plan which, as has already been said, is nothing but a national barbotte to take money out of the pockets of Canadian citizens.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think as a member of this committee I have an obligation to point out my different objections to this bill, and I do so after having listened attentively to some of the speeches made on the first clause and some of the arguments presented on other clauses.
After looking over the bill as it is, I am more than ever confused. The first six months I was in the house I wondered why I was elected: Since then I wonder how anybody else was elected. With a bill like this I am positive there is something wrong. It is very complicated, in fact the most complicated lot of lies and bluffs that have ever been structured into a bill and presented to the house for adoption. That you can be sure of.
The people of Canada might not know what they have in front of them or what is coming upon them fairly soon, because as I heard the Minister of National Health and Welfare last week on a television broadcast presenting this Bill C-136, the picture looked fairly good. I must congratulate the minister on the work done on that television program. I wish she could explain it just as well in the house, all the clauses of the bill as a whole. The picture was a colourful one, and I am sure brought a lot of honest thinking Canadians to the point of thinking that this was a good welfare measure and a good deed for them, and that it was another instance of the almighty Liberal government again dishing out goods and services throughout the country. But you can be sure that when this bill will come into operation the reactions are going to be somewhat different from what they are today.
In fact, if you inquire of some of the electors, the people of Canada, who will be affected by this plan, you will find that some of them are starting to have very serious doubts, and these doubts are going to be better and better founded as time goes by. The reason is not so much that they understand the bill as a whole but that they are catching glimpses of it here and there, and they do not like the smell of it.
Any hon. member who looks through it, and at its application now and in the years to come-more so in the years to come-cannot help having some objections to the bill. I for one am opposed to the principle of this bill because it is not one which permits a person to participate in its benefits because he wants them, but rather it is one from which a person will benefit because he has to. It is
Canada Pension Plan
only a different form of taxation. Look at it whatever way you wish, you still have a tax; and it is a strait-jacket, no matter how you look at it. It is a taxation method that is hypocritical and it is applied in the Robin Hood sense whereby you take from the rich and give to the poor.
This has been the general way of functioning of our government, that they tax the rich and give it to the poor-take away from Albert and give it to Peter; then take from Peter and give to Jacob; then take from Jacob and give it to the other guy. Finally you don't have any more interest in it-you just spread it around. That certainly does not help the situation any more. At the moment we are taxing sufficiently to build up a fund for the federal government varying between $5 billion and $7 billion. In fact I have an article here from the Winnipeg Tribune of February 25 that underlines this fact.
This bill is becoming the basis of a political auction to be used to attract voters in the next election. It is right here in the Winnipeg Tribune; this is the headline- "Social Security Auction". Most people, especially those who do not have a mathematical sense, do not understand exactly how large a sum $5 billion is; they cannot visualize it when they think only of a round figure with a "five" and nine zeros. It can be expressed in different ways, however, and this is what the Winnipeg Tribune does. Anyway, this is what the Tribune has to say about this particular bill:
Anyone who was naive enough to hope that the Canada pension plan would end political bidding in old-age security must feel sadly disappointed. Political parties and individual M.P.'s have responded to the scheme by initiating an auction for votes worse than anything in the past quarter of a century.
There are calls for blanket increases in amounts of pensions and for introduction of new categories of beneficiaries from all sides of the house. The result is that the plan is now a hopeless mixture of political insurance and political welfare.
The bidding can have very serious effects in future because of the vast sums of money involved. A recent issue of the "Mercer Actuarial Bulletin" gives an idea of the meaning of some of the figures being bandied about. Here is what it says:
The Canada pension plan is expected to create a fund which will reach $5 billion by 1975.
How much is $5 billion? Putting it in terms of time and terns of amounts we can better visualize, here are several ways of defining $5 billion.
If a 21 year old set out to spend $25,000 per hour, 8 hours a day, every week of the year, he would have to live to age 117 to achieve his objective.
That is an awful lot of money, and the government will have it in its treasury. It will accumulate, with interest upon interest,

Canada Pension Plan
and become an instrument oi enormous potential in the hands of any administration. Here is another example from the newspaper.
If you laid $5 billion in $1 bills end to end, they would encircle the earth at its equator 20 times.
A lot of money. Another example:
If a business had commenced operations in the year 1 A.D. with $5 billion capital and did so poorly that it lost $200,000 per month, every month, it could still operate for over another 100 years before it had lost its original $5 billion.
And so on. The article concludes by saying that even by current standards these figures are impressive.
To be sure they are. Yet this is what the government is imposing upon the Canadian people, and imposing by force-another tax totalling 3.6 per cent including what the employer has to pay and what the employee has to pay. Indeed, some hon. members have maintained during the discussion of one of the clauses in detail-I do not remember which clause-that the employer would have to pay more than 4 per cent rather than his share of the 3.6 per cent, because he would have to pay twice in the same year. This is a heavy burden to impose upon Canadian citizens who are already overtaxed and who are being squeezed out of the benefits which they could derive from Canadian production today because they lack sufficient purchasing power. Some people say we are facing overproduction today. This is not the case. What we have is under-consumption and the present bill will not help at all in such a situation.
As my hon. friend from Lapointe mentioned, there are wide inequalities in the rates of contribution according to the tax brackets within which individual taxpayers fall. This is sheer discrimination. If there is a principle involved, the law should apply across the board. This does not mean the law is a good one, but it is bad enough as it is without our making it worse. I do not agree with this aspect of the plan in its present form. First, there are far too many Canadian workers who do not have the possibility of earning $600. Again, those who do earn this sum and who work outside the country will not be able to benefit. I do not see the point of having a pension plan and advertising that it will cover all Canadians when in fact so many people will not be eligible. No matter how small a minority they represent, these people I have mentioned should be considered.

It is said that the province of Quebec will have its own plan. That is all right, but the plan has to be comparable with the one now before us. This will make them both bad. Today we heard the minister tell us that this bill is designed to ensure a decent retirement for our older citizens. As a result of this plan, she says, they can retire with a little ease and peace of mind. How can you talk about decent retirement when you have indecent living for 45 years of your labouring life? People have to slave each day of the year before reaching the age of 65, and by that time the cost of living will have increased so much that a new plan will be needed. Another thing which occurs to me is this: How does the minister propose to pay these pensions to all who will have retired in 40 years from now in view of the possibility -and the Financial Post talks about this- that only 20 per cent or 15 per cent of the population will be working, due to the impact of automation? Those workers will be contributing to the plan, but what about the rest? It was put forward with a tremendous fanfare and a great deal of window dressing. It was going to be good for the unemployed.
Since then we have unemployed; we have reached that stage today-and where do we stand? We are still standing in the same spot, off the road where we were standing when this program was set up. In fact we are worse off today because we have to pay them all. At that time we were thinking mainly of full time jobs, but today part time work has been brought in and these people are also receiving unemployment insurance benefit. What is going to happen to this plan when the situation comes about when we have only a small proportion of the people working because of automation and progress in this country? Are we going to do the same thing that we do now, put these people into holes for winter work and get them shovelling with long-handled shovels; because they have to work under the winter works program to get paid and get off unemployment assistance.
Things have not changed since the dirty thirties, as we used to call them. I think it was the hon. member for Chapleau who mentioned a little while ago that we like to call things by different names today from those that were used some years ago. This is a fact. In 1942 they did not like to call it conscription; they called it mobilization at that time. It was a better word because people did not know exactly what it was until they were brought in under it, and then they knew what it was. But it was the same thing. We

do not like to call these payments "relief', so we call it the winter works program. What is the difference between the relief of the 1930's and the winter works program of 1965? You still have to get out and shovel. Some of the work that is done today I saw done 20 years ago with mechanical shovels. Today it is all done with human arms and ordinary, long-handled shovels.
We will not solve these problems by putting on plasters of this sort; and this pension plan is just a plaster. In fact, it is more than a plaster; it is a plaster that sucks the Canadian economy dry, just as much as any bloodsucker could. When this Canada pension plan has been in operation for ten years, what will have happened to our Canadian economy? We will have a fund for the pension, but there will not be anything in the pockets of the people. Canadian production will surely be going up. You will have underfed people in the country. And we will be standing there like a bunch of ducklings, not knowing what is wrong or what happened to us. I am telling you now, Mr. Chairman, that this is the same procedure that has been applied in the past in a system that does not work, a system that is mathematically wrong. Today we are applying this pension plan in the wrong way. That is why I am opposed to the principle of the bill. After a man has worked from the age of 18 until he is 65-47 years-in this country

the best years of his life-working for progress, the welfare and the benefit of all Canadian citizens and contributing his share to our society, I think he deserves from this country a share larger than he will have been obliged to contribute in the form of a tax called a contribution under the Canada pension plan.
With regard to the proprietor or the owner of a company, this is what happens in their business; the more the company produces, the more profits he makes, the larger are the dividends to the shareholders. Why do we not operate this country in a logical way, in the way in which a private company is operated, namely in accordance with its development? Consider the debt this country has today. The Minister of Finance has just given us the estimates for the year 1965-66. If you look at the service on the debt of this country, what has to be paid out in interest and other forms of payment in respect of borrowed money-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: It is $1 billion a year.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
-we are paying over $1 billion a year, which is completely wrong.
Canada Pension Plan
If you consider all the debts of this country, private enterprise, provincial, school board, municipal and federal, you realize that we are more in debt than the amount of our gross national product. Where do we stand in relation to the time we discovered this country when the Indians had it? They did not have any debts at that time. They did not have anything else either, but they at least did not have any debts; they broke even. Today we are in the hole, after working for 200 or 300 years. The more we seem to develop this country, the deeper in debt we go. This is because something is wrong somewhere. We have enough natural resources in this country and enough potential to give everyone of the 19 million Canadians in this land the guarantee of three meals a day, whether now or at age 65. There are too many people in this country who are underfed and in misery at the moment. I say misery, Mr. Chairman, and it is a fact. They are underfed and have not the purchasing power to provide the needs for their families and themselves. We have this problem today, with 19 million citizens. What do we expect the position to be if our population ever increases to 50 million? We cannot look after the 19 million people that we have now, and therefore I do not see how we are going to look after 50 million. We have too many who are starving at the moment.
This pension plan is not going to help at all. At the moment it is a tax, but for how long? I know it is supposed to be paid at age 65, but at the moment it will permit the government to do anything it wants to do with this money-lend it, change it around, deposit it here, deposit it there, lend it to any cabinet minister and his ministry. In other words, the Minister of National Revenue should put on the tax himself and say it is just another tax. That would serve the same purpose as it is going to serve now. It is a far off election promise that when a man reaches 65 years of age he is going to have this pension; but it is just that. The people are going to find this out once they start paying into this octopus that will suck the Canadian economy dry.
The kind of pension plan that I would like to see operating in this country would be one based on national dividends. If a private company can pay dividends throughout the year, you should also receive dividends from the country. The more you develop your country, the more the dividends should be. It is a logical thing that the more you develop something, progress makes advances.

Canada Pension Plan
People who are working today, perhaps in five or ten years time will not be working because of progress and automation. Machinery will do the same work that human hands are doing now. They will do it cheaper and faster. And for whom will they be doing it? They will be doing it for the Canadian consumer. How is he going to buy the things he needs if he is not working? That is when the government will have to give him a national dividend with which to buy the production of the machines that will be functioning across this country. Such a national dividends system would replace this national octopus that we have today, which will squeeze, slowly but surely, the lifeblood of the Canadian citizens and the labour force across the country.
Whether it be a provincial or federal plan -a provincial plan would have to be comparable to this one-it would have the same effect. It would be cleaning the taxpayers' pockets more than at the present time.
The Liberal government knows that this is a tax. I asked the Minister of National Revenue in the house the other day whether it was a tax, and he said it was a contribution. He said to call it a tax or whatever you want, but it is a contribution. Then on the radio the same week end he said it was a contribution. It is a contribution put on the people by means of a strait-jacket and it operates as a tax. So why does the government not say so? You can call it a contribution but you are obliged to pay it. Let them come out squarely and say so. If they did, the people would then open their eyes to this pension plan and see what is at the bottom of it.
The government promised a pension plan during the last election campaign, but they did not promise what kind. They forgot to mention the kind of plan it would be. They did not say it would be a tax. If they had, they might have received further repercussions from the people at the time. Everybody thinks that the pension plan is a good thing, but when they get into it they will find out what it is. For once anyway I am glad I am on this side of the house.
Someone sitting opposite me, Mr. Chairman, keeps interrupting and seems to be having a regular good time with his jokes. He keeps ejaculating things into the subject matter which have no place at all. And furthermore, he is doing so from his seat, which is very unbecoming to the house. This sometimes happens across the aisle, when you get these interruptions from members in their seats,

which I do not like and which the house has to endure. But I am sure that some of these people make a more intelligent sound from their seats, regardless of where they are.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I should like to complete my argument about a national dividend, financing the plan through the Bank of Canada, the surplus thus supplying to the Canadian people the purchasing power missing today. Some people will say it is impossible to do this. I know it is impossible under the Liberal government; but they can do this sort of thing when it comes to stabilizing the pound sterling in England; $200 million went across there to stabilize their currency. Why can we stabilize the pound sterling but cannot do this for the Canadian citizens who are calling for old age security? Instead of having this pension plan, why not increase old age security to a reasonable level with which we are sure the people could live? When the minister brought in the pension plan she was pretty well aware that they could not live on $75 today. Why not raise this amount to an amount which would permit the senior citizens of this country to live as they should, having worked in this country for 20, 30, 40, or 50 years, the best years of their lives? This is a plan to which I object. Some will say that I am speaking only as a member from the province of Quebec. But that makes no difference; we are all citizens of Canada, and wherever there is injustice it is our duty to denounce it-just as it is my duty and obligation to denounce this plan as a whole.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I hear some hon. members say "Oh, oh." As far as I am concerned, they could say "Ah, ah." and it would not bother me in the least.
I should like the sponsor of the bill, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh), to realize that there is no joy in an easy victory. That is why I should like to be counted among those who will give her great joy when the bill is finally passed.
Mr. Chairman, I wish to state what my constituents and I think of Bill No. C-136. I should also like to put forward further arguments in support of the claims I made yesterday when I said that in spite of the numerous experts who testified before the committee, no one really knows where we will end up with Bill No. C-136 or what will be its effects on our national economy.

And to prove my argument, I ask my colleagues to refer to report No. 8 of the proceedings and evidence of the special joint committee, and more particularly to page 137 where can be found extensive statements by the deputy minister of finance and other actuarial experts employed by the Canadian government. I also suggest that my colleagues take a look at pages 404 and 442 and they will have an idea of the work put out by the experts to set up the pension plan which led to Bill No. C-136. If you refer to page 406, after a few remarks concerning the economic implications of the Canada pension plan, you can read this:
While it is not possible to specify the exact effects of these transactions, nor the reactions to them, it is possible to form some view as to the potential size of their impact on the economy under varying assumptions, and to establish a range for the orders of magnitude which seem likely to be involved.
That is proof that they are not really certain of the possible implications. At page 407, the same experts admit that the pension plan will change the rate of spending and saving within each of the three main categories, consumers, enterprises and governments. In fact, here is what they say:
For the consumer group, the effects are twofold. The employee's contribution to the pension plan represents a reduction in his income, and this initially must bring about either a reduction in his spending or in his saving.
So, the experts recognize that there will be a reduction in the income of the employee, which of course will bring about a reduction in his spending and saving.
And I continue:
At the same time, the benefits paid by the pension plan represent income for a different group of consumers, the aged (or the disabled), whose ratio of spending out of income is high, and whose saving rate is low, or sometimes negative.
The net effect is thus to transfer income from individuals working to a particular group of consumers having a low rate of saving. After this initial impact, of course, the employee may succeed in gaining higher wages, which produces further effects which are taken into account below.
For the business group, the employer's contribution represents an addition to business costs. This increase in costs would initially bring about a reduction in profits, and thus a reduction in business savings, or in dividends paid out to shareholders, except to the extent that it may be offset through consequential price increases or the granting of smaller wage increases than would otherwise be granted.
Therefore, experts recognize that the Canadian economy as a whole may be strongly affected.
On page 407, those same experts state:
Canada Pension Plan
Despite lack of knowledge of the shifting and incidence process, it is possible to make a broad quantitative evaluation of the effects of the pension plan under certain assumed situations.
Mr. Chairman, this is always based on assumptions. I quote:
This can be done by specifying the conditions which mark off the upper and lower limits to the shifting process, then working out the quantitative implications at these limits. This is the procedure generally followed in the examples which are given in appendix "B".
Consequently one refers to appendix "B" and one can see that our economic experts, those who went so wrong in the present financial system, realized that millions of Canadian citizens will have to depend on social assistance.
When analysing another problem, the same experts tell us, as reported on page 408:
In addition to the problem of incidence, there are two sets of reactions which are difficult to judge in arriving at some assessment of the impact of the pension plan. The first involves the amount of private saving that will be diverted to this public plan.
Mr. Chairman, it is known that lots of money will be diverted. I quote:
To the extent that saving which has hitherto taken place in the private sector is now stored in the public sector, there is no effect on private spending, but simply a transfer of saving.
The second reaction to be considered involves the use to which provincial authorities put the pension fund reserves. If provinces increase their spending as a result of the pension plan, this would involve a transfer from private saving or spending to public spending. Some comments will be made subsequently on both these aspects.
Therefore, unless they build up on assumptions, even experts do not really know where the Canada pension plan will lead us.
Mr. Chairman, could we have order in this house? If some Quebec members are not interested in a measure upon which they may be called upon to vote tonight or tomorrow, at least they could give others an opportunity to listen.

speechtext: We read the report.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
I heard one of my hon. friends opposite say that they read the report. Most of them murder English and cannot understand the English text before they have read the French translation.
Even the experts do not know exactly what the effects will be upon the whole Canadian economy. There is one sure thing: the principle of it, which almost everyone admits. I may be the last one to speak on clause 1, and this reminds me that most people admit that a post is made to tie something to it.

Canada Pension Plan
Everyone admits the principle, but most do not know what animal will be tied to it; they do not know if a horse or some other animal will be tied to it. But within the socialist doctrine, all those who are willing to accept this bill should realize the scope of this principle.
Mr. Chairman, I claim that the pension plan, the principle of which is about to be adopted by almost every party in this house, is a compulsory system which makes democracy as odious as a dictatorship. With hypocrisy added to it, a democracy which compels people leaves them only the opportunity of choosing their policemen, the tax-levying people who govern by decree-for instance, consider the unemployment insurance-those who will have the right to search your pockets or grab you by the scruff of the neck if you are bold enough to ignore the regulations and the prohibitions.
Of all the government's social security schemes that now exist, this is one of the worst with regard to the principle. The increasing interest the government takes in social security leads to a political and economic dictatorship.
All those plans appeal to the people when they are presented as an election promise, which is what happened in 1963 when the Canadian people as a whole believed that the Liberal party, if elected, would give to the poor a universal pension ranging from $75 to $250 a month. That was the bait, the hook.
That reminds me of the fisherman who uses a firefly as bait. The plan is attractive and you can tell the people: Bite without giving it a second thought; it does not matter if the hook chokes you and kills you, as long as you eat.
Mr. Chairman, I said earlier that even experts do not know exactly where we are heading financially and economically with this plan. Care was taken, I admit, to include in the bill an indexing which will permit an increase in pensions according to the cost of living index. I should like to attempt to explain briefly to the supporters of this legislation the opinion given by financial experts during the study of this bill. I see that the minister completely disregards the principles of economics and especially the principles of freedom to which Canadian citizens are entitled. I hope he will change his mind before the third reading. It was further stated:
According to the cost of living index, the benefits index will be increased.

That is a fine precaution when no one knows what will happen under the inflationary system supported by the three other parties except the Ralliement Creditistes.
For the past several years, those systems have reduced the purchasing power of the Canadian dollar and melted the savings of those who denied themselves in 1935, 1940 and 1945, to put aside a few thousands dollars to have a few more comforts in their old age and who now find that their $1,000, $2,000 or $5,000 in savings are worth practically nothing in Canada.
Page 142 of report No. 2 of the committee proceedings deals with the effects of the ever increasing cost of living. That is precisely why, to justify itself, the government added to the bill the provision regarding the cost of living related increase. Reference is made to a large number of countries which have set up identical, similar or comparable plans-less complicated perhaps, but comparable-which are based on the same monetary principles and, probably, on the same policy.
I wanted to mention those especially, because Denmark's and Sweden's social security programs are often referred to as being excellent. For instance, on page 136, after having dealt with the cost of living index increase, we can read:
The changes in this price index and in the basic amounts of the national pension that have occurred in the post-war period are summarized in table 1. The national pension (excluding supplements) for a single aged person living in Copenhagen rose from 2,388 kroner to 3,660 kroner between April 1946 and April 1959.
This is a substantial increase.
People often boast about Sweden's social security programs being most generous.
In this connection, on page 139, it is stated:
The first of these quarterly increments became payable in November 1950 when the pension price index (with June 1946 = 100) reached 108. Three more increments were added in May 1951, when the index jumped to 122. Others went into effect in August 1951 (index, 127), November 1951 (index, 130), May 1952 (index, 135), and August 1954 (index. 140). The index did not go above 144 during 1955, so that a total of eight increments continued to be paid throughout that year, equal to 40 per cent of the basic pension.
The plan advocated by our opponents is not inflationary? No, not much. All over the world, where benefit increases are based on the cost of living index, minimum pension increases are noted. We have another example of that on page 141. Here is a young country which, for many years has had no old age

pension plan such as the one now under consideration. Here is what is found in the state of Israel:
The national insurance law of 1953, which introduced contributory old age and survivors' insurance in Israel, established a system of flat rate pensions. The basic old age pension is fixed at 15 Israeli pounds a month for a single person; it is increased to 225 pounds if the pensioner has one dependent, 285 pounds if he has two, and 34 pounds if he has three or more dependants.
There is added, however, to the basic amount paid every pensioner a supplementary cost-of-living allowance. This allowance has become substantially larger than the basic pension itself.
I would advise those who often laugh when we speak of monetary systems whose scientific theories would allow a constant balance between the purchasing power and the use of products, goods and services offered to consumers through compensated discounts, providing a fair balance of prices, enabling the Canadian consumers to use up intelligently the things they produce, they import, they exchange in raw material or import from foreign countries, to study it more thoroughly.
Those who make fun of our monetary theories should seriously consider where we are going with our present financial system based on a tight money policy, money entirely produced by bankers who ration it out in times of peace and who are becoming masters of our lives: family life, social life, while becoming at the same time masters of parliament.
Did the governor of the Bank of Canada, Mr. Rasminsky, not say in his recent recommendations that we should use bold formulas, be inventive so that Canada's prosperity may match the hopes of the Canadian people, be inventive and not resort to nearly all the contributory pension plans of all the other countries already subjected to this rigid system, to introduce Bill No. C-136.
And it is claimed that people will accept it, as I said a while ago, by taking the bait whatever the size of the hook, which will choke us afterwards.
Mr. Chairman, once more I hope that before final passage of this bill I will see some of my colleagues of the other parties take seriously into consideration this new political philosophy to which parliament is committing itself today with Bill No. C-136.
I remember a year ago when the Minister of Finance spoke to us about an 11 per cent tax on building materials. For two days, a representative of the Conservative party rose and he kept the Minister of Finance on the carpet to claim exemption from this tax for grain wagons in all western Canada.
Companies Act
I wonder if it would not be a good thing to do the same today on the occasion of examination of Bill No. C-136 which commits us for the coming years to a direction rather different from that chosen by my friends of other political parties in the House of Commons, who are aware that freedom is as important as security and that security and freedom can especially be provided to all Canadians in this beautiful, great and parties except the Ralliement Creditistes. try with a tremendous potential.
While we are only a small country with 20 million people, must we follow blindly the political philosophies of Beveridge and Karl Marx?
We should have enough foresight and imagination to use the Bank of Canada and allow provincial governments to use it, because those governments are now short of borrowing power, and that is why they are ready to accept this bill, because they know very well that this would be another source of revenue.
Let us be logical and let us think about the serious implications this will have before final approval is given to Bill No. C-136.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider Bill No. S-22, to amend the Companies Act.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Lamoureux in the Chair.
On clause 1.

Mr. Chairman, in the absence of the Secretary of State, who would normally be piloting this bill, I presume the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance will be replying to our questions. At this moment I believe it is encumbent upon me to make a few brief remarks with regard to these rather extensive amendments, which do not amount to a reintroduction or complete revision of the past Companies Act. Perhaps this would have been preferable. I think that time has intervened, and rather

Companies Act
than perhaps go another two, three or four years, the officials of the registrar's branch of the Department of the Secretary of State have preferred to bring forward these amendments to what was the Dominion Companies Act in order to bring it up to date and to meet the requirements of today, as well as to meet some of the recommendations of the committee on the drafting of a companies act, which has been meeting, to my knowledge, since about 1957. This is a clear example of where lawyers meeting together did not enter into precipitate action. Certainly the members of the banking and commerce committee gave this bill very extensive examination, with regard to the registrar of companies, and outside representations made to them. There was also intensive study given to it in the other place. In fact they entered into what I feel is an unprecedented course of action by setting up a special subcommittee which made proposals for amending the act.
A number of amendments have been proposed since the bill received third reading in the other place. This chamber is going to be asked to accept certain recommendations of the committee on banking and commerce, and therefore the bill will have to go back for concurrence to the other house. But as is usual in this sphere of what one would call lawyers' law, there is agreement between the other house and ourselves, and I think it will be a mere formality.
The members of this party are in agreement with the amendments incorporated in Bill S-22, but if I might express some preferences I wish to say I feel that within the sphere of company legislation in Canada there is a difference between those companies which are incorporated under letters patent and those incorporated under a memorandum of association. The Companies Act as amended will try to get the best from both sides. It has drawn inspiration from some of the advances made under the letters patent type of incorporation, and some from the side where memoranda of association prevail. It is a very conscious attempt to bring the legislation up to the modern standards of the new Ontario companies act, and of course there is the new Manitoba companies act.
I was reassured by the registrar that very close attention had been paid to the draft companies act put forward by the committee on uniform legislation. In Canada, where we now have such an interchange and interplay at the corporate level, we know we must try to establish uniform standards and powers. Those of us who have had some

experience, to a greater or lesser extent, of incorporating businesses either under a dominion charter or some provincial charter, and then engaging in foreign registration, know too well that we have encountered some very frustrating differences of opinion and differences of provisions whether at the statutory or regulatory level in the various provinces.
From the point of view of doing business in Canada it is incumbent upon us at all levels, whether at the federal or provincial legislative level, to see to it that we get as much of a uniform companies act as possible. This is one of the areas which tend to inhibit company expansion, and when I talk about company expansion I am really talking about business expansion, because there is hardly any real volume of business carried out today except under a corporate structure.
Under the provisions of clause 2 the act is to be renamed the Canada corporations act. This is a change from the old idea of the Dominion Companies Act, but I think the explanations furnished by the registrar were quite satisfactory.
As we proceed we shall see how the act has been developed, but at this stage I will limit my remarks to indicate that we in the opposition are generally satisfied with the provisions of the bill and are prepared to support it. There may have been some changes made in the committee with which I personally would not agree, but these were decisions by the committee and I do not think much harm was done to the bill by the deletions recommended.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would just like to take this opportunity to say a few words on what is to become the Canada corporations act-the amendments to the Companies Act-chiefly because at some time in the past it has been, and perhaps very soon in the future it will again be, one of the statutes which will have great effect on my professional career.
As the hon. member for Edmonton West pointed out, this is not the optimum which company lawyers in Canada would have preferred. I think it is generally agreed that if it had been possible to obtain the uniform draft companies act which was worked out in the late fifties, and has been before the profession since that time, it would have been an immensely preferable solution to the problem.
The Dominion Companies Act was last substantially changed in 1934, completing changes which had been undertaken the

previous year. Company law and commercial practice generally have developed since that time. Many of the proposed changes are long overdue and I think this bill is a good solution to what has been a difficult problem. I am pleased to note that in the preparation of the bill and the amendments, inspiration was taken from the provisions of the Ontario corporations act, which was enacted into the law of Ontario some ten years ago.
I believe the hon. member for Edmonton West comes from a jurisdiction in which the memorandum of agreement form is commonly used. I come from a province in which the letters patent form is used, and I believe that the breakdown that took place in communication on the uniform draft companies act was really between bridging these two points of view. I would second the hon. member's remarks as to the desirability, not only from the lawyer's standpoint but that of commercial men, that company law should be made uniform throughout Canada, so that decisions of the courts and commercial practice may be the same throughout the country.

On clause 16-Name of company.

This is one of the areas in which there may be some difference in practice between certain jurisdictions. During the discussions in the committee I was anxious to be able to establish that an incorporated company might be able to carry on business under a name other than its incorporated name. This is an old, common law right but I think the present wording of the clause precludes this practice.
I am thinking, for instance, of a firm like T. Eaton (Western) Limited carrying on business and issuing invoices in the name of Eaton's. I know that a number of corporations, foreign companies, are registered under such names as, shall we say, "XY Company Limited". But these are very restrictive names as far as their operations are concerned, and they would like to be known as "XY of Canada Limited" because that is the way they intend to operate. It is my feeling they might come a cropper when seeking to operate in this way under the Companies Act.
As far as I am concerned I subscribe, in this field which concerns the qualifications for directorship and a few other things, to what might be called the Delaware theory. In other words I like to make it as easy as possible for a company to operate, so as to encourage the incorporation. There is still ample control possible, but for heaven's sake let us not introduce artificial barriers by prescribing difficult regulations. I had hoped that in this clause 16, which is the new clause 22 of the act, we might have had a little more flexibility. Those advising the hon. gentlemen in the other place, together with the registrar and the majority in the committee, did not go along with me so I will simply take the occasion to register my lone voice in the wilderness and ask for improvements in the future. I hope we shall ultimately see these things made possible. It is harmless from the point of view of the public and it is most efficacious from the point of view of ease of operation, and I am in favour of anything which makes a business operate more easily.

Clause agreed to.

On clause 35-Qualifying after election or appointment.

This is related to remarks I made on a previous clause with regard to ease of operation. Here again I would have hoped for a provision whereby a director could be named to a Canadian corporation without his having to be a shareholder. I know this is permissible under the Companies Act, provided the articles of association so provide, and I concede that in the case of many corporations where the board wishes to have a solicitor as secretary or treasurer there is no need to go through the complexities and the artificial procedures of having the solicitor apply for a share, go through the sham of paying for it, be registered as a shareholder and then conclude a trust agreement in which he signs a transfer in blank back to one of the controlling officers of the corporation, with the result that he does not have one penny invested in the business. I think it is a sham and a waste of time to go through all this and again I incline to what might be called the Delaware practice -and it is the Alberta practice in this case -that a director need not be a shareholder. This is very convenient, and the situation does not lend itself to subterfuge; as a matter of fact it eliminates subterfuge. It may apply in other jurisdictions-
Not Ontario.

Well, perhaps Ontario will catch up to us in the west some time. Ontario makes you run through the hoops for nothing, then. I would hope that we could convince the Canadian Corporations Act authorities to adopt this. At the present time, again, this is perhaps a cry from the outer wilderness to advance to a certain position, and I would heartily commend it to hon. members of this house who have some knowledge of corporate practice, in the ultimate revision of the act. I am not saying it should come in now, but in the ultimate revision of the act I think it should be a provision.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 39-Books of account and accounting records.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Edmonton West made some reference to the deletion that was made in the committee. I think he was referring to section 121(f) which appears under clause 39 of this bill. The reason for the deletion of that subsection in the committee was essentially to
[Mr. Lambert.)
permit the disclosure of information by the Secretary of State. I think this is an important deletion and it is one that should perhaps have a word of explanation.
The subsection which was deleted required the Secretary of State to obtain the recommendation of the chief justice or the acting chief justice of the court of the province in which the head office of the company concerned was situated, and he would not be permitted to make public the documents filed with the department until that had been done. I think it was the feeling of the committee that this should not be the case; that this should be public information. I believe that particularly the modern trend in company affairs is that we should have a better informed public. It seems that more sophisticated companies rely on more and more disclosure to their shareholders and to the general public, and the committee and I felt there should be this sort of disclosure. I would like to put on the record some remarks by Professor Williamson with regard to this clause. These remarks appeared in the Business Quarterly in the spring of 1963 when he was discussing take-over bids and insider trading. He said:
The recent wave of take-over bids for Canadian companies-offers usually made by a corporation directed to the shareholders of another corporation to buy up all or part of its stock-has shown the highly speculative nature, in many cases, of the decision whether or not to accept an offer, and has made clear the serious disadvantages from which the shareholder, who must make this choice, may suffer.
Complaints have been frequent in recent months that in some take-over cases, where the offer was to purchase less than all of the stock of a company, substantial profits were made by an inside group that was able to accept an attractive offer quickly while other shareholders were too late. In addition, the lack of information available to the ordinary shareholder who receives an offer for his stock can be a very serious handicap.
In another article on the securities regulations in Canada he also had this to say about the Canadianization of Canadian industry. This is from an article which appeared, again, in the Business Quarterly in the summer of 1964:
The "Canadianizing" of industry in Canada, currently so popular in government circles, may turn out to be one of the greatest disasters in Canadian economic development unless individual Canadians show a greatly increased willingness to invest in common stocks of Canadian companies. And if they are to be persuaded to buy common stocks then the image of the Canadian stock market will have to undergo a drastic improvement.

He was suggesting that Canadians could not be made to invest in Canadian companies unless they were given much more information than they have been up to the present. I believe this is perhaps one of the very important amendments which was made by the banking and commerce committee. We were unable to find that such a restriction had been written into any of the companies acts in any of the other jurisdictions, and the commitee and I felt this was a very important deletion.

Mr. Chairman, I would just like to speak for a moment on section 121(f), the disclosure section. I think that, as the hon. member for York-Scarborough pointed out, this is an essential and momentous section within the bill, in that if we are to encourage the public generally to acquire more equities in this country rather than put their moneys into savings, insurance, etc., and if in particular we are to achieve the objective that the Minister of Finance has indicated is so essential, namely buying back control of our own industries which have fallen into the hands of persons in other lands, I think it essential that the corporate name and the ownership of corporate entities be made fair, open, clear and distinct.
I think one of the factors which makes it very difficult to sell equity shares to the general public is the lack of information and knowledge that they can have of the dealings of corporations at the present time. We have had examples in the past few years of takeovers where the ordinary shareholder had absolutely no information of what was being done by insiders who were taking over these corporations. I believe that so long as this situation is extant, we are not very likely to get the average saver in Canada to invest his money in equities. It also, surely, is tragic when corporations that control some of our wealthiest natural resources, our most fabulous corporations in the natural resource areas, have two different financial statements. There is one for their American shareholders which, according to their S.E.C. regulations, must disclose all insider trading and any benefits to shareholders and directors; so if a Canadian who owns equity stock in one of these companies wants information, he has to get hold of the American shareholders' report. The Canadian shareholders' report does not require as nearly comprehensive information. I think if we are going to prevent the secrecy of corporate trading, if we are going to encourage public information in these 20220-811
Companies Act
areas which will enhance the possibilities of the average person investing in equity stock, and ultimately, we hope, result in these equities and the control of these Canadian corporations being once more vested in Canadians, we need a great deal more in the way of disclosure.
It is unfortunate that the uniform act could not have been accepted by all provinces so that in this area of disclosure we might have gone a lot further and a lot more effectively than we can with the Dominion Companies Act, when there are, of course, ten different entities and ten different corporations acts. Some of this might have to be done by securities legislation within the provinces. But I think the minister is to be commended for bringing in, at least in the Canadan bill, disclosure sections which will make more and fuller disclosures available to the owners of equity stocks under the Canadian Corporations Act.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources

Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask a question of the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance. As I read these clauses having to do with disclosure of a company's affairs to its shareholders, I notice it does not cover private companies. By private companies I mean those companies within the definition of the act where you have a limited number of shareholders and shares are offered to the general public. What happens in some of the smaller private companies, which may be family businesses which over a period of years may have been divided between two or more sections of the family, is that if the family shareholders control only 49 per cent of the shares they have no way under the present legislation of forcing the shareholders who hold 51 per cent of the business to reveal certain aspects of the company's affairs. I speak in particular of how much salary some of the directors receive as officers of the company, and so on. In this instance the private shareholders holding 49 per cent of the shares have absolutely no rights under the present statute. This primarily affects small family businesses across the country.
I would ask the parliamentary secretary whether these amendments contemplate giving more rights to minority shareholders in private corporations than they currently have, and if not, what is contemplated in the future? Because this subject concerns a lot of small family businesses across the country.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, my understanding is that this amendment is to give the Secretary of State's department more control over the companies which heretofore have been delinquent in making returns. This is putting teeth into the legislation so that these companies can be wound up if they do not comply.

I believe it is generally conceded that the companies branch of the federal government has been the most inefficient branch in the government during the last four or five years. At any rate, that is my opinion. If somebody wants to know why I have formed it, it would be quite easy to explain and go into some of the personalities involved. But it is the fact that it has created

a great deal of ill will among the companies. Perhaps it would be wise to ask the sponsor of the bill what was the percentage of the companies which were supposed to report which did not report? What sanctions were taken against them and why were they not exercised?
I do not know whether this matter will come up again for a long time but there has been terrific criticism on the part of many persons of the inefficiency of this branch. Quite frankly, I do not understand the sanction now being imposed, which means that the government will be able to take over a company which after a period of three years has failed to produce the report required by the Secretary of State. I would suggest that the companies branch is not sufficiently competent or does not have the personnel to deal with this matter. In other clauses reference is made to auditors, and I am sure we do not have sufficient auditors to audit the reports which are being submitted. Many of them are filed away and not acted upon. It seems to me that we are making quite a change here and I am wondering whether it is feasible. I do not disagree with the sanctions being put on, but I do not think we are in a position to enforce them.
Perhaps this matter has been considered by the committee, but as I understand it over one third of the companies who were supposed to report did not report. Another third of them reported improperly or in such a way that the report served no purpose; and another third reported as requested under the previous act and were operating in what was considered to be an acceptable manner. But as I say, I am wondering whether we can enforce this change we are making without bringing other factors into play.

No, Mr. Chairman. Perhaps some hon. members do not know the background to this, and I can explain some of the matters to which I am referring. In my opinion this state of affairs has been a disgrace for a number of years. Some years ago several hon. members made extensive speeches on this matter which indicated a complete breakdown in this department. Applications were before the companies branch for long periods of time without any attention at all being paid to them. For two or three years there was even no opportunity at all to make an application. Now we are saying in this clause that we have reached the stage where we not only

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I can understand the concern of the hon. member for Timiskaming. I might point out for the information of the house that it may have been that in the past we have been somewhat neglectful of the Companies Act, bearing in mind the fact that in Canada at the present time, as I understand, there are 28,746 corporations carrying on business and of that number 24,758 are under provincial incorporations and only 3,988 under federal charters. It is my understanding that due to the wording of the act there was some question in the past whether the companies branch here could dissolve a company or merely transfer its name for failure to comply with the regulations. The committee felt it would make it much stronger and more effective and accomplish the very point that the hon. member has raised.

Is it thought that the applications section has been broadened and strengthened so that applications will not be so long delayed? The point, as I see it, is that even in the case of good companies that made their reports we did not have anybody to go over them. It seems to me this does not say that you and I as individuals can walk in and have a look at companies' statements that are filed. What it does say is that the Secretary of State shall be responsible for seeing that they are properly administered and operated, and under certain conditions a judge can allow someone to look at particular files. In my opinion, although I may be wrong, the personnel have not been available in the past. ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-INVESTIGATION INTO DOCUMENT TAMPERING IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the other day I received a written answer to a written question relating to an allegation that the Royal Bank of Canada forged a particular document by changing the date on it and by so altering it as to make it appear that it was signed on behalf of a limited company by typing in the words "Tipton Cattle Company" and the word "president" after the signature of the individual. As a consequence of the allegation that the Royal Bank of Canada had forged a document, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police were contacted by the individual concerned, namely, Mr. Tipton of Francois Lake, B.C.
My inquiry of the minister and the answer are found on page 12330 of Hansard, and in my view the reply does not truly reflect the facts as they have been indicated to me. The reply to part I of the question contains the following statement with reference to Mr. Tipton:
He advised that all documents were in the hands of his solicitors, that these solicitors were taking necessary steps to bring the matter before the courts, and that they, the solicitors wished that any action with respect to Tipton's complaint be held in abeyance.
Mr. Tipton has advised me that is incorrect and does not truly reflect the conversation he had with the R.C.M.P. in that all he indicated to the R.C.M.P. was that they should deal with his solicitors and await a written reply from them. So, in that respect, I submit the answer is incorrect and misleading. It does not truly represent what took place.
The second part of the answer is, I submit, equally misleading because it reads as follows, and I quote:

The solicitors Indicate that the whole matter is subject to civil action and, therefore, no action can be taken by the R.C.M.P.-
I have here a photostatic copy of a letter dated September 25, 1964, directed to Sergeant Gordon, N.C.O. in charge, R.C.M.P. detachment, Burns Lake, British Columbia. It is headed, "Re:	Lorenzo Tipton & Norman
Tipton and the Tipton Cattle Company Ltd., Francois Lake, B.C." The letter reads in -part as follows, and is from Cullinane & Greene, solicitors, in Prince George, B.C.:
I wish to confirm that we are the solicitors for Mr. and Mrs. Tipton in the matter of a civil action which has been commenced against them at the instance of the Royal Bank of Canada. Bums Lake, B.C.
This is an indication that whatever civil action took place, or is still before the courts, was taken at the instance of the Royal Bank of Canada and not an indication, as the answer would lead us to believe, that the whole matter is subject to civil action. Perhaps I should read the entire letter into the record so it will be all here. I continue:
I understand that you recently saw Mr. Tipton with regard to a possible investigation of a document which was signed by Mr. Tipton and which Mr. Tipton assures me has since been altered by means of typing above his signature, the words "Tipton Cattle Company Ltd." and his signature is followed by the words "Press."
The fact is that on the date of this document, which is dated February 26, 1964, Mr. Tipton was in the city of Ottawa and did not actually return to the Bums Lake area until the evening of March 1st.
As an aside, Mr. Speaker, I can confirm this because Mr. Tipton was with me on that particular date. I continue to quote:
We do not have the original of this letter and can only supply you with a phQtostatic copy thereof but even examining the photostatic copy you will note that the words "Tipton Cattle Company Ltd." and the words "Press." have been typed with a different typewriter than the remainder of the document. Mr. Tipton's concern here is that on the basis of this changed document the Royal bank presumes that it is able to justify the wrongful seizure and sale of cattle belonging to the Tipton Cattle Company Ltd. Also, the actual date that Mr. Tipton signed this was March 19, 1964 which was almost a month after the cattle had been wrongfully seized and sold.
I understand from Mr. Tipton that he was a little reluctant to discuss this matter with you when you requested him to do so very recently, for reason that he had placed the matter in our hands. We wish to assure you that we have no objection of this matter being fully investigated by the R.C.M.P. as we feel that the person who altered the original document was acting most improperly and very much to the detriment of the Tiptons and the Tipton Cattle Company Ltd. We are prepared to cooperate fully with you in any way in this regard.
Yours very truly,
Cullinane & Greene

I submit on the basis of that letter, Mr. Speaker, that the second part of the answer is misleading. The solicitors do not indicate that the whole matter is subject to civil action. They merely pointed out that the Royal bank commenced civil action. I submit also there was an indication given to Mr. Tipton by one officer of the R.C.M.P. that they would be pleased to investigate this matter. This was subsequently countermanded, presumably by a senior officer on the force. I say that not only is the answer given by the parliamentary secretary misleading in that it did not fully represent the facts, but also that the R.C.M.P. have been negligent in their duties by trying to pass over their responsibility by refusing to investigate a matter when it was requested of them, a matter of a criminal character relating to an allegation of forgery of a document on the part of the Royal Bank of Canada.

AIR TRANSPORT-POLICY ANNOUNCEMENT RESPECTING ASSISTANCE TO SECONDARY AIRPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this afternoon I raised with the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) the urgent question as to when the government would announce a regional air carriers' policy for this country. My only purpose tonight is to put it again on the record in the hope that it will spur the minister and his government into some kind of action on a matter that is long overdue. This question was raised as
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion long ago as July 12, 1963, and it can be found on page 2133 of Hansard for that date, when the then minister of transport said this:
I believe that some clarification of the relationships and future role is essential-
The minister was referring to regional carriers:
-to meet the rapidly changing technical and economic circumstances of aviation-
He went on to say this:
-I hope to make some changes in this regard in the relatively near future. When I say that I mean within a very few months. It is one of the matters I consider of utmost importance.
Then speaking in the house, again, the then minister of transport, at page 2149 of Hansard for July 12, 1963, said this:
I would anticipate that it would be another two or three months before it would be possible to make the kind of complete statement that is required in order to deal with it in an adequate and proper way.
Later, at page 4794 of Hansard-this time we have gone from July to November of 1963-the then minister of transport said this:
I hope also, before the end of the year, to be making a statement on air policy.
Later on-and we know that there was a shift in portfolios necessitated by the need to elevate the now Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) into a new experience as house leader-the new Minister of Transport, the present minister, said this:
The whole question of future air policy is, as I think the hon. gentleman is well aware, under very active consideration at this time.
That can be found on page 256 of Hansard for February 26, 1964. Then he said:
However, I may say that no conclusions have yet been reached. As soon as they have been reached they will be made known to the house and to everyone else concerned. I hope this will be before too long.
It is over one year ago that the Minister of Transport said this. Subsequently, on April 21 of last year when the matter was raised by the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) as a grievance, he received no answer at all from the Minister of Transport. On April 27 I asked the Minister of Transport when he would announce the regional air carriers' policy, and the answer can be found on page 2599 of Hansard:
Whenever the policy has been devised.
Then we go to April 30 of last year, which was the night the minister took to television when, through sloppy management in this house he had been unable to make a statement on motions and he tabled his non-policy,

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion as he called it. The minister said this, which is to be found on page 2855 of Hansard:
-a reasonable role for regional air carriers providing scheduled and regular air service must be established-
That was 11 months ago when he said that we must establish a regional air carrier policy. Subsequently, in July of last year, at page 5811 of Hansard, the minister replied to the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer):
I intend to announce it just as soon as it is formulated and agreed to by the government.
The hon. member for Three Rivers had asked when the minister would announce his new national air policy. In September of 1964 the Minister of Transport, speaking on the estimates of the Department of Transport, said this at page 8162 of Hansard:
I am going to keep right on pushing just as hard as I can for the achievement of this-
That is an air policy. Then listen to this pious statement:
I hope before the end of the year I will be able to make good recommendations, too, about air policy.
In February this year, it will be found on page 11518 that I repeated the question and asked when we would have an announcement as to a regional air carriers' policy. This is what the Minister of Transport said:
I do not think, sir, I can say anything useful about the time that would be done, beyond saying that it will be done just as soon as we think we have something to communicate to the house which will really work.
Then again today I raised this question in the hope that it might sink into the minister's head that the regional air carriers of this country, as the former minister of transport said almost two years ago now, essentially require a policy enunciation by the government. The regional air carriers of the country want some kind of statement from the minister. They are worried about what
might be behind the minister's reluctance to say anything at this time. They are worried because they well know the kind of manoeuvres he can perform, especially at a time when he is anticipating an election. They are worried that he is holding up an announcement of a policy which has been arrived at in order to dangle before various regional carriers in this country some sort of carrot immediately prior to the next election.
It is not good enough for him continually to be saying "before the end of the year". This has gone on for two years now. This government must take the step of making an announcement and carry out that grand promise of the Prime Minister, that the actions which his government would take in the months ahead would excite the daring. Well, it is time we had a little excitement from the Minister of Transport in terms of a regional carriers' policy.

May I remind the hon. member of the basic principles recommended by the minister as a basis for a regional air carriers' policy for Canada, as set out by the minister on May 15, 1964, and as reported in Hansard at page 2855:
