speechtext:
Order. In the normal course of procedure in the house the most difficult and painful task for any Speaker is to be forced to the extremity of having to name an hon. member. Today I consider it my duty to name five hon. members. However, I do so not to cause their suspension from the service of the house, but on behalf of all its members to honour them on a quarter of a century in its service. In the circumstances perhaps the house will waive the provisions of standing order 34(2).
I name you John George Diefenbaker. I acknowledge your service to the country in war and in peace. As prime minister of this country you have held the highest office within the gift of the Canadian people. You gave your fellow citizens their own bill of rights. As leader of Her Majesty's loyal opposition you have vigorously asserted those rights and privileges that are the hallmark of our parliamentary system of government.
History will record and do honour to your achievements as leader of this nation through six significant years but we, your fellow Commoners, can pay you no higher tribute than to say you are, and have been, a House of Commons man.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to express to those gentlemen the admiration of the party I represent, because 25 years in the House of Commons is quite a feat, for one has to face not only his colleagues in the house but also the voters. maintopic: TRIBUTES TO MEMBERS COMPLETING 25 YEARS OF SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to join with the others and pay tribute to those who are today celebrating their 25th anniversary in the House of Commons.
Twenty five years is a long time, but I am sure it must bring back fond memories to those concerned.
We believe those five hon. members of the House of Commons have well served their land, their country, and have worked with sincerity and dedication for the interest of the people. We wish them many more years among us for we, the younger members, do benefit from their experience and this helps and encourages us to pursue our political careers.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: TRIBUTES TO MEMBERS COMPLETING 25 YEARS OF SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I doubt whether I have ever risen in this house with the same feelings that I have today. It is difficult to express to you, sir, what your words mean to me, and I know as well to my colleagues whom the house has honoured today in a way that I have never seen equalled in the years that I have been here.
I say to the Prime Minister that his words bring to me a re-emphasis of the pride that those of us who sit in the House of Commons understand. People outside cannot appreciate how from day to day we can face one another in the most difficult forum of all and retain a feeling of admiration for those who do not see eye to eye with oneself. There is no other legislative body like it, having to the same extent the tradition of the House of Commons based on the British model. Last week was the seven hundredth anniversary of the first parliament at Westminster, which has been our model since. That was the parliament that brought together the love of liberty of the Anglo-Saxons and the dedication to freedom of the Normans of French origin. We bring these two together within this institution.
All I can say is that occasions such as this, where warmth takes for a time the place of the harshness of debate, add to one's pride in this great institution. We stack our weapons and substitute verbal garlands. We seek to make parliament worth while.
I also want to refer to the dean of parliament, a parliamentarian who as the dean of the five new members will be for them a second Dizzy Dean, a great philosopher and a connoisseur of words.
The Prime Minister today epitomized the finest traditions of parliament when he added the query, what would the House of Commons be without me. I was reminded of an occasion when that question was asked by a former prime minister, Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, some years after he had been in the House of Commons but before he went to the Senate. He had met with that great wit of parliament, S. W. Jacobs, K.C., in Toronto, and asked him "What is it like in parliament without me?" to which Mr. Jacobs replied "It is like Hades would be without Satan". That is one way of describing parliament.
Sir, I can only say this, and this is not a swan song. I hope to continue in the days ahead in this house, to join with all members

To my hon. friend the parliamentary authority in this house, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), and to the hon. members representing the Social Credit party and the Creditistes I say, thank you all.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: TRIBUTES TO MEMBERS COMPLETING 25 YEARS OF SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it has not been very often during the last 25 years that I have found myself joined with the Leader of the Opposition in action by this house, but I now desire to express my appreciation to all hon. members in the house for their generous attitude today toward those of us who have been here for some years.
I recall in those early years that during an election campaign, local members who supported today's official opposition party said that I was too young to be a member of the House of Commons. Today I feel very grateful for that expression to which they gave vent in those years.
I find the statements today rather refreshing, because it has seemed to me that in the last few months or years it has been a rather popular pastime outside the house to attack this institution. My observation, for what it is worth, has been that, in spite of our weaknesses and suggestions that we are unable to perform the business efficiently at times- in spite of a desire by some of us to have reforms made-the institution itself is the best institution I know for operating the government of a country. It provides that degree of liberty and freedom of the individual subject that is required and, I am sure, desired by all hon. members. I cannot help feeling that nothing I have seen in my life leads me to doubt for one moment that this is the system which best guarantees the right of the individual to freedom and liberty.
So today, when I hear the house express itself so unanimously and so kindly, I find it refreshing to see the capacity of the house to come together and reveal its own inner self. I should like, with great warmth of feeling, to thank my colleagues in this chamber for their very kind expression.

SEVENTEENTH, EIGHTEENTH, NINETEENTH AND TWENTIETH REPORTS OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I have the honour to present, in English and in French, the seventeenth, eighteenth, nineteenth and twentieth reports of the special committee on procedure and organization.
The seventeenth report is largely concerned with improvements in Hansard and other parliamentary publications. The eighteenth report recommends the revision of standing order 65 to provide for a new structure of standing committees. The nineteenth report provides for the referral of estimates to the new standing committees and for a time limit on the discussion of the main estimates in committee of supply. The recommendations contained in both the eighteenth and nineteenth reports would be on a trial basis for the duration of the next session of this parliament.
The twentieth report recommends the extension of the use of electronic recording and transcribing equipment.

speakeroldname: Hon. Harry W. Hays (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF NEW DAIRY POLICY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like at this time to announce our new dairy policy. Just before I do that I should like to say one word as the youngest colt in this house. I have never seen the house just like this, so it seems to me I am learning something. I should like, as I say, to announce our new dairy policy which has to do with culture, the greatest of all cultures, agriculture.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF NEW DAIRY POLICY
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF NEW DAIRY POLICY
speechtext:
This pertains to the new dairy policy without which none of us could live.
The objectives of our Canadian dairy policy are twofold. The policy is designed to provide

dairy farmers operating economic units with an adequate income, while at the same time assuring the Canadian consumer a constant supply of the highest quality dairy products at stable prices which will ensure optimum consumption.
Because of its geography and climate Canada is a relatively high cost dairy producing country. Except for certain specialty products, such as mature Cheddar cheese, we cannot hope to be a significant competitor on world markets with dairy products from countries with lower production costs arising from milder climates. Because of our climatic disadvantages in dairy production it would be unrealistic to provide a level of support on all milk produced that could result in surplus production and a possible return to a costly accumulation of stocks.
A further objective of a national dairy policy must therefore be to maintain a reasonable balance between production and disappearance of milk and dairy products, account being taken of export possibilities and of imports. To this end it is proposed that government supports will apply only to domestic utilization as related to a base period. The policy will also recognize the interest of Canada's trading partners in the Canadian market for dairy products, and will permit imports to share in future market growth.
Last year Canada imported a record 17 million pounds of cheese. This was more than balanced by Canada's growing cheese exports of over 30 million pounds.
As an efficient exporter of agricultural products like cheese and wheat, Canada has a vital interest in obtaining better access to foreign markets, and in its own policies must therefore recognize the corresponding interest of other efficient agricultural exporting countries in being able to compete for a share of the future growth of the Canadian market.
To attain these objectives, and as part of the government's long range dairy policy, legislation to establish a Canadian dairy commission will be introduced at the earliest possible opportunity. This commission, working in co-operation with the provinces, would have responsibility for the over-all relationship between governments and the dairy industry.
The interim policy, to come into effect on May 1 for an 11 month period pending the establishment of the Canadian dairy commission, will follow the principles of the long range policy. The interim policy is being put into effect on May 1 for 11 months in order
Dairy Policy
to facilitate a widely supported change In the dairy support year to align it more closely to the milk production cycle. Starting next year the dairy year will begin on April 1 instead of May 1.
Two separate and distinct programs will be instituted. The first will provide for a basic support through a deficiency payment plan, coupled with direct subsidy and export assistance. The other will comprise a direct supplementary payment to producers. The over-all effect is intended to be a national average price for manufacturing milk used domestically and based on 1964-65 production of $3.50 per hundredweight.
The agricultural stabilization board will be authorized to provide an effective support level of 64 cents per pound for creamery butter, basis Montreal and Toronto. This level will be maintained, as it was last year, by authorizing payments to producers equivalent to the difference between the support level of 64 cents and the board's buying and selling prices. As at present, these payments will first be made by the processing plants to the producers. The plants will then be reimbursed by the board. This action, along with export assistance, is expected to maintain an average factory price to producers of manufacturing milk of between $3.10 and $3.20 per hundredweight.
At the same time the board will determine actual prices paid to producers, by processors, for manufacturing milk and will be authorized to make a deficiency payment direct to producers, equivalent to the amount by which the national average price for manufacturing milk falls below a prescribed support level of $3.30 per hundredweight. In other words, the goal of the deficiency payment plan will be a national average of $3.30 per hundredweight for manufacturing milk.
In accordance with the over-all policy, this price guarantee of $3.30 is to be extended only to that portion of manufactured milk used domestically. Accordingly the amount of any deficiency payment will be reduced by the cost of export assistance. This will mean that if manufacturing milk production and domestic use are in balance producers will, on the average, receive the full $3.30 per hundredweight. Should production exceed domestic use, the effective support level would in fact be reduced by the difference between the domestic price and the export price as determined by the cost of moving the surplus into export.
For example, if it were found that a national average deficiency payment of 15 cents per

Dairy Policy
hundred pounds was to be paid under this plan, and it the deductible cost of exporting surplus production amounted to 5 cents a hundred, the actual deficiency payment would be 10 cents per hundred. This follows the principle inherent in the long range plan under the proposed Canadian dairy commission that government supports should apply only to domestic utilization of Canadian production as determined by a base period.
Surplus milk produced by fluid milk shippers contributes to our total dairy stocks and hence to any amount that might need to be exported. Therefore any deduction of export costs from the deficiency payment fund would not include the cost of exporting surpluses arising from the fluid milk industry. The cost of export subsidies chargeable against the deficiency payments will be reduced by the percentage of the total supply of manufacturing milk which is represented by that produced as a by-product of the fluid milk industry.
In order to provide comparable assistance to cream shippers, any deficiency payment to shippers of manufacturing milk will also be made to cream shippers on an equivalent basis.
During the coming dairy year, pending establishment of the Canadian dairy commission there will be a supplementary payment to producers. It will approximate, in total, the difference between the $3.30 support level and $3.50 per hundred of milk, based on 1964-65 production of manufacturing milk.
Producers who during the base period marketed less than 10,000 pounds of milk or an equivalent amount of cream will not be eligible for the payment. Since that is less than the production of two very average cows or one good cow, the government does not believe they can rightly be considered dairy farmers.
In order to ensure a relatively higher level of assistance to our many eligible smaller farmers, this payment will be at a rate per hundred pounds that decreases as production rises. For eligible producers, that is, those marketing at least 10,000 pounds of milk last year, the rate of payment will be 25 cents per hundredweight for the first 47,999 pounds of milk marketed. It will be 20 cents per hundredweight for the amount between 48,000 and 95,999 pounds, and 10 cents per hundredweight for all milk marketed in excess of 95,999 pounds.
Thus a producer who in 1964-65 marketed 50,000 pounds of milk will receive a lump sum payment of $124. A producer who mar-

keted 100,000 pounds of milk will receive $220, and a producer who marketed 200,000 pounds of milk will receive $320. The estimated average payment per producer across Canada is slightly over $100. Payments will be made to cream shippers on the same scale, assuming an average fat test of 3.5 per cent. As in the past, producers who normally participate in the fluid milk market will not be eligible for direct subsidy payments nor will they be eligible for the supplementary payment.
The application of the program to major dairy pool areas will be consistent with the interpretation of manufacturing milk which has been used as a basis for the support program for the past two years.
In the interests of our producers I think I should remind them that under the new program it is as important as ever for them to negotiate the best possible price for their milk from the processing plants. The deficiency payment will be based, as all are, on a national average price obtained by dividing total returns to all eligible producers by the total number of eligible producers. Those producers who make good deals with the processing plants will lose none of the benefit of their own private enterprise. If, for example, the deficiency payment came to 15 cents per hundred pounds, the producer who averages $3.20 per hundred from his plant will average a total return of $3.35 per hundred. On the other hand, the producer selling to the plant for only, say, $3.10 per hundred would gross $3.25.
Complete details of the program are being developed by the agricultural stabilization board and will be made known to producers and the trade at an appropriate time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, you will admit that it is very difficult at this moment to assess the scope of the new dairy policy which the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) just announced. One would have needed an IBM machine in order to note all the data which the minister gave this house and make the necessary calculations to determine exactly the benefits the milk producers of this will derive from industrial milk during the 1965-66 dairy year.
At the outset, and on behalf of my party, I would like to point out to the minister that the dairy producers only asked for a minimum price of $3.50 per hundredweight of industrial milk shipped to processing factories.

We do not yet know if the dairy producer will get the requested minimum price, that is $3.50 per hundredweight, but the Canadian federation of agriculture, the farmers' unions and the catholic farmers' union informed us that if the price under the new dairy policy is $3.30, $3.35 or even $3.48, strong protests will be made with the government in order to get this minimum price of $3.50 which is absolutely necessary for every dairy producer.
We heard the minister mention $3.50 per hundredweight. Later he mentioned a price of $3.30, $3.35 applicable to a certain quantity of pounds of milk. But as I just said, one must make all those calculations before knowing exactly what the dairy producers will derive from this new policy.
As the minister mentioned the possibility of establishing a Canadian dairy commission, I must add that we, on this side of the house, had already requested it and even started working on it in February 1963.
Furthermore, since then we have repeatedly requested the establishment of such a commission as soon as possible.
As a matter of fact, in July 1964, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton), official spokesman for the Conservative party in matters of agriculture, stated in the house:
Such an agency should be set up in Canada as soon as possible.
The hon. member for Qu'Appelle also stated in July 1964:
As 1 am aware of the cost price of milk, I would say, moreover, that any government that does not give milk producers across Canada a minimum price of $3.50 per hundredweight is unfair to that segment of the population.
That was the attitude of the Conservative party in July 1964, and we still consider this matter as most important.
Furthermore, in July 1964, we had requested a special grant of 35 cents per hundredweight of milk for last year's production, and up to 100,000 pounds. We were also requesting that this grant be paid to all milk producers in eastern Canada, for they certainly need federal assistance.
As the minister knows, 3 per cent of the total government budget will be going to agriculture. These expenditures could be increased, taking into account the importance of agriculture.
In fact, according to statistics published in the Toronto stock exchange bulletin of September 1963, agriculture accounts directly or indirectly for 40 per cent of our gross national product. Now, if, as the bulletin claims,
Dairy Policy
agriculture provides directly or indirectly work for 35 per cent of our labour force, I feel that the federal government should not hesitate to increase the appropriations of the Department of Agriculture.
Considering that the United States earmark 8.2 per cent of their budget for agriculture as compared with 3 per cent only in Canada, it is easy to understand why our budget is not as it should be.
The minister also mentioned exports. We do not know whether the government intends to restore the subsidy on cheese exports, especially to the United Kingdom, but we know that the subsidy which was 4 cents a pound at the beginning of 1963, was reduced to 3 cents a pound by the present Liberal government that same year, and then to 2 cents a pound last year.
We do not know if the government intends to restore the 4-cent subsidy. We ask the Minister of Agriculture to see to it that it is restored.
Last year we shipped 30 million pounds of cheese to the United Kingdom. We could export much more because if we consider that in the first decade of this century we were selling almost 100 million pounds of cheese, there is certainly a need to find foreign markets which are there, close at hand, in order to help agriculture throughout Canada as well as the economy of the country.
In closing may I say that we will study closely that new dairy policy and that if the minister or the government do not provide for the country's dairy farmers a minimum price of $3.50 per hundredweight, the Conservative party will not be satisfied, nor will the dairy farmer. I can assure the minister that if that minimum goal is not reached a congress of the dairy industry will be held here in Ottawa in April.

speechtext:
The
farmers have waited until quite late in the year for this announcement to be made. It should be borne in mind that the dairy policy is to change by May 1, and if this statement is correct I doubt whether the minister will have the regulations ready by that time.
I believe the farmers of this nation, particularly those engaged in the production of secondary milk, would take the view that when the Canadian Federation of Agriculture made its recent presentation asking for a base price for secondary milk of $3.50, it was not being unreasonable. But the minister has weaseled and finagled on that amount. I

Dairy Policy
understand that the highest amount to be paid will be $3.50, but I believe this will be paid only to the wealthier farmers. It seems that the Minister of Finance is not interested in the small farmer who, it may be, has an old age pension and a couple of cows to supplement his income. But, though the minister may not know it, it is the people with two, three or five cows who made the agricultural policy of eastern Canada. The minister may not know this, but it is a fact.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF NEW DAIRY POLICY
speechtext: Don't forget the two pigs.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF NEW DAIRY POLICY
speechtext:
It seems to me that another factor is involved. We have a committee on agriculture which has met to consider other subjects during the present session. I am sure the members who serve on that committee are in a position to be of some assistance to the minister in the development of this program. We talk about deficiency payments; we talk about trying to establish a parity price taking into consideration, as correctly pointed out by the minister, the fact that we are a high cost production nation and that we have a climate which makes it difficult to maintain production on a year round basis. But this is all the more reason why we should take a look at the fundamental principles upon which our agriculture policy is based and, in particular, do something to stabilize the dairy industry. It seems to me that the government shows an unhealthy disregard for the agriculture committee when they do not trust and respect the judgment of even their own members by not referring this matter to that committee.
The solutions the minister has mentioned really have accomplished very little. The base cheese price has been left the same; the butter price, at 64 cents, has been left the same. The minister did not go into the aspects of the butter support price that was transferred from a producer subsidy to a consumer subsidy, the role this has played and what change should be made in this field. He has said there will be a two price system for the dairy industry, which of course relates to the industry as it affects domestic consumption and that part of the industry that goes into exports. But he has not said how this is going to be done; he has not indicated whether there is going to be an export agency established for dairy products.
He has said there will be a Canadian dairy commission and that this will co-ordinate the federal and provincial marketing agencies. This is to be highly commended, because it is the fact that two or three of the agencies

have really shown some initiative. I speak of the Ontario cheese producers as an example. This government, as the previous speaker said, cut the subsidized price, the floor price of cheese by 2 cents. The Ontario cheese producers were still able to go to England and sell their unpasteurized Canadian Cheddar in the English specialized market, but at a disadvantage of about 4 cents compared with some of the other countries with which they are in competition.
We know there is friction developing between the provincial agencies that are in the marketing field. The minister has not really said that the Canadian dairy commission is going to act as an agent. I think what he has really said is that the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and the interprovincial farm union, when they both asked for a base price on secondary milk of $3.50, were stating a reasonable, fair and acceptable figure. But he is now saying that this government, in a niggardly way is going to renege on the request that was made after careful consideration, not by one agency but by all the agencies, in trying to establish equality in the dairy industry in Canada.
I think this statement will not be satisfactory, and I believe the Prime Minister should give some consideration to the problem that has developed; because it is a very serious problem and one that we have not been able to solve. The problem is twofold. First, the secondary industry is facing a terrific handicap in competition with the fluid milk industry. Incidentally, the fluid milk industry built up its own negotiations over a period of years and has been able to establish a fairly decent farm price for milk; and at the same time we are producing milk as a valuable commodity for the consumers at a high farm subsidized rate and selling it at a very low price because of the way it is bought.
It seems to me that the Prime Minister should give some consideration to this problem because it does involve the establishment of a national marketing agency. It is the fact now-and I think everyone will agree-that there are no surpluses. The minister seems to be interested in the top end of the field, helping those farmers who need it least; but there can be much more production in the agricultural field and it becomes a national responsibility of the government to sell that production.
I think the Prime Minister has a responsibility in this matter, because this is a major change. I suggest that the minister consider

referring this matter at the next session to the agricultural committee, where the whole question can be gone into and witnesses can be heard; because I have met many farmers in Ontario who are completely dissatisfied with the method we have been using for the past few years and the operations of the stabilization board itself. It seems to me that this matter has been referred again to the stabilization board for them to make the decision which in my opinion should be made by the members of this house and the committees which operate in the house. I think the minister is being unfair to the Canadian people, unfair to himself and unfair to the House of Commons in not referring this important matter to the committee for immediate study.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we in this party agree with the two objectives that were outlined by the Minister of Agriculture when he announced this new dairy policy; that is, that we need to have economic dairy units established in Canada, and having done that to then have a price structure that will give them an opportunity to operate these units profitably. Whether the regulations respecting deficiency payments will in fact achieve those two objectives is questionable, but I am prepared to wait until we see the details of the administration of this new policy before either commending or condemning the minister in this connection.
The time is long overdue when the domestic market for dairy products and all other agricultural products in Canada should be insulated from the surplus or dumping prices in the international markets. Almost all the other countries in the world have already done this and it has, in their opinion, been an advantage which has worked to the good of the whole nation. Therefore I am pleased to know that the minister is accepting this principle in setting up agricultural policies and federal government support for the price structure within Canada, particularly within the domestic market.
This new dairy commission that the Minister of Agriculture is suggesting is probably a good thing, but I would like to mention that it is going to be necessary for this commission to work very, very closely with the milk and dairy control boards in all the provinces, because under our constitution agriculture is one of the few areas where there is joint responsibility spelled out.
The dairy farmers of Canada and the Canadian Federation of Agriculture have asked for a support price at the level of $3.50 per hun-
Dairy Policy
dred for manufactured milk. It does not appear, from the few details we have received this afternoon, that this base or minimum price is going to be achieved. However, Mr. Speaker, I do realize that there are some problems involved here because of the matter of overproduction and the need to establish quotas. I think the minister's suggestion that they use the 1964-65 production as a basis for the quota, if you like, is a good one. Whether he is on firm ground when he suggests that it will not be paid to anyone producing less than 10,000 pounds of milk a year, I am not sure. I do not know whether that is a good feature of it, but perhaps there is some credence in his contention that if you do not produce that much you are really not in the dairy business anyway.
We will wait with interest to see what the details of the regulations will be, and we hope the objectives which the minister mentioned at the beginning of his speech will in fact be achieved by this new policy.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF NEW DAIRY POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I only wish to say a few words about the dairy policy announced by the government this morning under the form of a report that we from the province of Quebec, had been awaiting anxiously.
Actually, we were expecting more improvements in the dairy policy in general. Just the same, I am pleased that the minister announced the setting up of a dairy commission.
After hearing the members of other provinces, especially those of western Canada, express their complete satisfaction at the establishment of that commission, I must say that we from the eastern provinces, and especially from Quebec, will be satisfied as long as there will be a specific section for the province of Quebec within that commission to deal with a special policy for Quebec.
More and more, in fact, we realize that what is often good for the western provinces is generally not good for eastern producers.
The thing is that, in Quebec our production methods are quite different from those used in western Canada and our dairy policy is not the same. To give but one example, I would ask the minister if he has thought of dealing with a problem which promises to be crucial in our province. I refer to manufacturing milk subsidies. Over 50 per cent of our milk producers in Quebec will sell some milk to consumers and ship the rest to processing plants.

Dairy Policy
At the present time a Quebec farmer who sells part of his milk on the fluid milk market cannot get any subsidies for the milk he will be sending to processing plants, simply because he is selling part of his milk on the fluid milk market. I do want to call publicly the attention of the minister to that matter which I already pointed out to him.
Mr. Speaker, I think there is a glaring injustice for the Quebec farmer who has to operate both ways, which is probably not the case for the western producer who sends all his milk to the processing plants because there is a larger market for manufacturing milk in that region.
It is for that reason that the minister must absolutely do something in that regard. The farmers who send their milk surplus to processing plants should be allowed to get the same grants as farmers who send all their milk to processing plants. I think that the contrary would be an anomaly.
The minister said in his report that a farmer will get the subsidy if he sells a minimum of 10,000 pounds of milk. Now, most of those farmers sell much more than 10,000 pounds of milk to processing plants after supplying dairies catering to the fluid milk trade.
I urge the minister to take that matter under consideration and I am sure that with some good will he will be able to do justice to that group of milk producers. At last, this morning, an announcement was made which we had been looking forward to. But our expectations were not fulfilled. The support price which has been announced will deceive, I am sure, most Quebec farmers.
I just happened to travel with the president of the federation of the catholic farmers' union who felt sure that the Department of Agriculture would accept a support price of $3.50. That price was not the one suggested by that organization. The initial price it suggested was $4. I am convinced that in the province of Quebec a farmer cannot economically produce milk unless he receives a support price of $4. This figure of $3.50 was a middle-of-the-road price arrived at after discussions with the department. I realize, today, that the minister has not accepted this figure which he had led the organization to believe would be the case, because this morning he has been talking about a support level of $3.30.
I am sure, Mr. Speaker, the farmers will react violently, because I feel the minister could have made an effort to give them satisfaction since the catholic farmers' union had

done their share in reducing their demands to $3.50. He should have made an effort, at least, to grant a minimum support price of $3.50.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre asked a question wtih regard to members of the militia being called up under Canadian army order 94-2 and being subsequently released without pension or other benefits. I took the question as notice.
The answer is somewhat complicated, as there are different categories of call-outs. In the first place, a call-out from the Canadian army reserves having previously established entitlement to an annuity under the Canadian Forces Superannuation Act must have served a minimum of one year as a call-out before he can augment his annuity. During his first year of service sufficient funds are protected in his pay account to pay for his C.F.S.A. contributions in respect of that service in the event that his call-out service extends beyond a year.
In the case of a call-out from the Canadian army reserves having previously established an entitlement to a pension under the Defence Services Pension Continuation Act, he may elect at the commencement of his call-out to augment his pension in respect of the call-out service. The third case involves call-outs from the Canadian army reserves who have never established an entitlement to a pension or annuity. No contributions are deducted from the pay of such men during the time of callout, and no pension or annuity is payable in respect of this service.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: Order, please. I understand that the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) is first on the list of speakers on this bill.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to make a number of observations in connection with this legislation. Over the years I have spoken on the subject of old age security and

social welfare, and today I intend to review some of the things that have taken place over the years and then direct my attention specifically to the bill in question which is now before the house. My first words must be of commendation to the committee of both houses which over so long a period devoted itself to one of the most complicated and difficult pieces of legislation with which the present parliament has been asked to deal; indeed, it is one of the most complicated pieces of legislation to come before the house for a number of years. That committee met for a lengthy period of time. It met not only while the house was sitting but also during the period of adjournment, and to each and every member of that committee the house and country owes its gratitude and thanks. It is a committee that had a very difficult job to do.
I think at the same time I should mention its members. Instead of all the members I would mention those in Her Majesty's loyal opposition who sat on that committee and gave the benefit of their contributions to the examination of the bill. I mention particularly the former minister of national health and welfare, the hon. member for Perth (Mr. Monteith), whose devotion to the question of social security is not of recent birth; it represents a lifetime given to a consideration of the problems of those who are underprivileged, and particularly those Canadians who are casting a larger shadow toward the east. That hon. member had with him the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Chat-terton), who made a long and careful study of this matter in all its aspects. With those hon. members were the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken), the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Cantelon), the hon. member for Northwest Territories (Mr. Rheaume), the hon. member for Wellington-Huron (Mr. Howe), the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Gundlock) and the hon. member for Portage-Neepawa (Mr. Enns). Each in turn and in co-operation with members from other political parties endeavoured to bring about recommendations as to changes to be made in the bill accepted in principle by the house.
I have read the evidence and I have also carefully studied the various amendments suggested. I believe there were amendments suggested that deserved a better fate than was theirs in that committee-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
-for too often there was on the part of those members supporting the
Canada Pension Plan
government an unbending attitude against amendments however beneficial or necessary they may be. I am not one who is a great admirer of committees in so far as the work they are able to achieve is concerned. None the less, I do say that this committee in its lengthy and comprehensive examination of this great problem approached the task, carried on that task and completed it in a way that does indicate that committees can become effective. At the same time I am concerned, as I read the fate that was suffered by various amendments made, that too often those amendments were turned down on a party basis, which of course is a denial of the purposes for which a committee is set up.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: What about your members?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we have heard from Vancouver, and it just shows how even a voice from the far Pacific can be heard clearly on occasion. No federal legislation has been subjected to more far ranging criticism and condemnation than this plan has from across the country. Criticism has forced the government on several occasions to produce new and altered versions.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: That is not true.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
I am not going to review the kaleidoscopic changes which have taken place, except to say that when mark I was produced, the first of these bills, the relationship that it bore to mark III is restricted almost exclusively to the acceptance of the name. We in this party have throughout the years always advocated that there is a major national responsibility to ensure the social welfare of the Canadian people. I refer particularly to those who because of disability, illness, age and the like are unable to have for themselves a reasonable and a fair share of the good things of life.
As for myself, when the family allowance bill came up there were some in my party, and in others, who were not agreeable to its provisions. I knew what it would mean. I took a strong stand, which ultimately was accepted by the Conservative party as a whole, and we joined in that legislation, recognizing that there is no limitation on the desire of everyone, regardless of party, to assure that we should achieve for all Canadians freedom from being victimized, if I may use the term, by social and economic forces beyond the control of the individual.
In the field of a national system of contributory old age pensions, in 1962 we placed on the order naper an amendment to the

Canada Pension Plan
British North America Act so as to permit of a comprehensive national contributory pension plan. It was our information from the law officers of the crown that to bring this about required an amendment to the British North America Act. Reading from Votes and Proceedings for October 1, 1962, we introduced an address to amend the British North America Act and have a new section 94, declaring as follows:
-that the parliament of Canada may from time
10	time make laws in relation to
(a)	old age pensions, and
(b)	pensions and other benefits incidental to, or conducive to the better operation and administration of, a scheme of old age pensions, but no law made by the parliament of Canada under the authority of this section affects the operation of any law enacted by the legislature of a province in relation to any of the matters specified in paragraphs (a) and (b) of this section.
I personally introduced this address. Before it received the attention of the house, the government was defeated on a vote of nonconfidence.
Now, sir, having said that we favour the whole field of social security legislation receiving its proper and considered place, I might begin by setting out a short chronology of the progress of this Canada pension plan. It was introduced by resolution on June 21, 1963. On July 18, 1963 the house was in committee on the first version. On October 29,
1963	the minister explained the delay resulting from the announced intention of Quebec to have a provincial plan. On December 2, 1963 the Prime Minister announced the possibility of changes resulting from the considerations being given by federal-provincial conferences.
On January 10, 1964 what I might call mark
11	was produced, the watered down version, which was set out in a letter by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) to the premiers of the provinces. On March 18, 1964 the second version was unveiled in the Commons and the first white paper was attached thereto. On April 14, 1964 version No. 3 was announced resulting from alterations in version No. 2 to match the plan which was going to be brought into effect in the province of Quebec. On August 10, 1964 white paper No. 2 was produced; and on November 9 the fourth version of the plan was introduced in this house.
No one knows the reason for the metamorphosis of this plan. There have been all kinds of explanations as to how it came about. The Toronto Star for November 12,
1964	contended that the minister was, more

or less, no more than a nurse to the plan; that during the five days during which the Kent and Premier Lesage talks went on in Quebec and Ottawa, she was unaware of what was going on. Indeed, the record as set out in the article to which I refer would indicate that the plan was evolved as a result of the diplomatic capacity of Mr. Kent. However, others who were closer to the matter might be able to outline some additional information in that regard.
Anyway the plan is before us. I need not give evidence in support of the contention that I made a moment ago, that the Progressive Conservative party strongly favours social security; because during the period I had the honour to be prime minister, from 1957 to 1963, this country made the greatest advances in social justice ever seen in our country. During that period of time payments to Canadian citizens in the field of social justice increased by more than 53 per cent.
As far as old age security is concerned, the old age pensioners of Canada do not forget that when in 1956 the government of that day decided to increase the old age pension by $6-indeed, contended that any other increase would be unjustified-we took strong exception thereto; and when we came into office we increased the old age pension very materially from $46, finally to $65 per month. We made changes in the residence requirements so that pensioners were permitted to receive payments on a permanent basis abroad.
We increased old age assistance payments by 50 per cent. We raised the income ceiling by 3 per cent. We greatly increased blind and disability pensions. All these things were done during that period when we were in office. During that same period the national hospital plan was brought into being. The legislation was passed by the previous government, but the financing had to be undertaken by the Conservative government. Hospital construction grants were increased by 301 per cent, and national health grants were increased by 27 per cent. Indian and northern health services were greatly extended. I could go on reviewing what took place during that period of time when we were in office.
I mentioned a moment ago what happened in respect of old age pensions. When the present government came into power it received a great deal of support across the country by a promise of a $10 increase to old age pensions. However, it took a long while before we were able to get the government to take action. The answer given by the

government to our suggestion was that this field was not unequivocal. But when one reads the statement of policy which was issued then by the Liberal government he will find in the fine print that the $10 was only to be paid in the event a contributory pension plan was brought into being. We did everything we could to bring about the $10 increase, and finally on October 1, 1963,1 moved the following amendment during our consideration in committee of the whole of a resolution to amend the Old Age Security Act:
That said resolution be amended by striking out the words "effective October 1. 1963" in line three thereof, and substituting therefor "and this house asks that the government give consideration to making the payment of such additional pension to commence as of April 8, 1963".
That has reference to the increase of $10. The chairman ruled that amendment out of order and we appealed his ruling. The Liberal members as a whole voted to uphold the chairman's ruling, but finally as a result of continued pressure put on the government we were able to bring about the introduction of the $10 increase, which raised the old age pensions to $75 per month.
A minute ago I mentioned our general stand in connection with the contributory pension plan. We had legislation ready in this regard when we went out of office, but we desired to provide for survivor benefits, without which the contributory system would not be effective. I mention these things so that no one will be misled by the propaganda which is raised from time to time to the effect that we are in opposition to social security measures. No party has a monopoly in this regard. I believe every party is composed of men and women with common objectives in so far as social security is concerned, each following the course which in its opinion will achieve the greatest good for the greatest number.
Sir, I could deal further with this subject but I think I have generally pointed out what is the fact, that our attitude as a party toward this problem was conclusively and absolutely proven during the period we were in office. I am not going to rehash the arguments which have been raised from time to time, but it does seem clear that the first version of this pension plan and one or two of its successors were concocted hastily and on an insecure basis, designed to dazzle the electorate. These plans had to be amended; yet today we are told that this pension plan is the proven child, the peerless offspring, of planned political parenthood. However, it
Canada Pension Plan
has had its insecurities during its existence. Efforts have been made to make changes so as to remove those things that were bad and those provisions that were weak. All I can say in that connection is that we believe there should have been a number of other changes made to assure that this legislation would have been universally effective, fully portable and based on the assurance that Canadians as a whole would receive equal treatment.
The committee of the Senate and the house on old age security met and heard many arguments as to how it should be financed.
I	should like to read a few of the views expressed by some members who now sit in the treasury benches. These views were given a few years ago by two of those hon. members who now occupy positions in the cabinet. The question to be answered at that time was, how should the pension plan be financed, and whether it should be done by payroll deductions. The present Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) gave evidence before that committee in 1950, and is recorded at page 949 of the proceedings and evidence as having stated:
The fundamental characteristics of a pay as you go system is that those who are working pay the cost of providing pensions for those who have retired. The financing of a pay as you go system is a matter of distributing the current cost of pensions over the population in what is considered to be a proper way. In other words, it is essentially a revenue problem, even though the scheme may be contributory in the sense that it is paid for in whole or in part by a special levy or contribution.
Then Mr. Sharp, director of the economic policy division of the Department of Finance, as he was referred to at that time, said:
I think it is pretty clear that a tax on wages and salaries would have a very direct effect on cost of production. I would think if there were a payroll tax, paid by the employer, the tendency would be for it to be passed on in prices immediately. There would be certain deterring factors and this is one of the difficulties of payroll taxes; if they do not apply on imports, you put the local producer at some handicap compared with his competitors abroad.
That is interesting in connection with the
II	per cent sales tax, to which the hon. member for Wellington South referred today. Perhaps this quotation will give him an answer to his question.
Mr. Sharp then continued and said:
However, I would think in general a payroll tax would tend to be passed on to the consumer and in that way it would have a direct effect on prices. It would not, of course, apply to everything purchased, it would apply only to goods and services that were taxed. It would not apply

Canada Pension Plan
to rents except in so far as they reflect the higher cost of construction in houses____The tax on incomes cannot be passed along so readily.
Then, finally, he said this:
Since the payroll tax is placed on all exports, it enters into the cost of producing goods for export. The sales tax is rebated. Now, a sales tax may have some effect on increasing the cost of living internally, thus affecting the wage rate, but it does not have the same direct effect a payroll tax has.
Then, the chairman of that committee at that time was Hon. Jean Lesage, the present premier of Quebec. He asked this question:
Mr. Sharp, what would be the economic effect of putting the sales tax on building materials, for instance? I am taking it as an example there.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
The effect certainly would be to increase the cost of production.
The present Secretary of State (Mr. La-montagne) gave his views on financing and old age pensions and I quote from page 1035 of the committee report:
Obviously, the tax on payrolls will add up to a larger amount in those industries utilizing a large labour force in proportion to the machinery used. The possibilities of proflt in these industries will be reduced unless some way is found to avoid the tax.. .Capital may even leave the country, seeking profits in those parts of the world where the living standards of the workers are lower and where no such taxes on payrolls present restrictions to profits...
The immediate result of the tax will therefore be a fall in industrial production, especially in those industries which employ a large proportion of labour.
I have left out portions in between, but hon. members can read them.
The conclusion seems inescapable. The tax on payrolls will fall back on the workers in the form of unemployment or a reduction in wages.
Now, those were the views of the present Secretary of State in 1950. In addition, he said:
We therefore conclude that the workers will bear nearly the whole cost of social security.
Then, the present Secretary of State gave a considered observation when he said:
-I do not believe in the balanced budget, and I think we will experience deficits in the near future.
Well, all of this is tremendously interesting and indicates the change in attitude of ministers today as compared with the views they held when they were economic advisers. It is well to give consideration to these matters because that committee was set up to endeavour, through discussion, to bring about the very best legislation possible. I could deal with the evidence given by Mr. Kent and others. I have it here, but I do not want to

take up too much time of the house. I did want the house to have the benefit of the economic views those gentlemen expressed in 1950 relating to the effect of a payroll tax.
Now, sir, this tax begins at 3.6 per cent on payrolls. Will it bring about the results that were pictured by Mr. Lamontagne, as he then was, and by Mr. Sharp, as he then was? Naturally, those are questions we ask, and I am sure the government, having given the fullest consideration to this matter with its economic advisers, will be able to provide the assurance that the black results to the economy expressed in 1950 will have been dissipated in the light of passing years. We in this party have placed our views clearly and definitely before the committee. We believe in a comprehensive contributory plan. We believe that no plan brought into effect should have in it inherent dangers that have not been fully viewed from every economic angle and the assurance that no ill results will follow.
On the basis of our belief in such a plan, we have given our full and complete support to the objective of a portable, contributory retirement plan for all Canadians. I say to you, sir, that one million Canadians, approximately, at present in receipt of old age pension are excluded from the plan. This plan, therefore, falls short of the objective I have mentioned. Persons in the greatest need, such as those already retired and those with small incomes or casual employment, will never benefit. After all the plan that is evolved should certainly assure that those in the greatest need will not be forgotten. Furthermore, it is proposed that those who will qualify will yet receive completely inadequate benefits, and our committee members advocated various changes.
They advocated that all persons over 70 receiving old age security benefit should receive an additional $25 per month being paid from the Canada pension plan fund when the first benefit payments are made from that fund. Today the old age pension is $75 per month, but the cost of living is rising very rapidly. The Liberal party promised that they would bring in a cost of living proposal so that, from time to time, the pension would be equated to the rise in the cost of living. This will not be the case until 1968. This gives no hope to those who today are struggling in the face of the rising cost of living to make both ends meet.
Furthermore, we recommended that all persons between 65 and 70 who meet the requirement test and who elect to draw the actuari-

ally reduced old age security payment should receive a minimum benefit of $25 a month to be paid from the plan. I mentioned a moment ago that there are thousands and thousands of Canadians who will reap no benefit. We believe that all persons qualified for any benefit under the Canada pension plan should receive, where a single person, a minimum pension of $25 per month. We contend that no one, regardless of the smallness of his income, should be placed in the position of a pariah. In other words, they should not be excluded from having pension rights.
We advocated, too, other necessary changes that we believed should be made, and these other suggestions will be brought to the attention of the house during the course of the discussion. What I am simply doing is outlining our views in regard to this problem.
There is no question but that today the old age pensioner is in great difficulty. Rents are up, prices are up, and there is grave need among tens of thousands, if not hundreds of thousands of old age pensioners who find themselves in a position bordering on penury. Yet there is no hope for them in this plan. They are just going to stumble along to the end of the road on the basis of a totally inadequate payment today.
I am not one of those who do not realize that costs must be considered, but this plan over a period of years will build up a terrific fund, and there is no reason why those who most need an increase over the present rate of $75 should be placed in the position of being denied any consideration for such an increase.
We also know that members of the committee advocated that to accommodate persons such as students, who may enter the labour force after 18, and people such as teachers and firemen who retire early, and people who suffer illness and unemployment, the number of zero years of earnings be increased by 25 per cent. All these things are designed to make the plan effectively workable.
We want a plan that is not an illusory one, that brings to those who do not examine it the visual effects of a mirage. Many Canadians who have not received a full explanation of the plan think the day of utopia is here; but the day of reckoning will come when the scheme goes into effect and those who need it most find themselves unqualified to secure their need.
As I have said, my purpose is simply to outline some of these things so that there will be a basis for the arguments that will be
Canada Pension Plan
advanced by others in this party, others with a fuller knowledge of the subject, others who have given it a more intensive study than I have been able to give it, others who belonged to the committee, and others outside the committee who gave this matter the fullest and most complete consideration. Therefore, while in every way desiring and being most anxious to assure that the legislation shall go through, we still hope that the hearts of those opposite can be softened to the extent that they will be prepared to allow this bill to go back to the committee for further consideration in another form.
Anybody who would disagree with that must recall that when plan No. 1 was produced we were told that it was the greatest thing that the mind of man, or even woman, had evolved. It was the summum bonum of all the perfections, but it died a natural death on examination. Along came the second edition and it went the way of all flesh. Then No. 3 came along and it represented the repairs that were made in drydock. They were not sufficient and the present plan, beneficial as it is in many areas, still deserves to receive further consideration.
It is not a matter of a long delay. This legislation will not come into effect until the beginning of next year. Another two weeks of consideration, with the members of the committee freed from any parental control or direction, or the suggestion of it, would be able to bring about changes that would remove any suggestion that any of the matters to which I have referred are final and absolute.
Somebody might say, "If you move an amendment you are going to kill the legislation." Nothing of the kind, Mr. Speaker. I say immediately that in the amendment I am about to move I make very clear this fact, that in no way is it to be considered as a vote of non-confidence or a vote disapproving of this legislation.
We are trying to assure that mark IV will be improved. Members of the committee tried without success. Always when they introduced amendments somebody seemed to be looking over their shoulders saying, "No, no don't take that." I do not say it happened because I am sure the committee members were free and untrammelled, and not subject to psychological influence, but the fact remains that for some reason the Liberal members opposed every change that was asked for by opposition members, and I think I can say that without exception.

Canada Pension Plan
I make it clear immediately that in no way is this amendment-and it is the only way 1 can bring it before the house-to be considered as killing the legislation. As I said a moment ago, in no way or by any interpretation is it to constitute a vote of nonconfidence. The purpose is to see whether parliament, whether this house can bring about what the members of the committee were unable to bring about; in other words, so that the House of Commons will speak on this and so members will have an opportunity to stand up and be counted.
I am sure that if the Prime Minister would only announce a free vote, and there is no reason why he should not, it would not take very long before the suggestion I shall offer in the amendment would receive support. I have talked to members in that informality that has always existed among members of the house, and I know there are members in all parts of the chamber who would like to see changes made. In order to give that opportunity, and so that there will be no mistake as to the consensus in parliament, and so that members may have the opportunity of voting without in any way being considered as against the government or for the government, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Perth (Mr. Monteith):
That all the words after "that" be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
That Bill No. C-136 be not now read a third time but that it be referred back to the committee of the whole so that the government may give consideration to and introduce amendments to the said bill to provide for a minimum payment of $25 per month out of the Canada pension plan account to all persons between the ages of 65 and 69 years who are retired from regular employment, and also to provide an increase from $75 per month to $100 per month for all those now 70 years of age or over.
I submit this in both official languages of the house, and before it is read, Mr. Speaker, might I make this observation, that it will be seen that in no way are we directing the government what it should do. In no way are we determining this question.
We are suggesting that the government might give consideration to this and introduce amendments to provide those things which are generally being asked for today across this country, and reasonably so. As far as further argument in connection with this matter is concerned, my colleagues to whom I have made reference, as well as others, will I am sure place before the house their views on this subject because there is no question before the Canadian people today which is more representative of the
[Mr. Diefenbaker.)
general views of Canadians as a whole than that which is embodied in the amendment which I have the honour to move.

I am wondering

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
I would suggest that the amendment is in order. It suggests that the bill should be recommitted to the committee of the whole, and such motions are standard practice on third reading. It asks that the government should take a certain matter under consideration and that the government should introduce certain amendments.
I would refer to the ruling of the Chair the other day that this was a money bill. With the greatest deference I have made

some remarks since then to indicate my feeling that this bill does not affect ways and means in any way and is therefore not in the category of money bills. This measure sets up a Canada pension plan account from contributions. Citation 415 or citation 423 of Beauchesne covers the situation. I would suggest to Your Honour that the question of whether this is a money bill is extremely pertinent. I put it to Your Honour that there is nothing in this bill, that is, in parts I, II and III, which in any way affects ways and means. I think the Chair should take this into consideration.
In any event, I think we can go back to a large number of precedents over the years and find that this is the standard form. I am sure Your Honour will be faced with similar types of amendments from other quarters of the house for consideration on third reading and I put it to you that the amendment is in order.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
I can understand the difficulty you may be faced with, Mr. Speaker, in deciding whether or not the amendment is in order. As usual, in order to make this kind of idea known, the amendment is very cleverly worded. There is no doubt in my mind that this is a money bill. A money bill is clearly defined on page 204 of Beauchesne's fourth edition in the last paragraph of citation 243.
A money bill was defined as follows in the Parliament Act, passed in the British house in 1911:
"A money bill means a public bill which contains provisions dealing with.. .money provided by parliament, or the variation or repeal of any such charges; supply; the appropriation, receipt,-
And these are the important words-
-custody, issue or audit of accounts of public money."
Even though the charge which would be made on the Canada pension plan as a result of the acceptance of this amendment might not come directly out of consolidated revenue, it would certainly come out of a fund of which the government has custody. Citation 243 clearly defines a money bill as including any fund which is within the custody of the government.
The second problem is presented by the words "that the government may give consideration to". This is, perhaps, the standard practice, because the amendment moved by the Leader of the Opposition is in fact in keeping with what is described in citation 415 where it says;
When a bill comes up for third reading a member may move that it be not now read a third
Canada Pension Plan
time but that it be referred back to the committee of the whole for the purpose of amending it in any particular.
The problem is that this amendment goes further than referring the question back to the committee of the whole. It sets out the kind of amendments which should be made to the bill when it does get back into committee. These words "the government may give consideration" are there in the amendment to gloss over or cover up the fact that only a minister of the crown may move an amendment which involves the expenditure of money, and the money involved in this case is money of which the government has custody, in accordance with the citation I read from Beauchesne.
I am not completely convinced that this amendment is out of order. It represents one of the things we have had to put up with over the years, with its clever wording. But it is known perfectly well that private members cannot move, for example, that an increase of $25 be granted, though they may insert these words requesting the government to give consideration to such a step.
If this amendment becomes an order of the house, I respectfully suggest that the balance of the amendment, spelling out in detail the nature of the amendments asked for, then imposes almost an obligation on the government to move this kind of amendment. Putting that alongside the well established practice that no member other than a minister of the crown can move this type of amendment, it is a kind of left handed way of putting an obligation on a minister of the crown to move it.
While I know we have been through this before and perhaps we could even find precedent that the wording of this type of amendment has been accepted before, I think it is really out of order because it is trying to do, in an indirect way, what members of the house other than ministers of the crown cannot do directly.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
