Mr. Speaker, with regard to the contention of the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Olson) I would respectfully suggest that if Your Honour declares this amendment in order and if the house approves it, there is no order from the house to change the balance of ways and means; the order of the house would merely be that the committee of the whole give further consideration to this matter. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, the committee of the whole would have to give consideration to it, by order of

Canada Pension Plan
the house, but it need not adopt the recommendations contained in the amendment. The house in committee could, after consideration, reject the proposals contained in our amendment. So I suggest that even if this is considered to be a money bill, the adoption of our amendment would not in any way affect the balance of ways and means.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would point out to the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Chatterton) that a member of this house other than a member on the treasury benches has no right to move an amendment respecting a money bill, even for the consideration of the house.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would bring to your attention, along the lines of the argument of the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Olson), that this amendment does in fact go considerably further than just the suggestion of the element of consideration. It states that "the government may give consideration to and introduce amendments to the said bill", and I would think that this quite definitely casts an obligation upon the government to introduce amendments to the bill. The amendment stipulates that consideration be given to introducing amendments to provide for a minimum payment of $25 a month out of the Canada pension plan account to all persons between the ages of 65 and 69 years who are retired from regular employment, and also to provide an increase from $75 a month to $100 a month for all those now 70 years of age and over.
I think both those latter elements under the heading of introducing amendments do bring into focus the particular restriction in the rules that such amendments which impose upon the government obligations to increase expenditures, which expenditures will be derived from general revenue, are out of order. This is quite clearly the case here and is a matter that has already been ruled on, namely that increased charges on the Canada pension plan account are in effect charges on general revenue. This is all set out and has been argued before this house in connection with the financial provisions of clause 110 of the bill. Subclause (4) of clause 110 states:
No payment shall be made out of the consolidated revenue fund under this section-
And so on. All through these financial provisions there is reference to the consolidated revenue fund. It is quite clear from the financial provisions of clause 110 that any charges on the Canada pension plan account
fMr. Chatterton.]
are in fact charges on the consolidated revenue fund and that the Canada pension plan account is a bookkeeping entry in the consolidated revenue fund. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I do not think there is any doubt at all that any amendment that is advanced which does require, or cast an obligation upon, the government to accept amendments which have the effect of creating additional charges on the Canada pension plan account cannot be considered anything but contrary to the rules.
I would also point out that when we talk about advancing an amendment such as this, namely that we refer this matter back to committee with definite instructions to create a charge on the Canada pension plan account, it is contrary to the resolution brought in by the government in introducing this particular bill; because it is quite clear from reading the resolution introducing Bill No. C-136 that all these moneys that go into the Canada pension plan account are moneys derived from contributors, from wage earners, and it is to those people that all benefits are to be payable. This amendment, of course, if accepted would cast an onus upon the government to use these funds, that are quite clearly stated to be for the benefit of wage earners and contributors, for the purpose of making payments to those who never would be covered under the Canada pension plan and who would never contribute to the Canada pension plan. That is precisely what this amendment would do in providing flat rate benefits payable out of this account in respect of moneys that come from contributors and for which benefits are to go to those contributors. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, this amendment runs contrary to the resolution introducing this particular bill.
The hon. member for Medicine Hat quoted many citations to Your Honour with respect to this question. I would refer the house to citation 249 of Beauchesne's fourth edition, which says:
"No cases can be found of any private member in the Canadian Commons receiving the authority of the crown, through a minister, to propose a motion involving the expenditure of public money."
Again I would argue, Mr. Speaker-and I believe it has been accepted already in a previous ruling on this bill-that there is no question that this amendment involves public money. This citation continues:
"No principle is better understood than the constitutional obligation that rests upon the executive government, of alone initiating measures imposing charges upon the public exchequer".

I would now refer to citation 250, part (2) thereof, at the bottom of page 215 in the same edition of Beauchesne:
An abstract resolution does not-
I would argue, Mr. Speaker, that this amendment is analogous to that:
-finally bind the house to make the grant, and it imposes upon the government the responsibility of either accepting or rejecting the recommendation.
Then the citation goes on:
Addresses to the crown requesting an issue of public money must originate in a committee of the whole house.
I say that this is precisely what this particular amendment does; it is an address to the crown requesting an issue of public money and as such, in accordance with that citation, it should originate in a committee of the whole house. I would now refer to page 216, citation 250 (3), which says:
No amendment affecting the purposes for which the grant is recommended by the crown can be allowed.
This is what this particular amendment does; it alters the purposes of this particular bill and is contrary to the resolution introducing the bill because it would, in effect, create charges on the Canada pension plan account for the benefit of other than contributors. This is against the whole theme of the bill. It is certainly against the first three parts of the bill, and it is against the resolution which introduced the Canada pension plan bill. Again, Mr. Speaker, I would refer to Beauchesne, citation 250 (4), which says:
The fundamental terms of a money resolution submitted to the house with the Governor General's recommendation upon which a committee of the whole is set up cannot be amended. Amendments will only be in order if they fall within the terms of the resolution.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, that would apply here. Again for the reasons I have already stated. For those reasons I would argue that this amendment is completely out of order and should be rejected.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just a few words on the same point of order, approaching the principle enunciated by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) from a different point of view. I agree with the submission he has introduced to you, supported by the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Olson), that this amendment affects the balance of ways and means in an indirect way instead of directly, which is prohibited. I refer to 20220-8134
Canada Pension Plan
citation 406 of Beauchesne's fourth edition, which says:
Amendments are out of order if they are-
(b)	inconsistent with or contradictory to the bill as agreed to by the committee;
(c)	inconsistent with a decision which the committee has given upon a former amendment;-
I suggest to Your Honour that since the principle of the bill involves a universal portable contributory plan, any amendment which would have the effect of adding noncontributors to that plan offends against the principle of the bill as accepted by this house both on second reading and throughout the committee stage of the bill. The two citations to which I have referred go to that point.
Also, Mr. Speaker, I would invite your review of the proceedings during the committee of the whole and ask Your Honour to inquire whether or not an attempt to add non-contributors to the bill has not already been made in committee of the whole and the amendment defeated by this committee. If that is so, this amendment attempts to achieve the purpose of an amendment which was rejected by the committee and therefore is inconsistent with a previous decision of the committee.
If Your Honour would be good enough once again to turn to citation 415 of Beauchesne's fourth edition, as found on page 287, paragraph 4 reads:
On the third reading of a bill, an amendment to refer back to the committee of the whole must not tend to change the principle approval on the second reading.
My submission to Your Honour is that the principle approved on second reading was a principle of a contributory pension plan, and I submit that this amendment moved by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) would offend against the principle of the bill by adding non-contributors to the bill. According to the citation it would go beyond the principle of the bill already approved by the house both on second reading and in committee of the whole.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the arguments adduced by the three members who have preceded me would be very weighty if they were related to the subject matter of the amendment, but I think they have gone very far afield. I suggest to Your Honour that this amendment is in accordance with amendments on third reading which have been considered valid by the Chair for many years. It is part of the custom and tradition of the house to move amendments in this form.

Canada Pension Plan
I suggest there is no direct order being given by the house to the government as mentioned in citation 249 (3). That we cannot do, and we are not giving a direct order. There is no suggestion in this amendment of a money resolution, which can be brought forward only from the treasury benches.
This amendment is contrived to determine what is the will of the House of Commons, and to bring to a vote the issue that is before us, so that there may be a distinct understanding as to what the house as a whole desires to do with the bill. I do not see that that is in any way altering the principle determined on second reading.
There are two matters in the amendment which have been repeated on many occasions in amendments on third reading. The amendment says "so that the government may give consideration to" and so on. That is not a direct order other than asking the government to have another look at the bill; that in view of the house there may be some changes which the government might take into account, having considered the debate which has progressed this far. So the request is simply that the government "may give consideration to". Then it goes on to say "and introduce amendments to the said bill". I emphasize the word "may". In other words, the house is simply saying that if the government will give further consideration to this bill and it finds on that further consideration that amendments are necessary to alter the financial matters in the bill, then the government itself is asked to introduce amendments. So that this amendment is drawn up with the fact in mind that no direct order is being given to the government, no change in the principle of the bill is being suggested, and no attempt is being made to interfere with the proper rights of the government in money matters.
All we are asking here is that the government reconsider the bill. If on reconsideration it finds that the suggestions made by the members of the House of Commons are reasonable, then the government itself, we suggest, may introduce certain amendments in accordance with the figures we have set out in the amendment.
I conclude, sir, by suggesting to you that this amendment is in order and that it follows a well recognized practice in this house.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I confess that I would rather be speaking to the merits or otherwise of the amendment than to its propriety in terms of procedure. Of course if

the amendment is allowed I will have an opportunity to do so, and to express our views as to what this kind of amendment would do to the Canada pension plan. However, at this point the question before us is one of procedure.
I have before me something that other hon. members, except my own colleagues, do not have, namely the draft of an amendment that we ourselves propose to move, if the opportunity arises, on third reading. It is precisely because we have taken particular care to make sure that our proposed amendment will be in order that I see faults in the one proposed by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker). I thought I should get that on the record so that hon. members will not say later that that is the reason for the stand that I now wish to take.
It makes you a rather prejudiced witness.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: In the amendment which we will propose, if we get the chance to do so later, we ask that the bill be referred back to the committee of the whole house so that that committee may reconsider it.
That is what we say.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Someone says from behind the curtain "That is what we say". The official opposition would refer the bill back to the committee so that the government may do something. This house has no authority to instruct the government what to do. But this house does have authority to ask its own members in committee of the whole to reconsider the matter.
I think that that is the first fault in the amendment moved by the Leader of the Opposition. He would refer the bill back to the committee of the whole so that the government may do something. It is the government to which the instructions are given-"that the government may give consideration", "that the government may introduce". In my submission, Mr. Speaker, if this amendment were to be carried, despite all the niceties of its language, it would in effect be an instruction by this house to the government to take a certain course of action in the committee of the whole.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Certainly.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Would the hon. member then suggest that the word "government" be

deleted and the words "committee of the whole" be substituted therefor?
How can a committee spend money?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
I certainly think it would be better if that were done, but we have an even better amendment which we will move when it is our turn. I think the amendment would be better if the word "government" was not included, and it referred the bill back to the committee of the whole to do things that a committee of the whole can do. What are the things that the committee of the whole can do? It can do those things that a committee made up of ordinary members can do, but all of the restrictions that we have been confronted with before are still in existence.
I shall not re-read the citations that have been read, but I should like to draw attention to one or two that have not been mentioned. Citation 246, paragraph (3), in Beauchesne's fourth edition reads:
The guiding principle in determining the effect of an amendment upon the financial initiative of the crown is that the communication, to which the royal demand of recommendation is attached, must be treated as laying down once for all (unless withdrawn and replaced) not only the amount of a charge, but also its objects, purposes, conditions and qualifications.
The proposal included in this amendment is that the house should consider altering the objects, purposes, conditions and qualifications of the Canada pension plan account. What has been laid down in the original resolution was on the financial initiative of the crown, and it is my submission that the house does not have the authority to change that unless there is another message from His Excellency the Governor General. I would point out that there is merit to citation 415, paragraph (4) read by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Turner), which deals with third reading and states:
On the third reading of a bill, an amendment to refer back to the committee of the whole must not tend to change the principle approved on second reading.
However, I disagree with the suggestion of the hon. member that citation 406 applies, because that citation is in the context of what happens in the committee of the whole. I see the hon. member nodding his head in agreement. Apparently he got ahead of himself.
Citation 415, paragraph (4), deals with the situation on third reading. Perhaps I should also read a portion of citation 418, which is as follows:
Canada Pension Plan
All amendments which may be moved on a second reading of a bill may be moved on the third reading with restriction that they cannot deal with any matter which is not contained in the bill.
The amendment proposed by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) asks the government to consider putting something into the bill which has not been there at all, namely the paying out of moneys from the Canada pension plan fund to persons who have not contributed to it. I am now getting very close to the substance that I should like to argue, that I think this amendment is one that is unfair in its purposes because it takes money out of the Canada pension plan fund to be used for something else. I do not think that is the way to solve our problems but perhaps I should not get into that discussion.
Mr. Speaker, we must stay with what has been the practice on third reading. When the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) spoke he said something I shall probably parallel. Neither of us expected this argument, so we have not got our precedents here. The hon. member said that the amendment is in line with traditional forms that have been used on third reading, but he did not produce any examples. I will follow suit and say that the amendment is in line with amendments of the kind that have been ruled out of order, but I do not have my precedents with me. The fact is, however, that any attempts on third reading to move a bill back into committee with instruction to introduce the expenditure of money have been ruled out of order.
Hon. members may be wondering how we are going to move an amendment. I say that our amendment is simply going to ask that the bill be referred back to the committee of the whole house for the purpose of reconsidering the basic amount of the old age security pension set out in a certain clause. We want to refer it back to the committee, but we are giving no instruction. We are setting no amount or dollar figure. We are simply asking that committee to consider something in a particular clause.
I mention that fact, not in an attempt to announce in advance what we intend to move but to indicate the kind of thing that can be done on third reading. On third reading one can move the reference back of a bill for consideration without going into detail, but one cannot move a reference back, supposedly for reconsideration of a clause but actually giving instruction or asking for an expenditure of money in a way in which a

Canada Pension Plan
private member is not permitted. There is no use trying to fool ourselves about this. An amendment or a proposal which would mean taking money out of the Canada pension plan fund to be paid to non-contributors is foreign to the provisions of the bill in the first place. On the other hand, what we will propose is entirely within the ambit of part IV.
Mr. Speaker, I suggest that you will have to look very closely at the terms of this amendment because it does seem to go beyond the kind of amendments that have been allowed on third reading.

Mr. Speaker, it is perhaps presumptuous of a new member in this house to follow an act such as we have just witnessed, and I use the word act advisedly. During the short time I have been a member of this house I have never before heard a member argue against an amendment by announcing a different amendment which he himself proposes to move at a later stage. However, I am sure you have been assisted by that hon. member's contribution, Mr. Speaker.
I should like to comment briefly on the statements made by government spokesmen to the effect that this amendment is out of order in that it somehow or other sins against the principles of the resolution and that, indeed, it is foreign to the very spirit of social security of this kind. I believe that when reviewing this amendment one has to take into consideration the statements made in the white paper which give some guidance-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. I am wondering now whether the hon. member is discussing the principle of the whole resolution rather than the point of order which has been raised. The spirit of this legislation, as set out by the minister herself when she introduced this resolution to the house, was stated to be that all Canadians would, by the provisions of this plan, be enabled to retire in security with dignity. All the proposed amendment would

do is refer the bill back to the special committee for reconsideration in an attempt to design the resolution in such a way as to carry out the government's intention. Mr. Speaker, that is my contribution to this debate.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
I shall be very brief, Mr. Speaker, but I am prompted to speak by the words of the hon. member for St. Law-rence-St. George (Mr. Turner). I should like to review what he said when he referred to the fact that we have a reason for presenting such an amendment. I should like to outline the reason the amendment should be allowed. First of all, the key word in the amendment is "consideration". I believe the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George indicated we were suggesting a change in the principle of this legislation. I say to you that is very unfair of him because, as was stated by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), we are in agreement with the principle. It is not the principle, therefore, that we are amending. We are amending a specific part of that legislation. Canada Pension Plan
again, these are instructions to a committee, not instructions to the government. It seems to me that on this ground this proposed amendment is faulty.
If the amendment is adopted, I am sure hon. members will recognize that it would really be inescapable for the government to introduce financial proposals. If the amendment means anything, then it instructs the government to introduce a financial proposal. This seems to be contrary to a number of citations. Citation 249 of Beauchesne's fourth edition, paragraphs (2) and (3), read as follows:
A motion requesting the government to introduce immediately legislation granting retirement allowances to all citizens over 60 years of age is out of order because it involves an expenditure of money.
An amendment declaring that government action in any matter should be taken forthwith and giving a direct order which, if approved by the house, would compel the government to adopt measures involving an expenditure of public money, could not be moved by a private member.
In spite of the argument to the contrary put forward by the hon. member for Grey-Bruce, I am impressed by the submissions made by the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Turner) when he referred to citation 406(b). Citation 415, paragraph (4), was referred to also by a number of hon. members. It is to the effect that the principle approved on second reading should not be contradicted by an amendment. Here again, it seems to me that this proposition is contradicting the principle as approved on second reading. I do feel that this amendment cannot be accepted by the Chair. I have looked at it as objectively as I could and for the reasons I have just expressed, in view of the arguments advanced by a number of hon. members which impressed me and which I adopt and make my own. I must say that the amendment proposed by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition is out of order.

AMENDMENT RESPECTING APPEAL IN HABEAS CORPUS PROCEEDINGS
speechtext: the second reading of and concurrence in an amendment made by the Senate to Bill No. C-35, to amend the Criminal Code (habeas corpus).

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING APPEAL IN HABEAS CORPUS PROCEEDINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wonder
whether the originator of this motion would like to speak to the amendment that has been made by the Senate. It is a substantial amendment and I should like to give the hon. member the opportunity to explain, if he so desires.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING APPEAL IN HABEAS CORPUS PROCEEDINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre. Following careful consideration, Bill No. C-35 was given third reading in the house on May 22, 1964. The bill then received most careful consideration in the other place for a period of ten months where several scholarly speeches were made by skilled and experienced lawyers who are members of that place. The bill has been considered carefully in committee with the assistance of certain experts and departmental personnel, and I am satisfied that the amendment is procedural in character and does not in any way alter the purport of the bill.
Bill No. C-35, as produced to this House of Commons in the form it was originally, simply provided an appeal on habeas corpus.

Criminal Code
Now, the amendments that have come back from the other place after this thoughtful scrutiny do precisely this: They define habeas corpus in a definitive way as being habeas corpus ad subjiciendum, thereby distinguishing this remedy from the ancient rights that are available under the writ of habeas corpus ad justijicandum which required the person to whom the writ was directed to be present and give evidence before the court of issue, and habeas corpus ad respondendum, which required the production of the named prisoner lawfully detained in order that he might answer further charges to be laid against him.
This, of course, is not what I, as the mover of Bill No. C-35 had in mind; it was simply to provide an appeal in the case of habeas corpus ad subjiciendum. Otherwise, what is provided in the amendments is simply to spell out succinctly the procedure that I was satisfied, in the former bill, would be determined by the courts as the cases were heard. I am quite satisfied with the amendments that have been made and would respectfully ask the concurrence of hon. members in approving same.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING APPEAL IN HABEAS CORPUS PROCEEDINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in studying this amendment it appears to me that we have been given what is, in effect, an entirely new bill. Ten months ago the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson) introduced Bill No. C-35 to this house and suggested in that bill an amendment to section 691 of the Criminal Code, subsection (1). This was the addition of three words. Incidentally, it is beyond my understanding why a bill which passed this house on May 22, 1964 and was referred to the Senate should return to this house on March 24, 1965. I was not aware that the other place was so heavily involved in business that it could not give attention to this particular matter without the lapse of such a lengthy period of time.
In examining the amendment submitted by the other place, I find that they are not amending section 691, subsection (1) of the Criminal Code but are amending subsection (2). It appears to me that the whole substance of the bill introduced by the hon. member for Leeds has been changed beyond recognition. The amendment of three words has become, in the hands of the Senate, an amendment of six paragraphs. I would have thought, in the circumstances, the hon. member for Leeds would ask to withdraw his bill and reintroduce it at the next session which
I understand is not going to be delayed too long.
There are quite a number of private bills that have been introduced in this session suggesting amendments to the Criminal Code. I wonder why the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) has not undertaken to deal with some of these. I wonder why he did not deal with this particular amendment, to which he gave his approval last May. In fact, he stated that he would have liked to introduce it himself. I do not know why he did not. It is the responsibility of the Minister of Justice to make improvements, if required, in the Criminal Code. He might want to have another look at it now. I notice that last May he said that the only means of getting directly out of prison is by using the procedure of habeas corpus. We have had a somewhat different example given us recently of how you get directly out of jail by a person with whom the Minister of Justice was concerned.
I question the procedure, sir, of a bill going from this house to the other place, ostensibly amending a certain section of the Criminal Code, and coming back to us with an entirely different amendment to a different section. Under the circumstances, I wonder if it is right for us to consider this as actually an amendment to Bill No. C-35. Had the other place modified the wording of the amendment put forward by the hon. member for Leeds directly applicable to section 691, subsection (1), then it would be understandable. However, when they have modified subsection (2) of section 691, and when they could have gone on to other subsections if there are other subsections there-I have not got the Criminal Code in front of me-then, we have a different bill. I think, under the circumstances, that this should stand for serious consideration by the Minister of Justice. In fact, he is not here to comment on the bill as he did on the original bill in May of last year. I should like to know from the Department of Justice and from the minister if the proposed amendment from the other place meets with the approval of the Department of Justice. Have the legal advisers in that department considered this and made any comment to the Minister of Justice or is this just being moved through the House of Commons without full consideration?
Let us just look at what is facing us, Mr. Speaker. The original bill said that subsection (1) of section 691 of the Criminal Code should be repealed and the following substituted therefor:

An appeal lies to the court of appeal from a decision granting or refusing the relief sought in proceedings by way of mandamus, certiorari, prohibition or habeas corpus.
Those last words, "habeas corpus" are the addition suggested by the sponsor of the bill. Now, what has come back from the Senate? This is what has come back from the Senate, and it is shown on page 1161 of Votes and Proceedings for March 24. I quote:
Strike out clause 1 and substitute therefor the following:
1. Subsection (2) of section 691 of the Criminal Code is repealed and the following subsections substituted therefor:
And right there we have a different bill. Then we have five more paragraphs dealing with important matters in connection with habeas corpus, which I do not deny at all, but I do not see where the relationship is between the amendment proposed by the Senate and Bill No. C-35 which went forward from this house. Under the circumstances, what are we to do?
In May 1964 we had the benefit of the advice of several members who spoke on the bill, and we had a summing up by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau). Is the minister prepared to give us a summing up with regard to this? If he considers that the change proposed by the Senate is more acceptable than the one of which he approved in May 1964, what are the reasons?
There appear to be substantial changes in the amendent sent to us from the other place. Under the circumstances should not the Minister of Justice have suggested to the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson) that he withdraw his bill, and give him a promise that in the next session, which is not far removed, the minister himself would introduce a suitable amendment to section 691 of the Criminal Code.
What we have in front of us is a very substantial rewording which should be subjected to scrutiny by the law officers of the crown and the Minister of Justice. It would be quite wrong for us on a Friday afternoon to rush through a bill of this nature, which may have more far reaching effects than we appreciate.
I listened to the arguments that were presented in May 1964. I fully appreciate the fact that some change with regard to habeas corpus is desirable and has been advocated by a number of very distinguished people, but is the change now in front of us the one that was in the minds of those people who debated the issue in May 1964? At least three 20220-814i
Criminal Code
of the hon. gentlemen who spoke on that occasion are missing from the chamber this afternoon. I would suggest to the hon. member for Leeds that he should allow this to stand for the time being, and I believe the debate might suitably be adjourned by someone, so that we could consider the matter at a later period, with the Minister of Justice present to give us his advice.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. S. Macdonald (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING APPEAL IN HABEAS CORPUS PROCEEDINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the chief point in the argument made by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) seems to be his concern that the house is being asked to approve an amendment which had not been considered by the law officers of the crown and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau). Perhaps I can allay that concern by saying that the rewording submitted and approved in the other place was given very extensive consideration by the law officers of the crown, to which the Minister of Justice himself was privy. I therefore give the assurance that the rewording has been subject to scrutiny by the Department of Justice.
The amendments put in here are essentially procedural in character, providing more elaborate methods of procedure to the basic substance that existed previously. In fact these amendments meet with the approval of the law officers. Substantially they allow for appeal in cases of habeas corpus. I would draw the attention of hon. members to the very protracted discussion which took place in the other place, and I assure hon. members that this does have the support of the Department of Justice, the approval of the law officers, and I therefore ask them to support passage of this worth-while legislation this afternoon.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING APPEAL IN HABEAS CORPUS PROCEEDINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the discussion that took place in this house on the previous occasion a great deal of credit was given to the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson) for the simplicity of language he had used in the bill. If that hon. member now tells me that nothing has been added and nothing taken away, then it seems one of our former attorneys general in the province of Ontario is very wordy. There is a lot of redundancy in this type of amendment and I think the parliamentary secretary on that score should be in favour of rejecting it.
If nothing has been added, and if it has not clarified anything, why should we clutter up the Criminal Code with a lot of verbiage?

Criminal Code
Again we see lawyers playing with words and dressing up something that could quite easily be handled without the extra verbiage that has been added in the other place.
I have an interest in this because I have noticed the same hon. gentleman who moved this amendment in the other place do the same type of thing on a number of occasions over a period of three or four years, not to help anybody or clarify anything, but to confuse the matter. I do not believe age gives anyone the right to have his opinion accepted in its most flamboyant and extensive wordage when something simpler will do.
The hon. member for Leeds was congratulated by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) for having said exactly what he wanted to say, without complicating it with a lot of words. A lawyer would have a lot more fun with these extra six paragraphs than with the three words originally proposed by the hon. member for Leeds. They were in Latin and I am not precisely sure what they meant, but I believe they were precise in their meaning. These six paragraphs have confused me and I am informed that the third one does not mean what it says.
This section of the Criminal Code is not as unknown as people might imagine. This is the section used by many persons detained in prisons in order to obtain a change of address for themselves for the purpose of defending themselves somewhere else. It is a method used to have the body produced in a particular court, and it is an important part of our system of justice.
The parliamentary secretary is being foolish when he says he is quite willing to accept all this verbiage because it accomplishes nothing that was not originally accomplished in three words. I know the hon. member for Leeds says this amended bill accomplishes exactly the same thing, but it is the result of the wrong functioning of the other place. This is not a sober second look at legislation; it is just confusion running rampant. The bill has been extended out of all proportion and I would hope the Department of Justice feels the same as I do about it.
Rather than adopt this phraseology we should revert to the original wording, which seemed to me and to most members of this house on a previous occasion to meet the need. While I am opposed to the amendment, I think it does some credit to the hon. member for Leeds that he has been able to arrive at a formula which says exactly the same thing

only in a long and protracted way. Nevertheless I hope the representatives of the Department of Justice will not hasten to accept this amendment and endorse it as being more acceptable than the original form. It is my view that the Criminal Code should be kept as precise and simple as possible because it is something which affects the rights and liberties of all our citizens.

The words we have been given here are not at all clear. I studied Latin for two or three years but I still do not know what these words mean. I know what habeas corpus means but I do not know what the other two phrases mean. We are supposed to write our laws so that any man, not necessarily a lawyer, can understand what is written in the Criminal Code. But I am certain that if you take a census you will find that 99 out of 100 people in Canada do not know what "mandamus" or "certiorari" mean. If one does not know the exact meaning of a thing he cannot talk intelligently about it. I have in mind now what the man in the street will think. open and was doubtful in the wording of the amendment which first came before this house.

Mr. Speaker, is it not true, then, that these amendments are not just expanding on the question but are introducing new subjects? I think these are major amendments and are not just explanations. There are three new ideas here, according to the parliamentary secretary. I do not want to misinterpret him, but is it not true, as the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson) said, that in the original bill that was introduced, containing the right to appeal, this question

was dealt with simply; but what is being done here is giving direction to the courts. This is the type of information that the courts would have available from other bills in other areas. It is the fact, is it not, that British justice says that justice delayed is justice denied, which is actually what the former attorney general wrote in section 6. This is redundant. The simple wording of the hon. member for Leeds in the bill conveyed all these things, or else I misunderstood either the hon. member for Leeds or the parliamentary secretary. What the parliamentary secretary is doing is giving an interpretation to this that is not really implied. This should be an explanation, and only an explanation, of the original wording.
If it is, I might be willing to accept it. If it is not, and if what he said in his explanation is that these things have been added -which perhaps I misinterpreted-that will provide other safeguards, limitations or extensions of what was originally in the bill, in my opinion it is new. You cannot have it both ways. I think the two explanations are very different and do not mean the same thing. If the first explanation is correct, then I am of the opinion, as a layman, that the simpler we keep it, the better it is; and that the precedent laid down by British justice which I just quoted, namely that justice delayed is justice denied, should be followed.
This is true in regard to every section of the Criminal Code and any civil case, and it does not have to be written into the act. In fact, we do not write it into the act, any more than in union contracts we write in that it is an act of God and therefore does not apply to anybody. These things do not have to be written in, because they are part of our law. I think we are now thoroughly confused because of this explanation as to what was originally intended, or at least I am confused as to what was intended.

However, out of an abundance of caution, and on purely technical grounds, seeking to provide the intention of the hon. member in his bill, it was decided that the original wording should be changed. This was done on a purely technical basis.
Criminal Code
As the hon. member mentioned, in the mind of the former attorney general there were areas of doubt that the courts might arrive at a decision which was not in accordance with the purpose of the bill.
The addition, therefore, was to make more clear the circumstances under which the original broad purpose would be carried out. It is to make quite clear what I think many people would, from an assumption of the purposes, conclude anyway; for example, under paragraph 6, that the justice was to be expeditious, and that a case was to be tried at the earliest possible date.
